candidates.title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
candidates.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

candidates.title: MoE--LoRA Methods for Multilingual Adaptation: A Systematic Empirical Study
candidates.abstract: Routed low-rank adapters offer a parameter-efficient means to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) across tasks. Hence, it is assumed that they can also be used to improve the support of low-resource languages in LLMs, which currently serve English far better than the thousands of other languages spoken worldwide. However, this assumption has never been verified empirically under a shared multilingual evaluation protocol. We address exactly this gap by comparing eight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) methods on a frozen base model, using 146 training runs across 200 unique languages and more than 10,000 evaluations. Our results suggest that a reduced-scale search can identify viable configurations of LoRA methods but does not reliably predict their relative performance, as the top-ranking configuration is never best at scale. LoRA reliably improves language-model fit on translation data, consistently degrades reading comprehension, and benefits low-resource languages most. These findings suggest that LoRA methods should be regarded as targeted tools rather than general-purpose means for improving the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

candidates.title: Mixed-Precision Quantization for Language Models: Techniques and Prospects
candidates.abstract: The rapid scaling of Language Models (LMs) has resulted in unprecedented computational, memory, and energy requirements, making their training and deployment increasingly unsustainable. Quantization has emerged as a crucial compression technique for reducing model size, alleviating memory bottlenecks, and accelerating inference. However, while uniform low-bit quantization (e.g., INT8, INT4) provides significant efficiency gains, it can degrade accuracy in sensitive components of transformer-based LMs. Mixed-precision quantization offers a promising alternative by selectively allocating precision across layers or within tensors to strike a balance between efficiency and accuracy. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of Mixed-Precision quantization frameworks for LMs (MXPLMs). We first review quantization fundamentals, including uniform and non-uniform quantizers, quantization granularity, and methods widely used in post-training quantization. We then categorize and compare recent MXPLM frameworks according to their bit allocation strategies and precision configurations across weights, activations, and key-value caches. A comparative analysis highlights differences in perplexity, zero-shot task performance, and deployment trade-offs. Furthermore, we contrast MXPLMs with earlier mixed-precision quantization methods for deep neural networks, identifying strategies that transfer and those that face challenges in the LM setting. Then, we discuss quantization-compatible hardware, KV cache and mixture-of-experts quantization, and summarize open issues and future directions, including hardware-aware design, activation quantization, and scalable optimization methods for billion-parameter models.

candidates.title: Learning Stratified Policies for Inference-Time Objectives
candidates.abstract: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.

candidates.title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
candidates.abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.

candidates.title: HADVQ: Hessian Aware Directional Vector Quantization
candidates.abstract: Ultra-low-bit quantization of large language models is a challenging task because aggressive compression severely distorts model parameters and disproportionately harms a small number of highly sensitive channels. We present a vector quantization method tailored for this regime. Our approach begins with random preconditioning, which regularizes the weight space and makes it more amenable to quantization. We then represent weights in polar coordinates and decouple the quantization of directions and magnitudes. To quantize directions, we leverage the structure induced by random preconditioning and design a structured codebook based on the $E_8$ lattice, yielding a compact yet expressive representation. To further reduce degradation, we detect extremely important channels using a proxy Hessian and preserve them with an additional cost of only 0.16 bits. Together, these components provide an effective quantization pipeline for LLMs in the extremely low-bit regime. Empirical results demonstrate improved accuracy, highlighting the benefit of combining geometric structure, lattice-based codebooks, and selective channel preservation.

candidates.title: Formal Adequacy Index (based on Polish-language material)
candidates.abstract: Linguistic formality is one of the dimensions of stylistic variation in speech; however, simply measuring its level does not allow us to determine whether the chosen mode of communication is appropriate in a given situation. The aim of this article is to present the concept of a formal adequacy index (based on Polish-language material), which enables a quantitative assessment of how well the formality of a text matches the expectations arising from the communicative context. The proposed approach is based on the separate modelling of observed formality, determined on the basis of the linguistic features of the text, and expected formality, determined on the basis of the characteristics of the communicative situation. Adequacy is assessed by comparing these two measures, taking into account contextual tolerance thresholds, which may differ for a lack of formality and an excess of formality. The potential applications of the index are illustrated by an analysis of Polish-language emails containing apologies for being late, written by human language users or generated by a large language model. The implementation presented here is preliminary in nature and requires further calibration and empirical validation. The main contribution of this article is the proposal of a general methodological framework for the quantitative study of formal adequacy in various communicative contexts.

candidates.title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
candidates.abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

candidates.title: Dynamic Task Allocation with Dialogue
candidates.abstract: Effective multi-agent collaboration requires agents to adapt task allocation as goals and responsibilities evolve. Prior task-allocation frameworks often assume static goals, full observability, or rely on large language models (LLMs) without explicit, verifiable beliefs about task allocation or intent. These assumptions limit their applicability to real-world collaboration, where agents often lack full information about each other's actions, progress, or local environment. To support dynamic task allocation under partial observability, we introduce a communication-augmented Bayesian task-allocation framework. Our agent uses dialogue to reduce uncertainty about the environment and collaborators, while keeping decisions grounded in explicit probabilistic beliefs. We evaluate our framework in an Overcooked domain extended with dynamically arriving tasks under both full and partial object-space observability. Our communication agent consistently outperforms a vanilla LLM agent in both settings. Additionally, our framework performs comparably to a non-communicating task-allocation baseline under full observability, but substantially outperforms it under partial observability as task complexity increases by an average speed up of 0.585 and completes on average 18 timesteps faster. These results indicate that our agent is more efficient in dynamic task allocation than baselines in partially observable environments, and that communication is important as available information decreases.

candidates.title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship. The code and data are available at https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors.

candidates.title: Can LLMs Understand What They Predict? Evaluating Latent Causal Structure Inference in Financial Markets
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated through their ability to predict future outcomes, implicitly assuming that predictive success reflects an understanding of the underlying system. However, accurate predictions can often be achieved without recovering the latent mechanisms that generate observable outcomes. To examine this assumption, we introduce LUCID, a benchmark that evaluates whether models can infer latent market structures from event descriptions and historical financial observations. Models generate event-induced causal graphs representing inferred market structure and are evaluated through a reconstruction-based framework. Our evaluation of 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs shows that adding their generated graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone, although a few metrics improve. These findings suggest that inferring informative, event-specific market structures from observable evidence remains challenging for the evaluated LLMs.

candidates.title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
candidates.abstract: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.

candidates.title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
candidates.abstract: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.

candidates.title: Precision vs. Pragmatics: Benchmarking Post-Training Quantization Trade-offs in Sovereign Korean Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: The rapid deployment of Sovereign Large Language Models (LLMs) in South Korea requires balancing high computational efficiency with strict preservation of linguistic pragmatics, particularly hierarchical honorifics (Jondaetmal) and cultural context. While 4-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) significantly reduces memory footprints for edge deployment on Neural Processing Units (NPUs), its impact on culturally sensitive Korean generation remains underexplored. In this study, we empirically benchmark the memory efficiency and pragmatic fidelity of 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization applied to a 2.8-billion-parameter Korean sovereign LLM (EEVE-Korean-Instruct-2.8B-v1.0) on an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Our results demonstrate that NF4 quantization reduces model memory footprint by 67.2% (from 5.64 GB in FP16 to 1.85 GB in INT4) while preserving grammatical honorific structure in formal workplace communication.

candidates.title: Cognitive Offloading with Large Language Model Agents in Cybersecurity Education: Perceived Burden and Engagement in a Single-Cohort Study with Ten-Year Institutional Context
candidates.abstract: Practice-oriented cybersecurity education often requires novice learners to build target web systems by hand before security analysis begins, imposing extraneous cognitive load. An earlier study introduced a Red/Blue teaming model in which a large language model (LLM) agent builds the target systems (vibe coding) under Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) control, so that learners audit, attack, and defend. This single-cohort study examines learner-level evidence from the 2026 cohort (n = 34) of a university web-security course, set against institutional Course-Quality-Improvement (CQI) satisfaction records for nine of the ten academic years 2017–2026. Evidence comprised self-reported coding-effort logs (n = 25), single-item final-course survey measures (n = 27), and peer cross-evaluation scores (71 ratings). Logged total coding effort had a median of 3.8 h. In the final-course survey, 96% agreed implementation burden had decreased and 93% that deeper engagement in vulnerability analysis and defense design was possible (raw means 4.67 and 4.44 of 5; Wilcoxon p < 0.001). The 2026 CQI score (91.55) ranked second among the nine records (descriptive). In this single-institution context, delegating system construction to an LLM agent was associated with lower perceived implementation burden, greater reported security-analysis engagement, and high satisfaction; multi-site replication is required.

candidates.title: Proposed new words and collective identity in human and language model agent groups
candidates.abstract: Groups develop distinctive words even when ordinary expressions are sufficient. Such words can symbolize collective identity, and observational studies link language use to community attachment. We examined identity change in temporary groups of one human and four disclosed large language model (LLM) agents, comparing discussions with and without a neologism proposal across recruitment waves. We recruited 100 Japanese participants in two sequential waves; an agent proposed a new word only in the first wave. Mean collective identity change did not differ significantly between waves. Within the proposal wave, favorable ratings of the proposed word were associated with change in identity, but this association did not survive correction for multiple testing (adjusted $$p=0.229$$ ). The three-way interaction among recruitment wave, message count, and team impression had a nominal $$p=0.027$$ but did not survive correction (adjusted $$p=0.082$$ ). In a sensitivity analysis, the interaction was not significant after adjustment for midpoint identity (nominal $$p=0.078$$ ; adjusted $$p=0.624$$ ). The nonsignificant between-wave comparison and exploratory associations that did not survive correction, together with wave confounding and post-discussion evaluations, limit causal inference and motivate randomized studies with repeated measures to test whether proposed group language affects identification.

candidates.title: Kompass: An Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Personalized German University Admissions

candidates.title: Theory of mind inspired mental state reasoning with large language models for empathetic response generation
candidates.abstract: As conversational AI expands into emotionally sensitive domains such as mental health support and counseling, empathetic response generation has become a key research challenge. Existing empathetic dialogue systems either reflect the user’s surface level emotions or, when relying on external commonsense knowledge bases, capture only generic patterns. We propose a Theory of Mind inspired framework in which a large language model first infers the speaker’s five mental states of Belief, Desire, Emotion, Intent, and Knowledge from the multi turn dialogue history and then uses them as conditioning signals for empathetic response generation. A preliminary study on a theory of mind benchmark indicates that the LLMs employed perform reasonably on mental state inference in both multiple choice and free form settings. On an empathetic dialogue dataset, injecting the self generated inferences improved response quality under both automatic metrics and LLM as judge evaluation. In the LoRA fine-tuned setting, the ToM condition performed comparably to COMET, an external commonsense knowledge baseline, with higher ROUGE-L point estimates for all four backbones and a significant advantage for one. Shuffled and corrupted descriptions consistently degraded response quality, whereas the ToM condition and a context-grounded factual-summary control performed similarly, indicating that contextual grounding is the primary source of the benefit. These findings suggest that speaker grounded mental state reasoning can be an effective strategy for empathetic dialogue systems.

candidates.title: Sniffing Large Language Models Over the Air
candidates.abstract: 1. Introduction TokenSniffer is an offline research pipeline for analyzing encrypted network traffic associated with large language model (LLM) interactions. It uses observable frame metadata to address three tasks, from detecting LLM usage to identifying the model deployment and recognizing the type of task being performed. LLM Usage Detection uses a LightGBM classifier to distinguish LLM traffic from ordinary application traffic. The training and evaluation scripts support fixed data splits and report test accuracy and macro-F1. Deployment Classifieridentifies the provider–model deployment associated with an LLM interaction. It uses a multiscale gated temporal convolutional network with masked attention pooling to classify sequences based on patterns across frames. Deployment-Specific Task Recognition trains a separate classifier for each model deployment. Each classifier predicts one of eight task categories, including writing, reasoning, mathematics, and coding. The training objective combines cross-entropy with weighted supervised contrastive learning to account for the relationship between augmented views of the same capture and examples from different captures. 2. Key Features Consistent traffic representation. All three stages use prepared sequences with 1,024 frame positions. Frame direction, normalized absolute frame length, and standardized log inter-frame arrival time are represented as separate input channels. Longer sequences are truncated and shorter sequences are padded with zeros. Normalization statistics are estimated from the training split and reused for validation and testing. Traffic sequence augmentation. The task recognition component supports timing jitter, frame dropout, and subsequence sliding. Training uses the original sample and its augmented views. The contrastive objective assigns each positive example from the same capture four times the weight of a positive example from a different capture before normalization. Training and evaluation with fixed splits. The included configurations and README commands support training with seeds 42–46. The neural classifiers select checkpoints using validation macro-F1 and evaluate those checkpoints on the held-out test split. Separate run directories make it possible to retain the outputs for each seed. 3. Package Contents TokenSniffer_source.zip contains the following files and directories under code/. llm_detection/ contains the LightGBM detector, frame preprocessing, data splitting, training, evaluation, and repeated-run scripts. deployment_classifier/ contains the deployment classifier, its training configuration, and entry points for preparing data, training, and prediction. task_recognition/ contains the task recognizer, augmentation methods, weighted contrastive loss, and training configurations for nine deployments. requirements.txt in each component lists the Python dependencies for that component. README.md documents the input format, task labels, expected directory structure, and commands for training and evaluation. 4. Basic Usage Extract the archive and create a Python 3.10 or later environment. Install the dependencies for the component you plan to run using its requirements.txt. Prepare the labeled JSONL records as described in the README. Each record contains aligned arrays for signed frame lengths and inter-frame arrival times. Use a fixed split manifest for LLM usage detection and separate training, validation, and test files for the neural classifiers. Run the training command for the selected component. For deployment classification and task recognition, set PYTHONPATH to that component’s src/ directory before running its training or prediction entry point.

candidates.title: Semantic-aware multimodal evidence integration with a lightweight large language model for rolling bearing fault diagnosis
candidates.abstract: Rolling bearings are critical components in industrial rotating machinery, and their failures may cause unexpected downtime, economic loss, and safety risks. Although deep learning and multimodal fusion have improved vibration-based fault diagnosis, two issues remain insufficiently addressed: magnitude-dominated time-frequency representations may discard phase-related impulse timing information, and heterogeneous diagnostic cues are often fused without explicit alignment in a semantically consistent representation space. This paper proposes M2-LLM-FD, a lightweight large language model-assisted framework for semantic-aware multimodal evidence integration in rolling bearing fault diagnosis. The framework converts each vibration segment into three complementary forms: time-domain patch tokens, phase-aware time-frequency tokens, and structured statistical prompts. A phase-preserving complex convolutional dimensionality reduction network is designed to process the real and imaginary components of the time-frequency representations, thereby retaining phase-sensitive information associated with fault-induced impulsive events. A structured multimodal alignment and fusion module then harmonizes temporal granularity and projects the aligned evidence into the pretrained language-model embedding space through semantic-anchor cross-modal attention. Furthermore, domain-specific prior knowledge is injected via structured statistical prompts, and the model is efficiently fine-tuned using Low-Rank Adaptation. \textcolor{red}{Extensive experiments on the CWRU, PU, and HUST datasets show that the proposed framework achieves consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, robustness, and cross-dataset generalization. Ablation and controlled analyses further validate the contributions of phase-aware time-frequency modeling, structured statistical prompts, and semantic-aware multimodal alignment to the overall diagnostic performance. The results indicate that combining phase-aware signal representation with large language model-compatible contextual evidence integration can effectively improve the robustness and generalization capability of intelligent bearing fault diagnosis.

candidates.title: On the Use of Large Language Models for Inter-Model Consistency Specification
candidates.abstract: Cyber-physical systems are developed using heterogeneous modeling frameworks that address different engineering concerns and abstraction levels. In practice, models from mechanical, electrical, and software engineering coexist across development phases, creating the need to specify inter-model consistency despite differences in terminology, structure, and execution semantics. A first step of such a specification is to identify which modeling constructs of two frameworks correspond, that is, whose instances have to be kept consistent, and along which dimensions. In this paper, we investigate how well Large Language Models (LLMs) perform this correspondence identification for pairs of modeling constructs, compared with expert references. We use two gold-standard datasets: 90 automotive construct pairs across AUTOSAR, ROS 2, CAD, Simulink, and a brake specification metamodel, annotated by three experts, and 32 smart-grid construct pairs across three IEC metamodels, whose reference labels are derived from a published rule-based integration. Each pair is labeled on an ordinal scale along three dimensions: syntactic, semantic, and behavioral. Six large language models from OpenAI and Google are evaluated under zero-shot, one-shot, and few-shot prompting, together with two agentic systems, OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code, run with web access allowed or disabled. We report Quadratic Weighted Kappa, Mean Absolute Error, accuracy, and macro-F1 with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired tests. On average, the LLMs agree with the references beyond chance and beyond string- and embedding-based baselines, but ordinal agreement remains weak to moderate. On the automotive pairs with traceable independent annotations, the agreement of the best configurations with individual experts does not differ significantly from the agreement among the experts, whereas most configurations agree less in the semantic dimension and, on the AUTOSAR–ROS 2 pairs, also in the syntactic dimension. Over both datasets, semantic correspondence is judged more reliably than syntactic correspondence. Vendor differences are small and dimension-specific, and in-context examples improve agreement only in selected dimensions. On the automotive pairs, the ordinal agreement of the agentic systems does not exceed that of the best direct configurations. On the smart-grid pairs, for which their prompts, unlike the direct prompts, define the dimensions in the terms used to derive the reference labels, they reach higher syntactic agreement. Web access does not improve their agreement consistently. Overall, LLMs can support experts in identifying correspondences, but they do not replace expert judgment.

candidates.title: Large Language Model Classification Validation Matching Task

Because classifications by an LLM are not fully reproducible, as repeated runs can assign a statement to different categories, we test whether human raters arrive at the same classification. To validate the LLM classification, we test whether human raters assign statements on 1) drivers of psychosocial risks, 2) solution ideas, and 3) derived interventions to the same categories as the LLM.

candidates.title: Instrumenting Failure: Scoring Language Model Agents at Every Decision Node in Imperfect-Information Games
candidates.abstract: Agent evaluations report task success and rarely say what an agent did at each decision. We score every decision node of three 12B to 14B instruct-tuned language models (LMs) playing five zero-sum imperfect-information games against four opponents on eight properties from decision and game theory, five of them against a CFR+ equilibrium reference. At each node, the LM also states a belief about the opponent's hidden state in a separate call. Without memory and at temperature 0, stated beliefs sit 0.250 to 0.288 in total variation distance from the equilibrium posterior, and where the action responds to the state its agreement with that belief exceeds chance by -0.04 to 0.19. The two calls frame the opponent differently, so the result is a behavioural inconsistency and makes no claim about internal beliefs. Under one prompt and greedy decoding, the LM's action never varies with the state in 10 of the 38 cells where the reference varies its own. Memory lowers the constant-action share in 9 of 13 testable ladders at temperature 0; at temperature 0.2 the cells at 1 fall from 16 to 5 of the 46 informative cells, while the belief results hold. A gate withholds, with a stated reason, any belief score the run cannot support, and seven of the eight non-zero defect rates are attributable to the instrument, a representation, or the LMs.

candidates.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Linguistic Annotation
candidates.abstract: Assessing large language models for linguistic annotation requires task-specific evaluation under documented conditions. We present dhAIBench, a Python benchmarking and annotation tool with a web interface for exploring and sharing results. It records prompts, configurations and predictions, enabling comparisons of annotation quality, confidence calibration, repeatability and estimated cost. We demonstrate the framework and the associated methodology through 293 runs of 48 models on nine linguistic annotation tasks spanning morphology, syntax, semantics, discourse-pragmatics, spelling normalization and learner-language correction. Models achieve high agreement with reference annotations on several tasks, including those on non-standardized, historical varieties as well as requiring contextual interpretation. The results support evaluating models against specific linguistic tasks, rather than relying on general rankings. To this end, we make the current and future benchmarks publicly available at dhaibench.silent3.ff.cuni.cz.

candidates.title: A Context-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Personalized Learning and Automated Course Development
candidates.abstract: The rapid growth of digital learning resources has created both opportunity and overload for learners navigating online education. This paper presents EDURAG, an AI-powered personalized learning and course generation platform that combines generative artificial intelligence with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to deliver adaptive, context-aware educational experiences. EDURAG integrates secure user authentication, a personalized analytics dashboard, automated course generation, structured lesson management, progress tracking, and a conversational AI teacher grounded in a curated knowledge base. The platform is built on a modern full-stack architecture using Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS on the client and application layer, with Prisma ORM and SQLite for structured data persistence, and JWT/Jose-based authentication secured by bcrypt password hashing. This paper describes the motivation, system architecture, implementation, and functional modules of EDURAG, and situates the platform within the broader literature on intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning, and retrieval-augmented generation. We discuss how the fusion of generative and retrieval-based methods mitigates hallucination and improves factual grounding in AI tutoring responses, while also examining limitations such as data quality dependency, domain coverage, and the ethical considerations inherent in AI-mediated education. The paper concludes that EDURAG demonstrates a practical, extensible architecture for trustworthy, personalized AI-driven learning and outlines directions for future research and development.

candidates.title: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated via truthful evidence in open channel
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents' beliefs can be manipulated through open channels such as social media, even when the information they receive is truthful. When agents fill gaps between fragments with self-induced relationships, they may accept those relationships as established facts and pass the resulting rumours to others. Drawing on cognitive theory of narrative understanding and film theory of montage, we introduce Generative Montage to operationalize this failure, termed narrative overfitting, by coordinating agents to arrange truthful fragments into misleading narratives. Across 1,090 rumour targets from six Twitter events, agents often accepted rumours overconfidently, with overall acceptance exceeding 65 percent in twelve of fourteen models. Acceptance remained above 50 percent after majority voting or review of the same evidence, showing how errors can reach downstream decisions. To explain this susceptibility, fragment interventions identify posts that influence belief within complete narratives. Synthetic controls then show that similar response patterns arise from valid evidence, separating belief influence from evidential support. This distinction motivates Grounded Monitor, a proof-of-concept neuro-symbolic runtime monitor that checks direct evidential support to guide agents' judgements, improving decision accuracy by 5.6 to 29.0 percentage points across original and anonymized settings. These findings expose a cognitive route to rumour amplification and support monitoring inferred relationships before agent-generated conclusions guide public decisions.

candidates.title: Idempotency Is Not Recovery: A Fault-Injection Study of Language-Model Agent Tool Actions
candidates.abstract: This is an earlier single-author preprint. A later revision with additional authors has been submitted to IEEE Transactions on Reliability for consideration. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Supplementary aggregate results are available separately at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24369921. When a language-model agent's tool call is interrupted, the action may already have changed an external system without confirmation. Retrying risks duplication; assuming success may conceal an action that never occurred. We study these failure modes in a controlled agent runtime combining authorization, an action ledger, target-side idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence sealing. We inject ten single-host fault classes and compare four configurations and three ablations using a target-side oracle separate from the runtime ledger. On each of Windows and Linux, 7,513 trials used 96 captured model responses from 24 constructed cases. In 200 known original crash and replay pairs, the full configuration recorded 0/200 repeated effects versus 117/200 for each simpler baseline. A ledger-related ablation had 170/170 orphaned effects versus 0/170 and 200/300 recovery successes versus 300/300 for the full configuration. Disabling reconciliation left 100/100 known post-effect crash outcomes ambiguous despite no observed duplicates. A separate supplement designed after the initial results and reusing the same inputs found a similar pattern under response loss or delay. The full runtime had about one-seventh of fail-open throughput, while injected evidence-write faults left 75/100 trials per platform unresolved. These findings distinguish duplicate suppression from recovery and identify their measured reliability and performance tradeoffs within the tested benchmark.

candidates.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
candidates.abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

candidates.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
candidates.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.

candidates.title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

candidates.title: Future Trends in AI and LLM Technology
candidates.abstract: With the increase in size, functionality, and complexity of artificial intelligence (AI) systems, future trends are expected to change to more human-like cognition, multimodal processes (combining text, images, audio, and video), and real-time thinking. The joint implementation of large language models (LLMs) and edge computing, cloud infrastructure, and dedicated hardware (such as AI accelerators) will augment deployment efficiency and decrease latency. Moreover, responsible AI practices that include transparency, fairness, preserving privacy, and energy-efficient architectures become more significant. Federated learning, smaller dataset fine-tuning, and domain customization are deemed to bring more acceptable and usable LLMs to industry. With the blurring of the lines between symbolic reasoning and neural networks, we expect to enter the domain of hybrid models that will be able to learn statistically, as well as make logical inferences. The trends will characterize the generation of intelligent systems in the future, as they will allow more flexible, environmentally knowledgeable, and ethically based applications in healthcare, education, government, and other fields.

candidates.title: Disaggregated LLM Inference in Space: A Communication Feasibility Study
candidates.abstract: Orbital data centers could enable large-scale AI inference, but efficiently serving a frontier language model to many users may require several compute satellites to cooperate over optical links. While disaggregated inference, which splits large language model (LLM) serving across machines, is well established in terrestrial data centers, its viability under the unique constraints of orbital deployments remains an open question. This article investigates how link capacity and satellite separation affect two types of disaggregated LLM serving, in both compact satellite formations and distributed constellations. Prefill-decode disaggregation (PDD) migrates a large KV cache once per request, while attention-FFN disaggregation (AFD) exchanges small activations at every mixture-of-experts layer for every generated token. The two respond to distance in different ways. PDD is limited mainly by link capacity and, with fast enough links, tolerates separations of up to a thousand kilometers. AFD is limited mainly by propagation delay, which accumulates layer by layer and forces attention and expert instances within about a kilometer of each other. Based on these results, we propose a hierarchical orbital inference architecture and provide network design guidelines for future orbital data centers, including the role of ground access latency.

candidates.title: Conclusion and Roadmap for AI and LLM
candidates.abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and large language models (LLMs) in the healthcare sector, educational infrastructure, legal analytics, and the academic publishing field has reshaped these sectors. Utilizing such architecture with transformers, LLMs show extraordinary performance due to their natural language comprehension and their ability to reason within context and generate textual material. There are, however, frequent problems in the deployment, such as mitigation of bias, interpretability, computational efficiency, and ethical governance. In the chapter, the results of studies in peer-reviewed journals are generalized; theories and practical limitations are critically appraised; and the specific application of the domain in such fields as cardiology, ophthalmology, education, and legal technology is discussed. It also discusses novel hybrid systems based on combining LLMs with knowledge graphs (KGs) as a solution to more factually grounded and less hallucinatory systems. The suggested framework combines modular design, a well-organized workflow pipeline, and human feedback cycles to be more flexible and reliable. The comparisons of performance in various areas demonstrate that LLMs with KG hybrids are particularly more accurate when comparing facts than the standard LLMs, but with a slight disadvantage in inference time software. The chapter culminates with a multi-stage plan of the future work, providing short-, mid-, and long-term plans with regard to domain adaptation, ethical AI models, and energy-efficient model design.

candidates.title: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.

candidates.abstract: This package accompanies the article "Large language model agents as operators of an exothermic chemical reactor" by T. Sainio, N. Groll, and G. Sin. It contains the machine-readable records of all 1224 reactor-operation episodes (shifts) of the article, a gallery of static HTML pages for browsing them, and every text that the agents received. In every shift, a large language model (LLM) agent operated a simulated non-isothermal continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) with three steady states and a high-temperature interlock, in real time, through a tool interface. The outcome of each shift was scored from the true state of the simulated plant. The LLMs were Claude Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 (Anthropic). Each shift record gives the design labels, the true plant trajectory at 1 s resolution, the measurements returned to the agent, every tool call made by the agent, every input change, the alarm and interlock events, the token counts of every call to the LLM, the scored outcome, the quantities that the article derives from the shift, and the text that the agent wrote (its messages during the shift, the reasons given with its forecasts, its debrief and its answers to the questions asked outside the shifts). candidates.title: NEBench R1: a Reasoning Benchmark for Evaluating Nuclear Domain Competence in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being explored for knowledge-intensive and safety-critical applications in nuclear engineering. However, existing nuclear-domain benchmarks provide limited content coverage or focus primarily on answer accuracy without systematically evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. This study introduces NEBench R1, a reasoning-oriented benchmark comprising 7,546 unique multiple-choice questions extracted from U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor operator licensing examinations covering 18 nuclear facilities. Each question is classified according to the NRC Knowledge and Abilities catalogs and accompanied by an official explanation serving as a reference for reasoning evaluation. Six LLMs were evaluated, with overall accuracy ranging from 34.0% to 73.9% across three distinct performance tiers. To assess reasoning quality, an LLM-based judge evaluated correctly answered responses using a multidimensional rubric. Although responses generally demonstrated strong problem comprehension, they scored lower in factual and procedural accuracy and distractor analysis, indicating that correct answers were not necessarily supported by technically sound justifications. Response clarity was also weakly indicative of technical quality. Furthermore, longer reasoning traces were associated with lower accuracy in both frontier reasoning models, suggesting that reasoning length may reflect question difficulty rather than improved problem-solving performance. Reasoning-token consumption may therefore provide an additional signal for identifying potentially unreliable responses. NEBench R1 establishes a benchmark for evaluating both answer accuracy and reasoning quality, providing a foundation for assessing the domain competence and reliability of LLMs in nuclear engineering.

candidates.title: Ablation study of correction methods in Polish language Retrieval-Augmented Generation chatbots
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations in large language models by grounding responses in retrieved evidence, yet the interplay of correction techniques across the RAG pipeline remains underexplored – especially for non-English languages. We present a modular RAG system evaluated through a systematic ablation study of 12 pipeline configurations on a 1,000-question Polish-language test set derived from a 1M-article Wikipedia corpus and manually validated. Four correction families are compared: (i) cross- -encoder reranking, (ii) query decomposition with multi-hop reranking and diversity enforcement, (iii) native Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, and (iv) post-generative Chain-of-Verification (CoVe). Results evaluated with RAGAS metrics show that multi-hop reranking yields the largest quality gains (Δ Faithfulness +15.6%, Δ Context Recall +38.4%, Δ Relevancy +20.3%) at acceptable latency (18.4 s), while CoVe in auto-correction mode can paradoxically degrade faithfulness at high computational cost (+41.6 s). Cross-encoder reranking achieves the best cost quality ratio (+16.7% Recall, +1.2 s). We discuss practical configuration tiers for real- -time, interactive, and offline deployments.

candidates.title: Rethinking Post-Training for Expressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
candidates.abstract: Zero-shot voice cloning typically emphasizes preserving the timbre and prosodic characteristics of a reference speaker. However, in real-world use, speech should adapt its delivery to the target text rather than remain tied to a fixed speaking style. In this work, we formulate this problem as text-adaptive prosody synthesis for zero-shot voice cloning and study how post-training can endow a cloning model with this capability. We develop a three-stage framework. First, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) provides a cold start by aligning the model with text-appropriate expressive speech. Second, Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) jointly optimizes prosodic expressiveness, acoustic quality, intelligibility, and speaker similarity. Finally, context-conditioned On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) enables self-improvement by transferring expressive behavior from strong-reference to weak-reference conditions. On Qwen3-TTS, our framework improves Emotion from 18.5 to 81.2 and Paralinguistics from 38.4 to 73.9. Extensive ablations validate the role of each stage.

candidates.title: LLM-D12: A Dual-Dimensional Scale of Instrumental and Relational Dependencies on Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: There is growing interest in understanding how people interact with large language models (LLMs) and whether such models elicit dependency or even addictive behaviour. Validated tools to assess the extent to which individuals may become dependent on LLMs are scarce and primarily build on classic behavioural addiction symptoms, adapted to the context of LLM use. We view this as a conceptual limitation, as the LLM-human relationship is more nuanced and warrants a fresh and distinct perspective. To address this gap, we developed and validated a new 12-item questionnaire to measure LLM dependency, referred to as LLM-D12. The scale was based on the authors’ prior theoretical work, with items developed accordingly and responses collected from 526 participants in the UK. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, performed on separate halves of the total sample using a split-sample approach, supported a two-factor structure: Instrumental Dependency (six items) and Relationship Dependency (six items). Instrumental Dependency reflects the extent to which individuals rely on LLMs to support or collaborate in decision-making and cognitive tasks. Relationship Dependency captures the tendency to perceive LLMs as socially meaningful, sentient, or companion-like entities. The two-factor structure demonstrated excellent internal consistency and clear discriminant validity. External validation confirmed both the conceptual foundation and the distinction between the two subscales. The psychometric properties and structure of our LLM-D12 scale were interpreted in light of the emerging view that dependency on LLMs does not necessarily indicate dysfunction but may still reflect reliance levels that could become problematic in certain contexts.

candidates.title: FRAAC: A French Multimodal Large Language Model and Dataset forPictogram-Based Augmentative and Alternative Communication
candidates.abstract: Pictograms are a core modality in augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), yet recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) cannot reliably interpret or produce pictogram sequences. Two obstacles explain this gap: the absence of a standardized pictogram grammar and the scarcity of parallel text-pictogram data. We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Pictogram Selection (RAPS), an annotation method that refines a rule-based transcription system's output with LLM-based concept extraction and retrieval over a pictogram vocabulary, handling cases where hand-written rules fail (named entities, numbers, polysemous words) without requiring new rules. Applied to French, RAPS yields a synthetic corpus of 1.4 million parallel pairs, of which 300k are publicly released. In a human ranking study where annotators order four pictogram transcriptions of the same sentence, RAPS outperforms the rule-based state of the art. Moreover, we show that standard reference-based metrics separate systems of clearly different quality but fail to rank strong systems against each other. Finally, we build an instruction-tuned model that supports interaction in several AAC modalities: it accepts pictogram or text input and answers in pictograms, speech, or text.

candidates.title: Boundary-Aware Adaptive Overlap Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Krishna Kumar Gupta Krishna Kumar Gupta
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems cut documents into chunks and usually copy the same number of tokens at every cut. This fixed overlap treats all cuts the same, even though some cuts split a sentence while others fall at a clean section break. We propose Boundary-Aware Adaptive Overlap Optimization (BAAO). BAAO scores each cut using meaning, shared technical words, context clues and document structure, then gives that cut its own overlap of 0 to 192 tokens. We compared BAAO with five fixed overlap settings and four versions of BAAO on Qasper. The tokenizer, 512-token chunks, ModernBERT embeddings, exact Qdrant search, top-k and a local Ollama model were the same for every method, and all settings were fixed on validation data before testing. On the test set, the full BAAO model stored 29.0% fewer tokens and 80.9% fewer copied tokens than the best fixed setting (Fixed-192). Its Recall@5 was lower, 0.1918 against 0.2000, but the 95% bootstrap range of the difference, [−0.0250, +0.0083], includes zero, so there was no clear improvement. A simple 32-token fixed overlap beat BAAO on both recall and storage. We also found that recall did not rise steadily with fixed overlap, that four of the five adaptive versions were among the best low-storage options, and that the version based on context clues almost matched Fixed-192 (0.1994) with about 30% fewer tokens. Our results show that adaptive overlap reliably saves storage, but better-tuned signals and fair storage-matched tests are needed before it can be shown to improve search.

candidates.title: Reinforcement Learning Post-Training for Reasoning Large Language Models: Methods, Systems, and Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central post-training approach for reasoning and agentic large language models (LLMs), particularly when task outcomes can be verified automatically. Comparisons across this literature remain difficult because a reported gain may combine changes to the learning signal, policy constraint, response granularity, data reuse, rollout system, and inference budget. This survey develops a mechanism-driven framework for separating these effects. It organizes methods along three axes — learning-signal type, policy/data regime, and optimization granularity — and decomposes their training stacks into reusable motifs spanning advantage construction, drift control, dense feedback, off-policy reuse, and rollout–update dataflow. We use this framework to synthesize representative method families, analyze cross-motif interactions, and conduct source-bounded case studies of how multi-component recipes and asynchronous pipelines should be interpreted. We further distinguish literature-established diagnostics from survey-defined reporting primitives and provide a matched-budget reporting checklist. Finally, we discuss how these interfaces may transfer to vision-language-action (VLA) models, World Action Models (WAMs), and embodied-agent post-training for unmanned systems, where reports should describe action representation, world-model error, interaction cost, and safety constraints. The corpus emphasizes mechanism clarity and records the maturity of evidence from recent preprints and system reports.

candidates.title: Large language model agent simulations of individual differences in social interactions
candidates.abstract: A key challenge in the behavioral sciences is the lack of formal models that capture individual differences in social interactions. At the same time, recent advances in artificial intelligence offer new opportunities to simulate and assess interpersonal behavior at scale. In this study, we introduce an agent-based modeling framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to simulate short-term social interactions. Within a dyadic interaction cycle, an LLM-based agent continually adjusts its interpersonal behavior (agency and communion) to its prior behavior, the partner’s behavior, and the combined influence of behavioral defaults (differences in default behavioral tendencies) and interpersonal reactivities (differences in reactions to partner behaviors). We derive a mathematical model that formalizes how interpersonal behavior unfolds across the interaction, evaluate the model in simulations, illustrate how the framework expresses these interpersonal dynamics in natural language, and outline the framework’s flexibility for simulating individual differences in practical applications across the behavioral sciences.

candidates.title: Adversarial Post-Training of Foundation Models for High-Frequency Trading
candidates.abstract: While autoregressive foundation models trained on limit order book (LOB) data show state-of-the-art performance for market simulation, pre-training with cross-entropy neither penalizes the compounding of sampling errors over free-running rollouts nor targets desired market properties. We introduce a post-training method for LOB foundation models using a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (GAN) objective. A critic, trained online on rollouts through the true, non-differentiable matching engine, guides updates from evolution strategies over rank-4 LoRA perturbations of the pre-trained generator, under a KL trust region. For efficiency, we use EGGROLL (Evolution Guided GeneRal Optimisation via Low-rank Learning), a memory-efficient variant of evolution strategies. On a held-out panel, adversarial post-training improves LOB-Bench realism by \(17.6\%\) (WS-21) and \(17.0\%\) (Mean-L1), while selection-matched random-perturbation and compute-matched continued-pre-training controls yield no improvement. Post-training is thus a necessary stage that more pre-training does not replace. Per-position divergence measurements show that it slows error accumulation over 500-message rollouts from 3.1 × to 2.3 ×. Adversarial post-training is also inexpensive, requiring under 50 M training tokens and 12 GPU-hours per seed, three orders of magnitude below the 48 B-token pre-training budget. Ablations over critic inputs, optimizers, and the population–rollout trade-off, together with an analysis of reward hacking, yield practical design guidelines for adversarial post-training.

candidates.title: InceptionRAG: Stealthy Poisoning Attack Against Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems enhance large language models (LLMs) with external knowledge but have been demonstrated vulnerable to corpus poisoning. Existing poisoning attacks against RAG largely focus on single-point explicit injection, where the malicious payload is fully encapsulated within a single document. Consequently, recent mitigation mechanisms have evolved to identify and diminish these threats effectively. In this paper, we first verify that existing mitigation mechanisms are insufficient for a new class of threats: indirect logic induction. Motivated by this observation, we introduce InceptionRAG, a stealthy attack mechanism that subverts the standard attack paradigm. Instead of injecting explicit malicious payloads, InceptionRAG fragments it into a chain of dormant passages. These passages appear harmless and can bypass existing mitigation mechanisms when examined separately. However, when retrieved together, they trigger LLMs to self-deduce target misinformation via multi-hop reasoning. To further improve the applicability of InceptionRAG in black-box settings, we propose zeroth-order suffix optimization (ZOSO) to automate the generation of authoritative suffixes. Extensive evaluations across three datasets and three LLMs demonstrate that InceptionRAG achieves an attack success rate exceeding 80% even under rigorous adversarial constraints. In particular, InceptionRAG shows superior evasion capabilities, effectively bypassing established defenses that mitigate traditional single-document injections. Our findings expose a concerning paradox: The stronger reasoning capabilities of LLMs increase their vulnerability to reasoning-based poisoning attacks. To mitigate the potential misuse of InceptionRAG, we propose a document isolation-based defense HODOR, which effectively mitigates the attack by decoupling the adversarial logical dependencies.

candidates.title: Securing Software in the Age of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer new capabilities for software security by interpreting source code and natural-language specifications, and generating plausible code. However, their probabilistic behavior, hallucinations, limited security knowledge, and inconsistent outputs make their direct use non-trivial. This dissertation investigates how LLMs can identify code requiring protection, discover and repair vulnerabilities in existing software, and improve the security of generated software code while accounting for reliability and deployment costs. The completed research provides results across three settings. LLM-CAL identifies cryptographic code for fine-grained TEE boundary establishment, reducing the Trusted Computing Base by 81.20%. RESTing-LLAMA uses semantic OpenAPI documentation to discover 11 vulnerabilities across real-world REST APIs with fewer requests and a lower false-positive rate than existing fuzzers. RAVEN combines agentic retrieval, repository-level dependency analysis, and iterative refinement to achieve an 83.13% repair success rate across 160 real-world CVE instances. The ongoing research examines the trustworthiness of LLM-based code generation through knowledge-poisoning attacks against RACG systems and an agentic Graph RAG framework for retrieving CWE-structured security knowledge. Together, these studies examine how LLMs can be adapted for securing existing and generated software.

candidates.title: Vision language model (VLM)-enabled counterfactual reasoning for illegal dumping profiling in metropolitan cities
candidates.abstract: Street view analytics (SVA) has gained increasing value in environmental criminology. However, most of the analyses are based only on limited factual information, which could lead to potential bias and limit opportunities to investigate the effect of a specific factor of interest while holding others constant. Generating counterfactual street views using vision language models (VLMs) provides a promising avenue for counterfactual reasoning and allows for the controlled study of individual factors. This study presents a novel approach that generates diverse counterfactual street views and compares them with their factual counterparts, using illegal dumping sites in urban environments as a case study. The baseline is a dataset of 757 Google Street Views (GSVs), of which 506 are illegal dumping sites and 251 are controls. Seven VLMs were benchmarked, and Nano Banana Pro was chosen to generate 1000 more counterfactual views with different featured factors. Of these, 921 passed quality screening and were retained for the main analysis. The data was analyzed by two high-powered VLMs namely GPT-5.5 and Claude Sonnet 4.6. In both evaluator graphs, visible litter and surface defects were associated with higher model scores for identifying illegal dumping sites, and well-maintained pavement with lower scores. The resulting graphs describe responses to controlled visual edits and provide hypotheses about environmental influences for future field validation. This approach can be scaled to broader studies of location-based environmental crime.

candidates.title: Tokens and market fairness in large language models
candidates.abstract: Commercial large language model (LLM) providers meter usage in tokens, and each provider defines the token through its own tokenizer. Prior studies have examined how token costs fall across languages and how per-token billing creates an incentive to misreport counts. The token itself has received less attention as a metering unit, namely as the quantity term in which the price of LLM capability is expressed. This paper develops the Fair Unit Test (FUT), a proposed normative framework of four conditions that a metering unit should meet to be fair to the party billed against it. The conditions follow from the ways in which control of a measure can disadvantage the buyer, and they correspond to requirements of legal metrology and financial reporting. Our analysis indicates that, under its stated classification rules, the token fails three of the four conditions and receives a partial pass on verifiability. This verdict combines documented properties of commercial tokenizers with the normative conditions of the FUT. The failures concern the definition of the unit, and under the FUT a change in the rate or the disclosure of token counts leaves them in place. For firms that buy LLM capability, these failures bear on the comparison of suppliers and on the forecasting of costs, and they make a buyer's estimates of its own consumption specific to one supplier. Their effects on prices and on market competition remain empirical questions for future research.

candidates.title: Rocks, Pebbles and Sand: Modality-aware Scheduling for Multimodal Large Language Model Inference
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) power platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, enabling rich interactions across text, images, and videos. Unlike text-only workloads, multimodal requests are inherently heterogeneous, differing by orders of magnitude in latency and memory footprint. Existing LLM serving systems, designed for homogeneous text workloads, struggle under this heterogeneity: large image and video requests monopolize GPU resources, causing severe head-of-line blocking and degrading the responsiveness of lightweight, latency-critical text queries. Recent multimodal serving systems mitigate this interference through disaggregation, isolating encoding and inference stages across GPUs. While effective at large scale, such designs introduce severe GPU underutilization in more practical, moderate-scale deployments. In response, we build RPS-Serve a modality-aware scheduling framework that leverages the extreme heterogeneity in multimodal workloads and introduces a simple abstraction: videos behave like rocks, images like pebbles, and text like sand. Then, it lets sand flow quickly through pebbles and rocks, maximizing GPU utilization while ensuring fast responsiveness for lightweight requests and controlled execution for heavier ones. To achieve this, RPS-Serve estimates the GPU admission cost of each request, classifies requests into rocks, pebbles, and sand using lightweight clustering, and applies priority-based scheduling with aging to balance performance across modalities. Evaluation across state-of-the-art MLLMs shows that RPS-Serve increases GPU utilization by 65% and reduces TTFT by up to 9.3 ×, on average across models, compared to disaggregation-based multimodal systems.
