candidates.title: Learning When Diffusion Language Models Should Regenerate
candidates.abstract: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.

candidates.title: Large language and atomic model: bridging atomistic representation and language reasoning for accelerating materials discovery
candidates.abstract: The combination of artificial intelligence and materials science promises accelerated discovery, yet existing approaches remain limited by a fundamental divide between physically grounded prediction and flexible reasoning. Large atomic models provide accurate structure-property relationships but are computationally expensive and lack general reasoning capability, whereas large language models excel at abstraction and inference but struggle with structured physical representations and reliable quantitative prediction. Efforts to bridge these paradigms have been impeded by competing training objectives: atomic models demand precise numerical optimization, while reasoning requires coherent sequential inference; when forced into a single objective, these requirements interfere, degrading both predictive fidelity and logical consistency. Here we introduce a Large Language and Atomic Model (LLAM), a multimodal framework with native structural reasoning capability that directly integrates atomistic representations with language-based inference. By aligning atomistic representations with the language embedding space through a lightweight cross-modal bridge, LLAM conditions both quantitative prediction and subsequent reasoning directly on crystal structures. Across diverse benchmarks spanning continuous property prediction and crystallographic classification, LLAM demonstrates strong performance while exhibiting improved reasoning capability. Case studies in optoelectronic-property interpretation, solid-state electrolyte optimization, and photovoltaic-material screening further demonstrate that LLAM can connect structure-grounded predictions with physically meaningful interpretations and application-oriented decisions.

candidates.title: Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it. We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.

candidates.title: Failure Recovery in Tool-Using Large Language Model Agents: A Structured Review of Detection, Correction, and State Consistency
candidates.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly act on the world through tools such as code interpreters, application programming interfaces, search engines, perception modules and robotic planners. Every tool call is an opportunity for failure: the model may choose the wrong tool, write malformed input, misread a returned value, trust an erroneous output, or leave external systems in a half-changed condition after a partial sequence of actions. This paper is a structured, qualitative review of how the literature detects such failures, corrects them and keeps the state of the agent and its environment consistent while doing so. It adapts the feedback-loop model and the loud/silent distinction of Sun et al. (2024) to organise a taxonomy of failures, groups detection methods into execution signals, output verification, model self-assessment, external critics and human oversight, correction methods into retry, repair, reflection, replanning, rollback and escalation, and consistency mechanisms into idempotency, compensating actions, checkpointing, action logging, state verification and memory hygiene. A study-by-study comparison of nine representative works, including 2025–2026 studies, records their methods, benchmarks, findings, limitations and treatment of state consistency. Within the reviewed corpus, explicit error messages are comparatively well exploited, silent failures appear to remain a major open problem, self-correction without external feedback is reported to be unreliable on reasoning tasks, and state consistency receives less attention than detection and correction. The paper closes with recommendations for evaluation and design and an agenda for future research. The review is not exhaustive and reports no new experiments.

candidates.title: SpaceMCP: Vision Language Model Spatial Reasoning via Model Context Protocol
candidates.abstract: Despite impressive advances in large language models (LLM), vision-language models (VLM) still exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities. Recent progress in feed-forward 3D reconstruction has enabled precise, real-time geometric understanding from visual inputs. In this work, we propose SpaceMCP, a framework that leverages these advances to introduce an MCP-style paradigm for spatial reasoning. Our approach augments a VLM with structured function calls, allowing it to query a scene graph for spatial information such as distances, object positioning, and camera properties. The scene graph is constructed in real time using feed-forward 3D reconstruction to recover metric geometry, combined with open-vocabulary segmentation to identify and localize relevant objects within the scene. Paired with the VLM's strong reasoning capabilities, the VLM is able to combine this primitive information to solve more complex spatial tasks. Without any training, SpaceMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, outperforming recent spatially post-trained VLMs and improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark. We argue that, given the contrast between the relatively slow progress in native VLM spatial reasoning and the rapid advances in feed-forward 3D computer vision, this paradigm offers a promising path forward for enabling robust spatial reasoning.

candidates.title: Hybrid Retrieval for Retrieval-Augmented Generation using Vector and Graph Databases
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) supplements a large language model with evidence retrieved from an external knowledge source. Vector retrieval is effective for semantic similarity, whereas graph retrieval represents entities and explicit relationships that can support multi-hop and corpus-level questions. This paper develops a comparative framework for evaluating vector-only, graph-only, and hybrid vector-graph retrieval under a shared generation setup. The review covers dense passage retrieval, GraphRAG, HippoRAG, LightRAG, and evaluation frameworks for retrieval-augmented systems. A reproducible evaluation protocol is proposed around 50 stratified questions and metrics for answer accuracy, evidence recall, faithfulness, citation coverage, latency, and resource overhead. Because no query logs, model outputs, corpus, or annotation records were supplied for this manuscript, Section 5 uses clearly identified synthetic values solely to demonstrate how a 50-question analysis and its figures would be reported. These illustrative values suggest a plausible trade-off: hybrid retrieval may improve coverage of relational questions while increasing latency and infrastructure complexity. They are not empirical findings and cannot establish superiority. The contribution is therefore a transparent comparative design, a reusable evaluation matrix, and a set of hypotheses for a controlled experiment. A publishable empirical claim requires rerunning the protocol on a documented dataset and replacing all synthetic values with measured results.

candidates.title: Semantic Consistency of Vision Tokens: A Vision-Centric Perspective on Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: In computer vision, vision-language and self-supervised encoders are two unique paradigms characterized by global language alignment and high-quality vision-only patch representations, respectively. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often use the former because of language alignment, despite the recent rise in vision-centric tasks resembling traditional dense vision tasks that would likely benefit from the high-quality patch representations, raising the question whether self-supervised models could aid MLLMs in vision-centric tasks. To investigate this, we define semantic (in)consistency of patch tokens from language-aligned encoders and identify two sets of tokens, semantically consistent (SCTs) and semantically inconsistent (SITs). Through systematic probing via the removal of SCTs or SITs from the input of modern MLLMs, we show higher reliance on SCTs than SITs, as removal of the former induces larger performance drops. This demonstrates that MLLMs benefit from semantic consistency of vision tokens. With this in mind, we devise a simple yet effective extension of the MLLM training objective that combines traditional language modeling with semantic guidance via minimization of semantic inconsistency. This strategy, named Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), combines the signals of both loss terms to push the vision encoder towards providing semantically consistent tokens, while preserving language alignment. Extensive evaluation shows that SGT outperforms all baselines and MLLMs with specialized vision encoders on vision-centric benchmarks while keeping strong scores on text-centric benchmarks, thus setting state of the art on average across all tasks. Our results highlight the importance of combining language alignment and semantic consistency through the lens of MLLMs rather than independently from them and pave the way towards the design of better MLLM vision encoders.

candidates.title: Security, Privacy, and Trustworthy Design for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a language model draw on an external knowledge store. Factual coverage improves, but the system also gains security and privacy boundaries that a stand-alone model does not have: a malicious or unauthorized document can shape what is retrieved, enter the model context, over-ride instructions, disclose sensitive information, or trigger an external action. This structured narrative review synthesizes RAG attacks, defenses, threat models, and evaluation practices in work published between 2020 and September 2026. The evidence is grouped by pipeline stage, from ingestion, chunking, and embedding through retrieval, vector storage, context assembly, generation, output, and tool execution. Four findings stand out. First, poisoning, extraction, membership inference, and indirect prompt injection are distinct but composable threats. Second, attack success often falls when realistic chunking, re-ranking, corpus redundancy, and permissions are introduced, while adaptive evaluation can expose residual weaknesses in defenses. Third, credible security requires layered controls spanning provenance, access control, retrieval-time anomaly detection, context isolation, output monitoring, and tool permissions. Fourth, current benchmarks rarely evaluate authorization state, multi-tenant isolation, cache invalidation, deployment cost, or external actions. The review contributes a RAG security reference architecture, an attack-defense matrix, and a reporting framework for deployment-aware evaluation.

candidates.title: Outside the Purview of the Reward: Capability Drift in Multilingual Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.

candidates.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Fine-Grained Image-Interpretation Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models on Bilingual Radiology Questions: Cross-Sectional Benchmark Study
candidates.abstract: Background Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding in radiology and digital health; however, their diagnostic performance across diverse clinical scenarios and fine-grained visual reasoning tasks requires systematic evaluation. Objective The study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and fine-grained visual reasoning performance of 5 multimodal LLMs with bilingual medical imaging questions. Methods This cross-sectional benchmark study evaluated bilingual medical imaging questions using zero-shot prompting on 5 LLMs: GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Pro, Doubao, Yuanbao, and Llama 4 Maverick. Subgroup analyses by language (English/Chinese), question type (image/text), imaging modality (computed tomography, radiography, magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound, and nuclear medicine), and anatomical system (neurologic, respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, genitourinary, and musculoskeletal) evaluated intermodel accuracy and intramodel consistency. Image-based visual reasoning performance was assessed across modality, anatomy, lesion detection, and localization. Results A total of 298 questions (198 image-based, 100 text-based) were evaluated. Gemini 3 Pro achieved the highest overall accuracy (n=268, 89.9%, 95% CI 86.0%‐92.9%), significantly outperforming Doubao (n=235, 78.9%; P <.001), GPT-5.2 (n=233, 78.2%; P <.001), Yuanbao (n=216, 72.5%; P <.001), and Llama 4 Maverick (n=216, 72.5%; P <.001). All models performed better on text-based than image-based questions (Yuanbao, P <.001; Doubao, P =.02; GPT-5.2, P <.001; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.002; Llama 4 Maverick, P <.001). GPT-5.2 ( P <.001), Llama 4 Maverick ( P =.03), and Yuanbao ( P =.03) favored English questions, while intramodel performance remained stable across modalities (Yuanbao, P =.46; Doubao, P =.21; GPT-5.2, P =.26; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.96; Llama 4 Maverick, P =.45) and anatomical systems (Yuanbao, P =.82; Doubao, P =.52; GPT-5.2, P =.35; Gemini 3 Pro, P =.13; Llama 4 Maverick, P =.97). Despite near-perfect macroscopic visual recognition (modality and anatomy: 99.0%‐100.0%), accuracy dropped in complex tasks. Gemini 3 Pro outperformed Yuanbao ( P <.001), GPT-5.2 ( P =.002), and Llama 4 Maverick ( P <.001) in lesion detection (175/198, 88.4%) and outperformed Yuanbao ( P <.001), Doubao ( P =.004), and Llama 4 Maverick ( P =.004) in lesion localization (189/198, 95.5%). Conclusions Gemini 3 Pro demonstrated optimal, comprehensive performance and cross-lingual stability. However, current multimodal LLMs face a technical bottleneck in complex visual interpretation—particularly in fine-grained lesion detection and localization—emphasizing the need to prioritize local feature perception in future model development.

candidates.title: DiFiT: Distribution-Fidelity-guided Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models, but answer accuracy only partly reflects its effect. Pruning can change the probabilities of alternative response tokens even when greedy answers remain correct and unchanged. We compare full and pruned response distributions under shared reference prefixes. Average predictive drift grows with compression on fixed correctly answered samples. Separate analyses associate larger drift with more confidence-decision disagreements and sampling failures. We propose DiFiT (Distribution-Fidelity-guided Token pruning) to learn discrete selection from reference answers and full-token response distributions. Dual-View Distillation matches probabilities across the vocabulary, while answer supervision supports task quality. A learned scorer and differentiable Top-$K$ learn which visual evidence to retain. A multi-budget mask objective supports different retention ratios through one shared ranking over a frozen model. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DiFiT reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% relative to FastV at 10% retention on four-task greedy-correct controls. It preserves 98.74% of baseline performance on MME at 30% retention.

candidates.title: TraceKV: Policy-Preserving Low-Rank KV Cache Compression for Reasoning Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) impose substantial KV cache demands from both large multimodal contexts and growing reasoning traces. Low-rank KV compression has emerged as a promising paradigm that stores low-dimensional latents of KV states and can be combined with quantization. However, existing low-rank methods often induce growing predictive policy drift from the dense model when compressing reasoning KV states, resulting in reasoning failures. We identify two key causes of this degradation: calibration-state mismatch between static contexts and on-policy reasoning states, and unequal error sensitivity across KV states. To address these challenges, we propose TraceKV, a training-free low-rank KV compression framework that unifies on-policy calibration, sensitivity-aware SVD, and global rank allocation under a single policy-preserving principle, substantially reducing policy-KL divergence during reasoning. Experiments across multiple VLMs and visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate superior accuracy--memory trade-offs, achieving near-lossless reasoning accuracy with 5.64$\times$ KV cache compression when combined with quantization. Optimized low-rank attention kernels further deliver up to 1.83$\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup. Code will be available at https://github.com/AK-DREAM/TraceKV.

candidates.title: How Far Can Frozen Vision-Language Models Go on Event Data? A Training-Free Study on EventBench

For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.

candidates.title: TQIR: Trellis Quantization with Integer Reconstruction for Bandwidth-Efficient Edge LLM Acceleration
candidates.abstract: Autoregressive large language model (LLM) inference is often limited by external-memory bandwidth, while existing ultra-low-bit trellis quantization reconstructs floating-point weights and leaves runtime Hadamard-transform and decoder costs unresolved. This paper presents TQIR, an algorithm--hardware co-design that decouples storage precision ($S$) from decoded-weight ($W$) and activation ($A$) compute precisions, enabling a better accuracy--hardware trade-off. TQIR performs trellis matching with floating-point candidates offline while constraining each candidate to an INT8 or INT4 codeword that can be reproduced exactly for integer GEMM at runtime. To reduce transform cost while preserving the integer weight path, TQIR relocates the reverse Hadamard transform to the activation side and employs an $H_{128}$ Subspace Hadamard Transform, together with a subspace-aligned $128\times2$ trellis tile that preserves the original 256-weight sequence length. The configurable decoder, synthesized in a TSMC 16-nm process, delivers 307.2~Gweights/s in 0.0509~mm$^2$ and achieves 13.93$\times$ and 1.52$\times$ the normalized decoder-area efficiency of Ecco and Codeword Decomposition, respectively. These results show that fixed-rate trellis compression can reduce weight traffic while sustaining an integer-GEMM datapath matched to the evaluated memory and PE rates.

candidates.title: SubGPU Pipelining: Intra-GPU Fine-Grained Spatial Parallelism for LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) decode is dominated by short, predominantly memory-bound kernels that make bursty use of on-chip execution resources and memory bandwidth. This paper introduces SubGPU Pipelining, a fine-grained, intra-GPU spatial execution model that cuts an operator graph into ordered contiguous segments, binds those segments to spatial stages backed by disjoint streaming-multiprocessor (SM) pools, and streams microbatches through the resulting schedule. Selecting the graph cuts, segment-to-stage binding, per-stage SM allocation, and microbatch size is a coupled optimization problem: each choice changes the overlap pattern, shared-resource contention, cache state, and execution times of the others. We evaluate SubGPU Pipelining through both simulation and silicon experiment using the GPT-OSS 120B workload with 32-GPU B200 deployment settings. The analytical shared-resource simulator searches across SubGPU pipeline structures and batch sizes to map the per-user/per-GPU throughput Pareto frontier. At matched per-GPU throughput, the modeled SubGPU frontier provides up to 2.2x higher per-user throughput than temporal execution, and at matched per-user throughput it provides up to 1.9x higher per-GPU throughput. To test physical feasibility and further validate the simulation results, silicon experiments are performed, using one B200 GPU to emulate a 32-GPU B200 deployment. The experiment evaluates one selected two-stage pipeline configuration at global batch 2,048 using CUDA Green Contexts and TensorRT-LLM kernels. Results show that SubGPU Pipelining improves mean DRAM read-plus-write throughput from 71.8% to 83.6% of peak, and reduces the 36-layer decoder iteration time by 10.33%.

This paper aims to explore optimization techniques for complexity reduction of LLMs without substantially degrading performance. Model pruning, parameter reduction, and early stopping techniques will be investigated. The study will evaluate existing lightweight models like TinyBERT and explore novel strategies for creating efficient LLM variants suitable for edge deployment. Metrics like model size, inference latency, and task-specific accuracy will be used to assess the trade-offs. The tradeoffs to enable practical LLM deployment in low-resource environments while maintaining acceptable performance levels are discussed.

candidates.title: Anytime-Valid Empirical Likelihood Inference from LLM Annotations with Adaptive Human Auditing
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate unlabeled data as a fast, low-cost alternative to human annotation. However, their outputs can be biased and miscalibrated relative to human labels, potentially leading to misleading analysis and inference. We propose AAELI (Adaptive Human Auditing and Anytime-Valid Empirical Likelihood Inference), an online framework for estimating the population mean of human labels under a limited auditing budget. AAELI uses LLM outputs to guide adaptive human auditing and combines them with audited labels through predictable empirical-likelihood $e$-processes to construct anytime-valid confidence sequences. Our main theoretical result shows that a predictably learned efficient projection preserves the first-order profile empirical-likelihood statistic under adaptive auditing, without requiring a prescribed convergence rate for the projection estimator. This yields an exactly anytime-valid betting construction whose continuous-mixture form incurs a scalar rather than vector-dimensional mixing penalty. Supporting results establish adaptive empirical-likelihood asymptotics and show that a learned audit rule attains the oracle variance within the stated class of augmented estimating-equation designs under the same audit-probability floor and long-run expected budget. Experiments on synthetic data and three real-world datasets demonstrate that AAELI maintains empirical anytime coverage while requiring fewer human audits than the strongest competing baseline to reach a target precision.

candidates.title: From Search to Decision: How Post-Training Shapes Information-Seeking Capabilities in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Information seeking in large language model (LLM) systems increasingly involves decisions about when to acquire information, where to search, and how to evaluate and use evidence. Recent post-training methods have improved several such behaviors, but their objectives and evaluations span different tasks and system settings. This paper organizes research around six interrelated information-seeking capabilities and examines the learning signals, optimization methods, update loci, and credit-assignment mechanisms used to develop them. We synthesize empirical progress in targeted behaviors, end-to-end performance, search control, and generalization. Existing studies report gains in retrieval routing, query refinement, multi-tool exploration, evidence-grounded reasoning, and resource-aware search, although the scope of behavioral evidence varies across capabilities. We identify open challenges in estimating prospective retrieval utility, coordinating information-seeking decisions, and adapting to unfamiliar retrieval environments, and discuss evaluation practices for interpreting future progress.

candidates.title: Desalination LLM: Large Language Model Agents Design Efficient Graphene Membranes for Water Desalination
candidates.abstract: Graphene nanopores can, in principle, combine high water permeability with strong salt rejection, but finding pore geometries that do both usually requires many molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. We describe a design framework in which a large language model (LLM) grows a nanopore atom by atom, using pretrained predictors of water flux and ion rejection to judge each candidate. Two recent models, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, were tested with the same prompt and the same design protocol (30 steps, up to 30 trials per step, at most three atoms removed per trial, and a 90% ion-rejection floor). We wanted to know how much of an agent’s performance comes from the model and how much from the surrounding scaffold, so each model was run twice: once as a tool-using agent with access to the predictors, and once in conversation only, where it chose atoms and estimated performance without any feedback. Three scaffold-only baselines that contain no language model were run for comparison. With tools, both models stayed above the rejection floor at every step. Claude Opus 5.5 produced a single, island-free pore with a predicted flux of 122.3 ns−1 at 93.2% rejection, and GPT-6.1 Sol reached 131.7 ns−1 at 90.2%. Without tools the two models erred in opposite directions. Claude Opus 5.5 overestimated rejection and removed too many atoms, ending at 64.3% rejection, whereas GPT-6.1 Sol was overly cautious and recovered only 30% of the flux reached by its scaffold. A greedy search restricted by simple manufacturability rules matched or exceeded both agents in flux. Compared with the MD dataset and the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) designs of earlier work, the agents placed a larger share of their high-rejection pores above 120 ns−1. Taken together, the results indicate that predictor feedback, rather than the language model on its own, is what keeps LLM-guided pore design on target, and the six-condition protocol gives a simple way to make that attribution for other models.

candidates.title: Retrieval-augmented Large Language Models for automated discharge summary generation in post-surgical ICU cancer patients
candidates.abstract: Introduction Discharge summary generation is an essential yet time-consuming component of clinical documentation, particularly for post-surgical cancer patients admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), where clinically relevant information is distributed across structured electronic health records (EHRs) and unstructured clinical notes. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for automating this task, they remain susceptible to hallucinations and often struggle to incorporate previously unseen patient information. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has been proposed to address these limitations by grounding text generation in retrieved clinical evidence. Methods This study separates the contribution of retrieval from that of fine-tuning using a paired two-by-two design: three open-source LLMs: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, StableLM-Zephyr-3B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, were each evaluated as pretrained and parameter-efficient fine-tuned models, with and without a hybrid RAG pipeline combining sparse (BM25) and dense (FAISS) retrieval, giving 12 configurations. Using structured data from the MIMIC-IV dataset and two disclosed note-derived fields, all configurations generated multi-section discharge summaries for the same fixed evaluation set of 50 patients and were assessed with ROUGE, BLEU, and BERTScore, with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired per-patient comparisons. Results Fine-tuning improved every model on every metric, with confidence intervals excluding zero, and fine-tuned summaries matched the length of physician-authored references; the smallest model (StableLM-Zephyr-3B) achieved the highest ROUGE-1 (0.278) after fine-tuning. Retrieval augmentation, implemented as style-reference retrieval from training cases, produced no measurable change in this setting for either pretrained or fine-tuned models. Discussion These findings indicate that small, parameter-efficient fine-tuned open-source models offer a practical option under constrained compute for automated ICU discharge summary generation, and that the value of retrieval augmentation should be demonstrated against fine-tuned baselines rather than assumed.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation For Document Question Answering: A Review Of Retrieval, Embedding, Vector Search And Grounded Answer Generation
candidates.abstract: Abstract—The rapid growth of digital documents creates a need for systems that can find relevant information and answer questions accurately. Traditional question-answering systems rely on predefined knowledge bases or keyword search and may fail to understand the meaning of complex questions, while large language models alone can produce fluent but unsupported answers. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with the generation abilities of large language models. This paper reviews RAG for document question answering. It explains sparse retrieval with BM25, dense retrieval with dual encoders and sentence embeddings, approximate nearest-neighbour vector search, re-ranking, and the integration of retrieved passages into generation, including fusion-in-decoder and self-reflective retrieval. Practical issues such as chunking, context length and the tendency of models to overlook information in the middle of long contexts are discussed, together with evaluation of faithfulness and relevance. A five-layer system is proposed in which users upload PDF documents that are extracted, cleaned and chunked, embedded with a sentence-transformer model and stored in a vector database; queries retrieve relevant chunks that are passed to an LLM to generate grounded answers through a Streamlit interface. Research gaps, objectives and a comparison of retrieval methods are presented.

candidates.title: Comparative Vulnerability Analysis of Long-Context Retrieval Across Commercial and Edge-Hosted Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: While contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) advertise expansive context boundaries reaching up to millions of tokens, empirical systems-level testing reveals that actual operational fidelity non-linearly degrades. In complex multi-needle retrieval and long-form analytical workloads, reliable recall routinely contracts to an estimated 20% of nominal capacity. This paper provides a rigorous comparative benchmark of six industry-leading architectures across both local edge-hosted open-weights deployments and commercial cloud environments. Utilizing a high-resolution, continuous 1% spatial depth tracking methodology, our baseline empirical testbed uncovers a critical processing anomaly on a bare-metal edge rig hosting a local open-weights model, exposing an abrupt 54x processing latency explosion (surging from ∼1.95s to 106.72s) occurring at the precise geometric midpoint (52% depth) of inference execution. To map closed frontier ecosystems without network noise, these baseline metrics are utilized as control parameters to initialize precise mathematical telemetry simulation matrices for commercial cloud platforms, capturing a downstream latency shift to the 88% boundary as context horizons scale to 32,000 tokens. Finally, we present an algorithmic, cost-effective middleware framework featuring dynamic semantic interleaving, high-attention mirroring, and vector-density position routing. Deployed within an enterprise production-grade retrieval pipeline, this architecture successfully mitigates intermediate retrieval failures by 42.6% and contracts commercial token billing consumption metrics by 31.8% without necessitating model re-training.

candidates.title: Chain of Physics: Supporting Fault Diagnosis with Engineering-Inspired Large Language Model Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Fault diagnosis in complex systems requires linking observed changes in physical quantities to the failure mechanisms that produce them. Experienced engineers perform this task by combining sensor information with knowledge of system behavior and fault propagation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can support this process, but their diagnostic reasoning depends on the availability of asset-specific engineering knowledge and on how this knowledge is represented and used during inference. This work introduces Chain of Physics (CoP), an LLM-based fault-diagnosis framework built around a Constrained Knowledge Graph (CKG) generated automatically from asset-specific reference documentation. CoP addresses failure-sensor association from textual engineering knowledge. The CKG stores diagnostic chains connecting failure modes, changes in physical quantities, and monitoring sensors. During inference, semantically similar graph paths are retrieved for each question and used as both information and in-context examples for the reasoning process. Candidate failure modes are extracted from the question and analysed independently through dedicated LLM calls, which generate plausible failure-to-observation chains. A final decision module compares these chains with the available answer choices. CoP is evaluated on the FailureSensorIQ benchmark across four industrial asset classes and three LLMs. Compared with direct prompting and conventional Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), CoP improves diagnostic accuracy across all evaluated models, with gains ranging from 7.8 to 19.6 percentage points and from 11.7 to 18.2 percentage points, respectively. The results show that structured engineering knowledge can improve LLM-based diagnostic reasoning when graph retrieval is combined with in-context examples of fault propagation.

candidates.title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2. Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.

candidates.title: Improving Factual Grounding and Citation Reliability in Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines information retrieval with large language model (LLM) generation to answer questions using external documents. Although retrieved passages provide contextual evidence, their presence does not guarantee that every generated claim is supported or that a citation is correctly associated with the claim it accompanies. This paper presents the design and preliminary evaluation of a document-based RAG application integrating hybrid retrieval, claim-level evidence assessment, and citation-label validation. The application uses Angular, Java Spring Boot, PostgreSQL with pgvector, and locally hosted models through Ollama. Documents are extracted, divided into overlapping chunks, embedded using nomic-embed-text, and retrieved through a ranking function combining semantic and lexical relevance. The qwen2.5:3b-instruct model generates answers from retrieved context. A validation stage assigns evidence statuses and separately checks whether citation labels correspond to retrieved sources. Evaluation used 17 predefined questions over a five-page fictional employee handbook. Seven responses were classified as SUPPORTED and ten as NOT_SPECIFIED. Citation-label checking identified 12 VALID_LABELS responses and five MISSING citations. These results are preliminary: the experiment used one document and one recorded run, and citation-label consistency does not establish semantic entailment. The study treats evidence support and citation consistency as distinct reliability dimensions and identifies larger-scale comparative evaluation as future work.

candidates.title: Closing the BF16-FP16 Convergence Speed Gap in RL Post-Training with Stochastic Rounding
candidates.abstract: BF16 is widely used to pretrain large language models because it has the same dynamic range as FP32 and converges similarly to FP32 training. However, in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where learning rates are typically low, we find that standard mixed-precision BF16 training converges more slowly than FP16 training at the same learning rate. We attribute this gap to weight sticking: when FP32 shadow weights are quantized to BF16 using round-to-nearest, small updates often leave the BF16 weights used for rollout generation and training unchanged. Consequently, several optimizer steps may be needed before updates to the shadow weights are reflected in the BF16 weights. Raising the BF16 learning rate reduces weight sticking and matches FP16's convergence speed, but it also increases the KL divergence from the reference model. We instead apply stochastic rounding when quantizing the FP32 shadow weights to BF16. This approach matches FP16's convergence speed across different models and datasets while reducing the KL divergence relative to BF16 training with a larger learning rate. Unlike FP16, it keeps BF16's wider dynamic range and needs no loss scaling.

candidates.title: Trait Hitchhiking in LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now a standard stage of language model post-training, and the compute devoted to it is growing rapidly. While it has been shown to improve capabilities, particularly for tasks with verifiable rewards, it can also change behaviours and internal properties that the reward does not explicitly target. We present a formalism to describe the evolution of "traits" during RL post-training and, in doing so, recover the Price equation from evolutionary biology. We use this to develop a mathematical model for what we call "trait hitchhiking": the amplification or suppression of non-targeted traits as training redistributes probability across completions. We evaluate this Price update expression on language models trained with GRPO and show that the Price estimates closely track the sampled trait dynamics. These results identify trait hitchhiking as a mechanism by which RL post-training can silently amplify undesirable traits.

candidates.title: How Post-Training Influences Verbalized Algorithmic Computation in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Post-training improves language-model reasoning, but how it changes the use of internal information and verbalized chain of thought (CoT) remains unclear. We study successive SFT, DPO, and RLVR checkpoints of Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on multi-digit addition, using carry values as known intermediate state. Probes recover carry information from internal activations with similar accuracy in SFT and RLVR, although manipulating this information does not reliably control model outputs. In contrast, the usefulness of verbalized reasoning differs: CoTs produced by RLVR yield higher accuracy across receiving checkpoints than those produced by SFT or DPO. We also show that carry-related statements receive higher importance scores after RLVR than matched random controls. DPO shows similar sensitivity to carry-related statements but without comparable accuracy gains. These results suggest that post-training changes the usefulness of written reasoning and sensitivity to its content in meaningful ways, although greater sensitivity does not necessarily coincide with better problem performance.

candidates.title: Dynamic Knowledge Grounding for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Uncertainty-Aware Evidence Fusion with Adaptive Retrieval Control
candidates.abstract: Despite the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as a paradigm to provide grounding of LLM output in external knowledge, current RAG approaches have three core limitations: (1) uniform retrieval for every query, which wastes computation and adds irrelevant noise; (2) evidence fusion via shallow combination, failing to model differential relevance and reliability among retrieved passages; and (3) no explicit grounding verification to prevent hallucination from propagating despite retrieval augmentation. We present FORGE (Factually-Optimized Retrieval for Grounded gEneration), a principled framework that addresses all three limitations through three tightly integrated modules: the Adaptive Retrieval Controller (ARC), which learns an uncertainty-driven policy for when, what, and how much to retrieve; the Evidence Fusion Network (EFN), which performs multi-granularity cross-attention fusion with passage-level reliability weighting; and the Grounding Verification Module (GVM), which provides token-level factual consistency checking with calibrated confidence scores. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis establishing: (i) \(\:\mathcal{O}\left(\sqrt{T\text{l}\text{o}\text{g}K}\right)\) retrieval regret bounds for the adaptive policy; (ii) information-theoretic optimality guarantees for evidence fusion under the rate-distortion framework; (iii) PAC-Bayes generalization bounds for grounding verification; and (iv) end-to-end hallucination rate reduction guarantees. Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, HotpotQA, FEVER, ASQA, ELI5, PopQA, TruthfulQA) demonstrate that FORGE achieves state-of-the-art performance with 2.1–4.8 point improvements over the best baselines while reducing hallucination rates by 38.7% and retrieval costs by 42.3%.

candidates.title: Comparative Study on the Translation Quality of "Three-Character Classic" by Large Language Models and Multimodal Large Models
candidates.abstract: With the widespread application of large language models (LLM) and multimodal large models (MLLM) in the field of machine translation, how to evaluate the translation quality of different models for ancient Chinese classics has become an urgent issue to be explored. This study takes the children's educational classic "Three Character Classic" as the research object, selects eight representative original sentences, and translates them into English using both LLM and MLLM. The translated texts are then quantitatively compared using the BLEU automatic evaluation tool. The aim of this study is to determine which type of model performs better in the English translation of classical Chinese texts and which model is more suitable for the translation tasks of Chinese classical literature. The study found that, here, fill in the actual experimental data: the BLEU and METEOR scores show which type of model performs better. This study provides empirical reference for AI-assisted English translation of Chinese ancient classics and also offers an empirical basis for the applicability of automatic translation quality assessment tools in the context of classical Chinese translation.

candidates.title: An evidence-traceable benchmark of clinical reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Benchmark scores for medical large language models (LLMs) are difficult to interpret when scoring criteria cannot be traced to clinical evidence. Here we developed Med Evidence Bench (MEB; https://www.medevidencebench.org.cn/), comprising 1,536 physician-constructed items across three levels: guideline knowledge, standardized clinical scenarios and real-world laboratory scenarios. Each criterion stating a medical claim is linked to a versioned source-text span. Across ten LLMs, the Evidence Trace Score (ETS) was 0.975-0.997 for guideline knowledge, 0.292-0.658 for standardized scenarios and 0.182-0.447 for real-world scenarios, and rankings varied across levels. For real-world scenarios, scores for identifying clinical information (mean, 0.770) exceeded those for matching evidence (0.165) or formulating recommendations (0.160). On 1,296 criterion-level judgments, automated grading agreed with the majority vote of three physicians (macro-F1, 0.930; 95% confidence interval, 0.915-0.945), although agreement was lower for evidence application. These findings from Chinese-language materials indicate that guideline recall does not ensure patient-specific evidence use and do not establish clinical effectiveness.

candidates.title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
candidates.abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.

candidates.title: Sophon: A Procedural Diagnostic for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) score 85-94% on spatial benchmarks (BLINK Spatial, What's Up CLEVR) yet collapse to chance on simple geometric questions when object, scene, and texture priors are stripped away. We introduce and open-source Sophon, a procedurally generated diagnostic of paired colored point-cloud stimuli across three coordinate systems (1D linear, 2D Cartesian, 2D polar) and four question types (binary, categorical, comparative, quantitative). Across four open architectures (LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2.5-VL, Idefics3), accuracy clusters at 47-52% while frontier models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4) clear 77-83% and humans reach 84-94%. We use linear probes and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to trace the open-weight failures. Probes of the vision encoder (ViT) and language decoder (LLM) recover Sophon spatial information at 83-85% and 80-86% accuracy, respectively, and the language tower's reasoning circuit answers text-only controls (point clouds as sets of coordinates) at +40 pp over visual stimuli. Language tower per-layer attention attribution localizes visual integration to mid-stack layers. At readout, models elevate the correct answer-set tokens but select among them randomly. We localize the mechanism by tuning individual and grouped components across every architecture's stack, including the vision tower (ViT workspace and reader), the projector, and the language tower (LLM workspace and reader). These experiments demonstrate that this mid-stack workspace holds circuitry capable of organizing the spatial signal so that the frozen reader can decode it. LoRA fine-tuning adjusts that circuitry such that 7B-class VLMs answer Sophon spatial reasoning questions at frontier aggregate accuracy. This work suggests that these models do not have a capability gap for spatial reasoning but suffer from a routing bottleneck that targeted fine-tuning repairs.

candidates.title: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries
candidates.abstract: In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the nature of expert specialization remains controversial. Reports of domain-associated expert preferences contrast with analyses attributing routing primarily to token identity or syntactic patterns. To clarify these differing accounts, we look beyond expert-level routing to investigate the neuron-level organization of domain-specialized computation using Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP), a measure developed for this analysis. Using mixed-domain calibration data, we identify domain-specialized neuron sets with 58-74% overlap across multi-source samples of the same domain, compared with 15-24% across domains. To understand how this organization evolves during training, we trace neuron importance throughout pre-training and post-training across three fully open MoE families. Neuron importance continues to reorganize between pre-training checkpoints despite comparatively stable expert-level importance rankings, while post-training largely preserves neuron rankings. Building on these neuron-level perspectives, we further introduce RAMP-based Pruning (RAMPr) to select neurons across experts for balanced multi-domain capability preservation. At 75% neuron retention, RAMPr preserves average 91-98% of original full performance across six models. At 50% retention, our pruning method can reduce resident GPU memory by 36-43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17-39% effectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/Neuron-Level-Specialization-in-MoE

candidates.title: Tri-Stack-PIM: A Heterogeneous Multi-Die 3D-Integrated Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Efficient LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference during autoregressive decoding is fundamentally memory-bandwidth-bound. Existing three-dimensional (3D) stacked processing-in-memory (PIM) architectures alleviate the off-chip bandwidth wall, yet remain constrained by several limitations: physical layer (PHY), controllers, and direct memory access (DMA) engines compete with arithmetic units for advanced-node base-die area; hybrid-bonding keep-out zones fragment the base-die floorplan and impede physical design; compute tiles built in a dynamic random access memory (DRAM) process are restricted to low logic density, capping achievable throughput; and nonlinear operations offloaded to the host reintroduce a communication bottleneck. We present Tri-Stack-PIM, a heterogeneous three-die architecture that resolves these tensions by dedicating a top DRAM die to storage, a middle buffer die on a mature process node to PHYs, DMA engines, and near-memory compute units, and a bottom base die on an advanced node exclusively to single-instruction-multiple-data (SIMD) multiply-accumulate (MAC) arrays. We further introduce a Unified Buffer-Aware Ready-based (UBAR) hardware out-of-order micro-operation scheduler that enforces cross-die dependency correctness at runtime while maximizing issue-slot utilization through a multi-term priority function, recovering up to 90% of the cycles that an in-order policy would forfeit. A joint architecture-dataflow co-exploration identifies Pareto-optimal configurations that reduce the energy-delay product (EDP) by 33-66x over naive parameter selection. Evaluated across multi-head, grouped-query, and multi-query attention (MHA, GQA, MQA) mechanisms with batch sizes 1-32, Tri-Stack-PIM achieves geometric-mean speedups of 4.95x, 2.57x, and 1.68x across all three attention mechanisms and batch sizes over a graphics processing unit (GPU) baseline, AttAcc, and H2-LLM, respectively.

candidates.title: RE-PRESENT: Evidence Triangulation across Alternative Candidate-Space Views for Efficient LLM Ensemble Inference
candidates.abstract: Heterogeneous large language models (LLMs) exhibit complementary strengths, motivating routing and multi-model inference methods that seek to identify reliable predictions for each input. However, exploiting this complementarity remains challenging even when a correct prediction is available within the ensemble. We investigate this challenge across heterogeneous LLM ensembles and find that a simple single-round aggregation rule is highly competitive with learned routing methods, yet substantial oracle headroom remains. Further analysis shows that the evaluated single-round response signals provide limited discriminative power for identifying reliable predictions. In contrast, controlled re-presentations of the same question elicit complementary evidence about prediction reliability. Motivated by these findings, we introduce RE-PRESENT, a training-free framework that selectively re-presents disputed questions and directly aggregates candidate-level evidence across alternative views. Across seven multiple-choice benchmarks and two heterogeneous model ensembles, RE-PRESENT improves over strong single-round aggregation while offering a favorable accuracy--cost trade-off compared with self-consistency and multi-model debate.

candidates.title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains, yet its standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective treats every corpus token as a fixed target, regardless of its utility to the current model. In a controlled study on the same 1B-token mathematical corpus, we observe sharply different outcomes across base models: NTP improves Llama-3.2-3B's performance on mathematical benchmarks but substantially degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base's performance, indicating that, under a fixed training recipe, the same training sequences can have model-dependent effects. To address this problem, we introduce On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD), which reformulates mid-training from offline text imitation into active, query-driven knowledge acquisition. At selected anchor positions, OPMD samples trajectories from the evolving student policy and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, training the model on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. This on-policy objective reduces the training-generation mismatch of teacher-forced NTP. On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves the Qwen student over its base performance and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline, which degrades on both benchmarks. OPMD integrates into CPT pipelines without added inference-time overhead and offers a model-aware alternative to passive domain adaptation.

candidates.title: PancreaGuide for Computed Tomography Report Interpretation and Perioperative Consultation in Pancreatic Cancer: Development and Retrospective Evaluation of a Knowledge-Augmented Large Language Model Agent
candidates.abstract: Background Accurate interpretation of pancreatic cancer status and resectability-related information, together with effective perioperative communication, remains a major challenge in pancreatic cancer care. In routine practice, unstructured computed tomography (CT) reports and complex clinical information may limit the accessibility and consistency of clinical information delivery and increase the communication burden on clinicians. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for clinical information support; however, existing applications are often task-specific and rarely combine CT report interpretation with perioperative consultation within a unified patient-oriented framework. Objective This study aimed to develop and retrospectively evaluate PancreaGuide, a knowledge-augmented LLM agent designed to support clinician-supervised CT report-based interpretation of pancreatic cancer resectability-related information and standardized perioperative consultation. Methods We developed PancreaGuide, an agent-based framework integrating structured prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and a domain-specific pancreatic surgery knowledge base to support clinical information interpretation and perioperative consultation. A retrospective cohort of 444 patients who underwent contrast-enhanced CT at West China Hospital between 2023 and 2025 was analyzed. Three LLMs, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Gemini, were evaluated in both base and PancreaGuide-integrated configurations. CT report-based interpretation of resectability-related information was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, F 1 -score, receiver operating characteristic curves (ROCs), and decision curve analysis (DCA) using a surgery-based proxy reference. Perioperative consultation quality was evaluated across 5 dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, safety, and robustness. Results Higher classification metric point estimates were observed after integration of the PancreaGuide framework across all 3 backbone models. In CT report-based interpretation of resectability-related information, Gemini+ achieved the highest accuracy of 87.4% (95% CI 0.840‐0.902) and a sensitivity of 95.9% (95% CI 0.927‐0.978). All models showed improved sensitivity and specificity estimates after PancreaGuide integration, with improved agreement between model-generated interpretations and observed surgical management status. ROC and DCA suggested improved discrimination and estimated net benefit using the surgery-based proxy reference. In perioperative consultation, PancreaGuide-integrated models received higher expert-rated scores than their corresponding base models across all 5 evaluation dimensions. Gemini+ achieved the highest overall score (mean 3.88, SD 0.38), followed by ChatGPT+ (mean 3.8, SD 10.36) and DeepSeek+ (mean 3.75, SD 0.35). The greatest improvements were observed in completeness and robustness, with consistent gains across clinical consultation domains. Conclusions PancreaGuide provides a unified, knowledge-augmented framework for clinician-supervised CT report-based interpretation of resectability-related information and perioperative information support across multiple LLM backbones. The CT-based findings should be interpreted as agreement with observed surgical management status rather than validation against an independently adjudicated anatomical resectability. PancreaGuide may serve as an auxiliary information interpretation framework to improve the accessibility and consistency of clinical information delivery, while it should not replace formal radiological assessment, multidisciplinary evaluation, or clinician judgment.

candidates.title: SSL-R1: Self-Supervised Visual Reinforcement Post-Training for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has demonstrated the great potential of enhancing the reasoning abilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, the reliance on language-centric priors and expensive manual annotations prevents MLLMs' intrinsic visual understanding and scalable reward designs. In this work, we introduce SSL-R1, a generic self-supervised RL framework that derives verifiable rewards directly from images. To this end, we revisit self-supervised learning (SSL) in visual domains and reformulate widely-used SSL tasks into a set of verifiable visual puzzles for RL post-training, requiring neither human nor external model supervision. Training MLLMs on these tasks substantially improves their performance on multimodal understanding and reasoning benchmarks, highlighting the potential of leveraging vision-centric self-supervised tasks for MLLM post-training. We think this work will provide useful experience in devising effective self-supervised verifiable rewards to enable RL at scale. Project page: https://github.com/Jiahao000/SSL-R1.

candidates.title: RAP: Relation-Aware Post-training for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance on diverse multimodal tasks, yet current post-training methods remain largely answer-centric and do not directly optimize behavioral reliability. In practice, a trustworthy MLLM should remain consistent when the same evidence is presented in different forms, become cautious when critical evidence is missing, and explicitly recognize contradictions when different evidence sources conflict. To address this gap, we propose RAP (Relation-Aware Post-training), a simple and unified framework that post-trains MLLMs via behavior alignment over transformed evidence views. RAP organizes training data into relation pairs that encode four fundamental evidence relations: equivalence, irrelevant perturbation, causal deletion, and evidence conflict. The model is trained to produce a structured output consisting of an answer, supporting evidence, and a decision mode, and is then optimized with a single relation-aware objective that enforces the desired behavior across paired views. RAP is model-agnostic, lightweight, and reframes multimodal post-training from answer optimization to relation-aware behavior alignment, providing a practical direction for building MLLMs that are more grounded and more reliable under evidence variation, incompleteness, and conflict.

candidates.title: OP-CL: On-Policy Guided Continual Post-training for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Continual post-training is essential for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving tasks, but it often leads to catastrophic forgetting. The core challenge is to achieve rapid adaptation to new task formats and semantics while preventing policy drift from accumulating into forgetting during sequential training. Existing paradigms address this trade-off only partially: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) enables rapid adaptation but often disrupts prior knowledge, whereas Reinforcement Learning (RL) better preserves existing capabilities through on-policy updates but typically converges slowly and struggles on open-ended tasks. We propose OP-CL, a two-stage on-policy guided framework for continual post-training in MLLMs. In Stage 1, On-Policy Corrective Supervision transforms model rollouts into corrective supervision, providing efficient learning signals for acquiring new-task behaviors, especially on open-ended tasks. Since such rapid adaptation may still introduce policy deviation, Stage 2, Reward-KL Stabilized Reinforcement further stabilizes continual adaptation by adaptively regulating KL regularization to limit excessive policy updates. The two stages therefore address two complementary requirements of continual post-training: efficient acquisition and stable retention. Experiments show that OP-CL consistently achieves a better balance between new task adaptation and old task retention than representative SFT- and RL-based baselines.

candidates.title: Large language model agents in watershed environmental response: a hypothesis-and-theory framework for the cognitive orchestration layer
candidates.abstract: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.

candidates.title: Beyond Model Choice: A Harness-Centered Framework for Designing Clinical Large Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Clinical large language model agents depend on both model capability and the surrounding system that selects information, constrains actions, and verifies execution. In this Viewpoint, we argue that this harness should be an explicit unit of clinical agent design, evaluation, and reporting. Our aim is to help clinical informatics and development teams specify this layer and to help evaluators and institutional governance teams assess its contributions and risks. Selected benchmarks show substantial performance differences across harness configurations, but architecture comparisons, bundled improvements, and within-model component comparisons support different levels of causal attribution. We propose a revisable 3-tier framework: tier 1 specifies general orchestration functions, including prompts, tools, output schemas, control flow, memory, and generic verification; tier 2 specifies their clinical adaptations for knowledge integration, differential reasoning, missingness and temporality, safety verification, and workflow alignment; and tier 3 specifies a failure-driven evaluation cycle applied to both. Our contribution is a framework that makes these connections explicit. We provide classification rules, an illustrative clinical example, a proposed evaluation protocol, and a minimum reporting checklist. Observable execution traces are distinguished from private model reasoning, with provenance and privacy safeguards supporting retrospective reconstruction. Evaluation should separate task success, clinical correctness, process safety, and operational reliability. Lightweight fine-tuning can complement harness design; their interaction requires controlled study. The framework is a proposal for empirical testing, not a validated taxonomy or evidence of deployment safety.

candidates.title: Learning to remember: advances in memory mechanisms for large language models
candidates.abstract: Memory has become a central mechanism for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond fixed context windows, stateless interaction, and static parametric knowledge. This survey organizes the literature around three complementary dimensions: the life cycle of memory, the storage substrate, and the system role that memory plays in LLM-based agents, while using cognitive-science-inspired memory concepts as a lightweight conceptual motivation rather than as a separate technical contribution or implementation family. On this basis, we distinguish three mechanism families: nonparametric memory, where information is stored outside model parameters in text, graph, multimodal, or database-like structures; parametric memory, where information is stored or accessed through activations, key-value caches, learned modules, adapter-based parameterizations, or model weights; and memory for agent evolution, where stored experiences support reinforcement learning, continual learning, procedural reuse, context engineering, and agent harness design. Evaluation is treated as a separate cross-cutting component rather than as a memory mechanism. Unlike surveys that focus primarily on retrieval-augmented generation or long-context modeling, this paper emphasizes the full memory life cycle: construction, maintenance, retrieval, consolidation, forgetting, governance, and evaluation. By aligning conceptual motivations, computational memory mechanisms, benchmarks, and deployment concerns, the survey provides a structured roadmap for designing memory-augmented LLM agents that are persistent, adaptive, auditable, and safe to update over time.

candidates.title: HINT-RAG: Hypothesis-Contrastive Differentiable Retrieval Augmented Generation for Medical Image Report Generation
candidates.abstract: Translating medical images into accurate natural language descriptions is a critical challenge in cross-modal understanding. However, existing RAG-based methods typically retrieve references according to visual similarity, where visually similar images may correspond to different clinical findings and report semantics. Visually matched but semantically mismatched samples can introduce misleading multimodal evidence, thereby reducing the accuracy of generated reports. To address this challenge, we propose a hypothesis-contrastive differentiable retrieval augmented generation (HINT-RAG) framework, a perceive-query-disambiguate cross-modal learning paradigm for ambiguity-aware medical report generation. Specifically, the perceive module formulates uncertainty-aware hypotheses to capture plausible clinical semantics from the input image. The query module leverages these hypotheses to perform contrastive differentiable retrieval, aiming to identify discriminative evidence from clinically confusable candidates rather than merely visually similar samples. The disambiguate module adaptively fuses visual features and retrieved evidence to resolve cross-modal ambiguity before report decoding. Extensive experiments on public datasets show that HINT-RAG achieves leading performance in both natural language generation and clinical efficacy metrics.

candidates.title: DeRAG-Oracle: A Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation Architecture for On-Chain Risk Telemetry
candidates.abstract: Smart contracts on the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) cannot natively access unstructured enterprise data due to prohibitive on-chain storage costs and the lack of native text-parsing capabilities. Existing oracles remain bottlenecked by their reliance on strictly deterministic, structured data feeds. We propose DeRAG, a decentralized oracle architecture combining BNB Greenfield object storage, a FastAPI middleware powered by the Google Gemini Large Language Model (LLM), and Chainlink's Custom Runtime Environment (CRE). DeRAG distills complex, unstructured enterprise data into ultra-compact structured payloads that provide a deterministic representation of the probabilistic underlying inference, which can then be securely pushed to on-chain smart contracts. Evaluated over N=30 iterations, the architecture achieved a 100.0% execution success rate with a mean execution latency of 6.882 seconds, reducing raw enterprise data into average payloads of 369.43 bytes. By shifting heavy computation and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) off-chain, we demonstrate a robust bridge between enterprise data and Web3, enabling stable intelligence delivery designed to minimize on-chain data footprint.

candidates.title: An Empirical Study of Reasoning Degradation in Quantized Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities on complex tasks through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, yet at the cost of substantially increased inference overhead. While post-training quantization (PTQ) has emerged as a prevalent approach for reducing deployment costs, its impact on the reasoning capability of MLLMs remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a comprehensive empirical study on the reasoning capability of quantized MLLMs. Employing two representative weight-only quantization methods, AWQ and GPTQ, we systematically evaluate 10 models spanning the Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL, and InternVL3 families across 20 multimodal benchmarks, and analyze the performance-efficiency trade-offs introduced by quantization. We find that quantization incurs significantly greater degradation on multimodal reasoning tasks than on perception tasks, with the disparity becoming especially pronounced in long-chain reasoning scenarios. Mechanistic analysis attributes this degradation primarily to error accumulation during long-sequence decoding, reasoning trajectory drift, and systematic shifts in output patterns. Despite these adverse effects, quantization still yields substantial end-to-end speedups in reasoning-heavy, long-output scenarios. Finally, we empirically analyze two training-free factors that influence quantization performance, namely calibration set design and selective layer preservation, and discuss their implications for future multimodal quantization research.
