candidates.title: Predictive Retrieval Preparation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Anticipating Future Knowledge Needs and Precomputing Reusable Retrieval Resources
candidates.abstract: The increasing adoption of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has established external knowledge retrieval as an important component of modern large language model (LLM) systems. By combining parametric language generation with non-parametric external knowledge, RAG enables generative AI systems to access information that may be unavailable in model parameters or may require frequent updating. Nevertheless, conventional RAG architectures remain predominantly reactive: document retrieval, query processing, relevance ranking, and contextual preparation are generally initiated after a user request arrives. Although existing optimization techniques have improved retrieval efficiency through vector indexing, embedding reuse, caching, approximate nearest-neighbor search, and retrieval pipeline optimization, they do not necessarily address whether the knowledge resources required by future requests can be anticipated and prepared before those requests materialize. This paper introduces Predictive Retrieval Preparation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (PRP-RAG), a conceptual framework that investigates whether future knowledge requirements can be predicted from historical user interests, ongoing research activities, emerging information trends, document relationships, and temporal behavioral signals. Rather than pre-generating complete answers, PRP-RAG focuses on preparing the knowledge and retrieval resources that future RAG requests are likely to require. Its architecture integrates predictive knowledge-demand modeling, future information requirement generation, proactive document acquisition, document parsing and segmentation, embedding precomputation, retrieval index preparation, candidate knowledge organization, and adaptive retrieval execution. A central component is a knowledge-resource reuse mechanism that distinguishes reusable underlying knowledge assets from query-dependent retrieval decisions. This distinction enables potentially valuable document representations, embeddings, metadata, and indexed knowledge resources to remain useful even when the initially predicted question does not occur. The framework further investigates cost-aware preparation scheduling, including the possibility of performing document processing and embedding computation during periods of relatively low GPU utilization, favorable electricity prices, or lower-cost cloud GPU availability. A unified optimization formulation is developed to evaluate the expected benefits of predictive knowledge preparation while accounting for prediction uncertainty, document acquisition, parsing, embedding computation, index construction, storage, maintenance, information freshness, and subsequent resource reuse. The paper establishes an experimental methodology for evaluating retrieval latency, knowledge preparation expenditure, retrieval quality, resource reuse, prediction accuracy, and total system cost. Particular attention is given to prediction-error-tolerant knowledge reuse, where prepared knowledge resources may provide value across multiple future requests rather than only the specific questions initially predicted. The proposed framework does not assume that proactive preparation is universally beneficial; its effectiveness depends on the predictability of future knowledge demand, the reusability of prepared resources, preparation expenditure, document freshness, and retrieval compatibility. By shifting the focus from predicting future answers to anticipating and preparing future knowledge requirements, PRP-RAG investigates a complementary direction for improving the computational efficiency and responsiveness of retrieval-augmented generative AI systems.

candidates.title: Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching
candidates.abstract: Traditional similarity-based schema matching methods fail to resolve semantic ambiguities and conflicts in complex, domain-specific mappings due to a lack of commonsense and domain-specific knowledge. In parallel, large language models (LLMs) without sufficient background knowledge tend to hallucinate, further complicating schema matching. To overcome these limitations, we introduce KG-RAG4SM, a Knowledge Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Schema Matching. This method integrates novel retrieval mechanisms, including LLM-based, vector-based, graph traversal-based, and hybrid techniques with advanced reranking schemes to extract the most relevant subgraphs from large external KGs. Our approach achieves superior results without requiring re-training, as evidenced by improvements of 39.79% in precision and 30.56% in F1 score over LLM-based state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods (e.g., Jellyfish-8B) on the MIMIC dataset, and enhancements of 69.20% in precision and 21.99% in F1 score over pre-trained language model (PLM)-based SOTA methods (e.g., SMAT) on the Synthea dataset. Additionally, KG-RAG4SM scales effectively across KGs from commonsense KGs to domain-specific ones, while its instruction-tuning knowledge exclusion component ensures truthful performance in end-to-end schema matching tasks despite the suboptimal relevance of KG context. Our empirical analysis and case studies from real-world scenarios show that the hallucination problem in LLMs for schema matching is well mitigated by our solution.

candidates.title: BRAT: Bounded Residual-Aligned Training for Stable Multi-Pass LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language model post-training often reuses each batch of sampled rollouts for several gradient passes to amortize the cost of generation. Under such multi-pass reuse, existing objectives fail in different ways: unclipped updates collapse as the policy drifts away from the sampling policy, adding a negative baseline avoids collapse but reinforces every sampled response, and PPO-style ratio clipping cuts off gradients abruptly. We first ask why reuse is fragile. Measuring how well an update estimated from a small rollout group aligns with the KL-regularized target on held-out rollouts of the same prompts, we find that this alignment drops by nearly an order of magnitude from in-sample to held-out rollouts across three base models, suggesting that repeated passes largely overfit the sampled group. Motivated by this finding, we propose Bounded Residual-Aligned Training (BRAT), motivated by a proximal update toward a bounded reweighting of the sampling policy. BRAT assigns each token a gradient weight that decreases linearly with its probability ratio and vanishes at a trust-region boundary, and normalizes group-centered rewards by their maximum magnitude, keeping advantages zero-mean and bounded without extra hyperparameters. With four reuse passes, BRAT avoids training collapse, limits policy drift, and achieves higher average accuracy with lower seed variance on most benchmarks.

candidates.title: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
candidates.abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

candidates.title: Two-Sided Conformal Evidence Sets for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface passages that support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it, yet existing calibrated grounding methods are typically one-sided and model only supporting evidence. We introduce Conformal Evidence Sets (CES), a two-sided framework that returns separate support and refutation sets with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least $1-α$ on each side under exchangeability; a Bonferroni union yields joint coverage of at least $1-2α$. On labeled candidate pools from the contrastive VitaminC benchmark, CES closely tracks nominal coverage across $α\!\in\!\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\}$, with maximum deviations of $3.0$ percentage points for support and $5.4$ for refutation, and reaches essentially the same empirical coverage--size frontier as a test-tuned fixed-threshold heuristic without any test exposure. Stress tests mark the boundary of that guarantee: under FEVER distribution shift both sides under-cover, by up to $12.7$ percentage points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap. Scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer, and a live end-to-end pilot expose a clear separation: when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, evidence inclusion remains calibrated even with an imperfect scorer, whereas the support/refute verdict tracks scorer quality directly. Calibrated evidence coverage and reliable verdicts are therefore distinct properties and should be reported separately.

candidates.title: Global Context Guidance for Diffusion Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Diffusion large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, enabling parallel generation through iterative denoising. Recent guidance methods improve diffusion LLMs by introducing a weak model to guide the prediction of the base model during denoising. However, the influence of the weak model during denoising remains less clear, and computing its prediction requires an additional forward pass at each denoising step. We present in this paper an in-depth analysis of how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising. Our analysis reveals that diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context while often underutilizing global context. Based on this observation, we introduce Global Context Guidance (GCG), a feature-space guidance method that enhances global-context utilization without constructing an explicit weak model. Extensive experiments on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods, while incurring much lower inference overhead.

candidates.title: Enhancing Mathematical Reasoning in Turkish Large Language Models with Search-Based Inference and Model Merging
candidates.abstract: We improve Turkish mathematical reasoning in Large Language Models by combining LoRA fine-tuning, weight-space model merging, and search-based inference. Using Turkish-Llama 8B-DPO with Turkish translations of MetaMath, NuminaMath, and TigerLab, we find data quality beats scale (Mix-30k best among fine-tuned; large MetaMath underperforms). Linear merging delivers the largest gains (GSM8K up to 0.63), while Ties is modest and Breadcrumbs/Slerp degrade. Search with MCTS and Tree of Thoughts improves mean LLM-judge scores for reasoning quality on a 0-100 scale. Limitations include machine translation, limited scale, and search stochasticity.

candidates.title: Benchmarking Membership Privacy Risks in Preference-Based LLM Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Modern language models are commonly adapted after pretraining to follow instructions, align with user preferences, and improve deployment behavior. Such post-training often relies on preference data from users, annotators, or model interactions, which may contain sensitive prompts, private responses, proprietary tasks, or confidential judgments. Understanding the privacy implications of this data is therefore essential. Membership inference attacks (MIAs), which test whether a record was used for training, are the de facto standard for empirical privacy auditing in machine learning. However, preference-based post-training changes the unit of membership: a training record contains a prompt, a preferred response, and a dispreferred response, rather than a single input-output sequence. Audits that ignore this structure can under-report leakage. We therefore introduce a benchmark protocol that adapts strong reference-model MIAs to complete preference records. Our protocol asks whether membership is exposed by either response alone, by the model’s preference between them, or by the two responses jointly. We find that auditing the response pair can reveal membership evidence missed when the record is reduced to a single score. Across three preference datasets, two model families, and seven post-training objectives spanning three post-training families, measured leakage depends strongly on both the audited record statistic and the training objective, with imbalanced risk between preferred and dispreferred responses. We further evaluate the impact of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and differential privacy (DP), finding widely varying privacy-utility trade-offs. Overall, preference-based post-training leaks in ways that standard single-response audits can miss, motivating formal privacy methods that protect complete preference records while preserving post-training utility.

candidates.title: AbductionBench: Benchmarking Abductive Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Abductive reasoning is the inference of plausible explanations for observed evidence. Evaluating this capability requires more than a single task: a system may need to generate an explanation, discriminate among competing hypotheses, revise its hypotheses as evidence arrives, or decide what evidence to seek next. Yet these capabilities are typically evaluated through isolated benchmarks with different task formulations and scoring procedures, so claims that a model is ``good at abduction'' may reflect only a narrow aspect of this capability. We introduce AbductionBench, a unified framework whose taxonomy characterizes abductive tasks. We instantiate this framework on 27 datasets spanning ten domains and evaluate eight LLMs from four model families evaluated on single-choice selection tasks. Beyond harmonizing heterogeneous tasks, AbductionBench separates final-answer evaluation from analysis of the observable reasoning traces and interaction histories produced alongside those answers. We analyze written traces as observable model outputs rather than faithful representations of internal computation, characterizing evidence use, hypothesis comparison, uncertainty, contradiction handling, and answer commitment. Jev matches or exceeds small LLMs when selecting among explanations over compact evidence but falls substantially behind on longer cases, suggesting that candidate discrimination and extended evidence integration place different demands on a system. In interactive tasks, the proportion of actions judged relevant declines at later steps, and a relevant first question is associated with a correct final answer; in the passive task, models rarely revise their initial hypothesis as new evidence arrives. Together, these findings highlight the value of evaluating abductive reasoning through both final answers and observable evidence use, hypothesis revision, and information gathering.

candidates.title: Selective Cooperative Perception via Blind Spot Reasoning and Agentic Dialogue with Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.

candidates.title: Lightfoot: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Exact, Model-Free Document Deletion
candidates.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems pay costs that research comparisons rarely measure: model calls at query time, building the graph, and removing documents correctly. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Retrieval makes no language-model call, indexing makes one per passage, and deleting a document is a database transaction with no model calls: 14 seconds for 10% of an 11,402-passage corpus, after which the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. On a corpus of near-duplicate names, HippoRAG 2's capped synonym lists leave 565 fewer edges than a rebuild, while Lightfoot remains exact. Under identical extraction, embedding and answer models on held-out questions of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, Lightfoot is competitive with HippoRAG 2: with Holm-corrected paired tests it is better on MuSiQue at recall@5 and recall@10 (+4.8 and +5.5 points) and on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@10 (+3.4), and tied on HotpotQA, while HippoRAG 2 keeps a non-significant 3.0-point edge at 2WikiMultiHopQA recall@2. Seeding the walk from entities named in the question accounts for most of the 2WikiMultiHopQA gain. Answers tie on all three datasets, and the retrieval pattern holds with three larger embedders, up to Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The gain is not the reranker's: with the same cross-encoder, dense retrieval trails Lightfoot by 9.3 and 17.8 points recall@5 on the two multi-hop sets. Lightfoot also builds the cheapest index, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2; LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours for the same deletion, and fast-graphrag cannot delete.

candidates.title: Efficient LLM Adaptation with Forward-Only Passes
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference serving is undergoing rapid growth and large-scale deployment, motivating us to rethink how the inference process itself can be leveraged to enable efficient task-specific LLM adaptation. In this paper, we propose a forward-only approach for efficient LLM adaptation with forward-only passes in LLM inference serving. We exploit the angle concentration of activations induced by each singular value decomposition (SVD) component to measure its contribution-dispersed or concentrated-to the angle concentration of the hidden states. Based on this, our forward-only search then efficiently identifies the weight matrix with the highest dispersion that merits rank reduction. We then selectively remove the higher-order components and retain the lower-order components in SVD. Empirical results across diverse datasets demonstrate the competitive accuracy of our forward-only approach, while theoretical analysis shows lower peak memory and greater speedup than the gradient-based approach and greater speedup than the exhaustive search approach. The experiments further present the robustness and generalization of our forward-only approach to various LLMs with up to 57B parameters. The code is included in the supplementary material.

candidates.title: RAG-X: Systematic Diagnosis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medical Question Answering
candidates.abstract: Automated question-answering (QA) systems increasingly rely on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground large language models (LLMs) in authoritative medical knowledge, ensuring clinical accuracy and patient safety in AI applications for healthcare. Despite progress in RAG evaluation, current benchmarks focus only on simple multiple-choice QA tasks and employ metrics that poorly capture the semantic precision required for complex QA tasks. These approaches fail to diagnose whether an error stems from faulty retrieval or flawed generation, limiting developers from performing targeted improvement. To address this gap, we propose RAG-X, a diagnostic framework that evaluates the retriever and generator independently across a triad of QA tasks: information extraction, short-answer generation, and multiple-choice question answering. RAG-X introduces Context Utilization Efficiency (CUE) metrics to disaggregate system success into interpretable quadrants, isolating verified grounding from deceptive accuracy. Our experiments reveal an ''Accuracy Fallacy'', where a 14% gap separates perceived system success from evidence-based grounding. By surfacing hidden failure modes, RAG-X offers the diagnostic transparency needed for safe and verifiable clinical RAG systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/AswiniS94/RAG-X_Evaluation.

candidates.title: MINE: Entropy-coded Memory-efficient Inference for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: We present MINE (Memory-efficient INference Engine), a lossless entropy coding approach that accelerates single-stream inference of Large Language Models (LLMs), where existing lossless compression methods yield speedups only for specific data types such as BF16 and under additional assumptions. Single-stream decoding is strongly memory-bound, since every weight must be streamed from memory once per generated token and requests cannot be batched in local or low-latency deployments. At the core of MINE is dtANS-LLM, a GPU entropy coding scheme adapted from the prior dtANS to the needs of LLM inference. It exploits the non-uniform distribution of weights, which persists even after quantization, and exposes hyper-parameters that trade compression ratio against decoding cost. We auto-tune these parameters for each tensor and GPU to obtain the Pareto front between model size and decoding latency. MINE integrates into vLLM as a plugin and selects the best kernel configuration for a given memory budget. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a 2.1-bit EntQuant checkpoint, MINE achieves speedups of 2.52x and 1.48x over the fastest baseline on an RTX 4060 Ti and an RTX 5090, at effective bitrates of 2.24 and 3.43 bits per weight. MINE is available as open source.

candidates.title: A Social Choice Theory Approach Towards Quantifying Causal Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models can answer causal questions correctly while relying on shallow associations, lexical cues, or familiar answer patterns rather than the causal structure described in the prompt. This makes causal reasoning an important target for trustworthy language-model evaluation, since output accuracy alone may not reveal whether a model will generalize reliably under distribution shift or in downstream decision-support settings. We present a white-box auditing framework that uses social choice theory to quantify the role of individual attention heads in causal prediction. Our hypothesis is that, if a model engages task-relevant causal structure, then a sparse subset of attention heads should become disproportionately pivotal when the prompt requires interventional or counterfactual reasoning rather than simple association. Treating attention heads as voters in a cooperative game, we estimate each head's Banzhaf power: how often the head is pivotal in shifting the model toward the correct ``yes'' or ``no'' answer on a causal task. We apply this method to CLadder, a benchmark spanning associational, interventional, and counterfactual reasoning, using Qwen-2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. We further compare Banzhaf-based pivotality with a gradient-based functional-specialization probe that identifies heads whose representations distinguish causal task types. Across models, both approaches reveal sparse, localized attention-head subnetworks concentrated mainly in middle and late layers. However, similar mechanisms appear in both correct and incorrect generations, suggesting that the models often detect the form of causal queries without reliably executing the required causal reasoning. The Banzhaf and gradient methods highlight overlapping but distinct heads, suggesting complementary roles for representational encoding and final answer routing. By converting internal model behavior into component-level evidence about answer-generation pathways, this work contributes to AI assurance initiatives for foundation models. It supports more transparent evaluation and targeted testing of components and failure modes relevant to using LLMs inside larger AI-enabled systems.

candidates.title: Retriever as an Attack Surface: Exploring Fairness Vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have recently been shown to be vulnerable to fairness and bias manipulation, with prior attacks predominantly targeting the data layer via corpus poisoning. In this work, we expose a fundamentally different and largely unexplored attack surface: the retriever itself. Motivated by the widespread deployment of off-the-shelf neural retrievers as plug-and-play components in modular RAG pipelines, we formalize the Adversarial Fairness Attack against RAG (AFA-RAG), where an adversary manipulates only retriever parameters, leaving both the corpus and generator untouched, to systematically skew evidence exposure toward a target demographic while preserving semantic relevance and stealth. To instantiate this threat, we propose AFA-RL, a reinforcement learning framework that treats the retriever as a strategic ranking agent interacting with a RAG environment. AFA-RL learns adversarial ranking policies that subtly reshape retrieved evidence to bias downstream response generation, guided by a fairness-aware reward with strict relevance and distributional constraints. Experiments across multiple datasets and large language model backbones show that AFA-RL can cause disproportionate fairness degradation with negligible impact on standard retrieval metrics. Our results uncover a previously overlooked supply-chain vulnerability in modular RAG systems and underscore the urgent need for robustness guarantees at the retriever level.

candidates.title: Predicting Partial Answer Quality and Utility in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become a promising paradigm for multi-hop question answering, where a reasoning model iteratively issues queries to a retriever and incorporates newly retrieved context into subsequent reasoning steps. While this iterative process can improve final answer quality, current evaluations of agentic RAG largely focus on end-to-end outcomes and provide limited visibility into how a model's answer state changes during generation. In this work, we introduce an in-trajectory probing framework to study intermediate answer states in agentic RAG. Specifically, after each retrieval-reasoning iteration, we force an agentic model to stop reasoning and generate an intermediate answer based on its current state. This allows us to define two iteration-level measures: partial answer quality at each iteration, and partial utility as the change in partial answer quality across iterations. Our analysis across multi-hop QA benchmarks reveals that partial answer quality often plateaus before natural termination, with many later iterations contributing only small measurable improvements. Accordingly, we formulate two prediction tasks, partial answer quality prediction and partial utility prediction, and study trajectory-derived signals from intra-iteration, inter-iteration, and query-iteration perspectives. Experiments show that partial answer quality is more predictable than partial utility, with supervised models achieving Pearson's r above 0.43 for quality prediction. Finally, using predicted answer quality and utility for early stopping reduces average iteration count by about 11% while preserving about 98% of the final answer quality achieved by natural stopping.

candidates.title: Does Reasoning Improve Psychological Depth in Large Language Models?
candidates.abstract: Benchmark gains from reasoning-enhanced large language models encourage the assumption that these models should broadly perform better on complex generative tasks, but this remains underexplored in open-ended, creative domains shaped by nuances of reader experience. We tested this assumption through the lens of psychological depth in short stories. We compared DeepSeek-R1 vs. DeepSeek-V3, our closest available contrast for reasoning-oriented post-training, and GPT-5 vs. GPT-4o, through 60 blinded pairwise evaluations in which seven human annotators and an ensemble LLM-as-a-Judge rated prompt-matched story outputs. Human evaluations showed no universal reasoning advantage: GPT-5 was slightly preferred over GPT-4o (60.0-62.9% across two reasoning-effort settings), whereas DeepSeek-R1 fell behind DeepSeek-V3 (42.9%). Although this pattern was marked by low inter-annotator agreement (Krippendorff's $α= 0.070$), our annotation-quality checks suggested genuine evaluative subjectivity, plausibly reflecting distinct annotator decision schemes rather than annotation failure. In contrast, the LLM-as-a-Judge showed a strong pro-reasoning bias (98.3% of pairs vs. 55.2% of human votes), consistent across its five configurations and partly tracking sentence length. These findings suggest that, at the frontier, reasoning-related quality differences are small enough to be dominated by reader subjectivity, and that LLM-as-a-Judge evaluators can obscure this subjectivity in nuanced creative-generation tasks.

candidates.title: A Tutorial on Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommender Systems
candidates.abstract: Recommender systems are essential to real-world online services due to their substantial business value. Increasingly, large language models (LLMs) have been adopted for recommendation tasks, owing to their strong reasoning capabilities and their effectiveness in handling cold-start items. A large body of work has sought to adapt retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for LLM-based recommender systems by retrieving information from external databases and integrating it into the LLM's input to improve recommendation quality. Despite the rapid growth of the field, existing tutorials lack a clear taxonomy and a dedicated review of RAG methods for LLM-based recommender systems. To fill this gap, we present the first tutorial on this topic. First, we discuss the types of information used in LLM-based recommender systems, including target-user information and external databases for retrieval. Second, we present the design space of RAG for LLM-based recommender systems, outlining the key design choices at each stage of the pipeline: (1) retrieval, (2) augmentation, and (3) generation. Lastly, we introduce open questions for future research on this topic.

candidates.title: What Does Hard-Negative Fine-Tuning Teach Multimodal Large Language Models? Controlled Evidence from a Compositional Benchmark
candidates.abstract: Fine-tuning on hard negatives is a popular way to improve the compositional reasoning of vision-language models, but when accuracy goes up it is rarely clear what the model actually learned. We ask this question for multimodal large language models. We use CompHall, 2,860 forced-choice questions (spatial, attribute, counting and part-whole) with two graded hard negatives each, three model families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Idefics2), and controls that such studies often lack: gray-image evaluation, three seeds, option-order tests, control arms trained on different question types, and independent benchmarks. We find four things. First, CompHall is not a pure test of vision: part-whole questions can be answered from the text alone (66-95% without the image), and per-image accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe (r = -0.05), so we see no evidence that compositional failures drive hallucination. Second, the original fine-tuning method scored mostly image-placeholder tokens and hurt both LLaVA models. With a corrected loss, fine-tuning raises accuracy on the spatial-relation questions of CV-Bench in all three families, by +3.2, +23.1 and +6.0 points (averaged over both option orders). Control arms show that the gain needs spatial training questions, and for LLaVA-NeXT about two-thirds of it appears even on relation words that were only wrong options in training. Third, the gain is not general: on CompHall itself it is significant only for LLaVA-NeXT (+6.9 points) and not detectable for Idefics2, it reaches about 3 points at most on true/false statements, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuned on other question types learns to answer "true" too often. Fourth, both losses raise the yes-bias of LLaVA-1.5 on POPE.

candidates.title: Performance-Adaptive Instruction-Template Assignment for Clinical Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Instruction-tuning corpora are commonly constructed by pairing fixed input--output examples with static or randomly sampled instruction templates. However, for clinical reasoning, different candidate instruction templates may emphasize different learning signals, including diagnostic conclusion, evidence synthesis, and explanation structure. This paper studies instruction-template assignment as a training-time corpus-construction problem: given fixed clinical input--output examples and a pool of candidate templates, can performance feedback guide template assignment during fine-tuning? This paper presents Performance-Adaptive Instruction-Template Assignment (PAITA), a framework that uses validation feedback to assign instruction templates to fixed clinical input--output examples during fine-tuning. Unlike static assignment, which repeatedly applies one template, or random assignment, which samples templates without regard to observed performance, PAITA balances exploration of alternative templates with exploitation of templates associated with stronger validation feedback. We evaluate PAITA primarily using LLaMA-3-8B and further examine instruction-template assignment across additional model settings using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and BioMedLM-2.7B on the Clinical Reasoning task; Clinical Diagnosis and Medical QA serve as auxiliary evaluations. PAITA improves clinical reasoning conclusion accuracy over static assignment (0.397 vs. 0.372; +2.5 percentage points, p=0.001) and random template assignment (0.397 vs. 0.383; +1.4 percentage points, p=0.044), with additional gains in several reasoning-quality metrics. Auxiliary results and template-assignment analyses further suggest that performance-adaptive assignment can provide benefits beyond instruction diversity alone. These findings support instruction-template assignment as an important design variable in supervised instruction tuning of clinical LLMs.

candidates.title: LSH-KV: Efficient KV Cache Retrieval for Long-Context LLM Inference via Locality-Sensitive Hashing
candidates.abstract: As large language models increasingly support long-context inference, the computation and memory access overhead of attention and KV caches have become critical bottlenecks for inference latency and system scalability. Existing approaches mitigate these costs through KV cache dropping, approximate attention, or system-level optimizations, but often incur non-trivial trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and implementation complexity. In this work, we propose LSH-KV, a coarse-to-fine KV retrieval framework for efficient long-context LLM inference. LSH-KV uses locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) as a lightweight, training-free coarse partitioning layer for similarity-preserving organization of global KV entries. Within each hash bucket, LSH-KV further uses product quantization with offline-precomputed codebooks for efficient approximate similarity estimation, followed by exact re-ranking to preserve attention accuracy. To further improve system efficiency, LSH-KV introduces a score-aware block-level cache management strategy that aligns KV movement between CPU and GPU with retrieval relevance. Experimental results on long-context benchmarks demonstrate that LSH-KV significantly reduces end-to-end inference latency while preserving generation quality, even when selective attention is performed using only a fraction of the input tokens. These results show that LSH-KV enables scalable, robust, and accurate inference under long-context settings. The code is available at https://github.com/HarryFunn/lsh-kv.

candidates.title: LEDGER: A Long-Context Benchmark of Corporate Annual Reports for Grounded Financial Retrieval and Extraction
candidates.abstract: Finance reporting is a natural proving ground for large language models, and the very-long-context capabilities of recent models across all sizes make rigorous evaluation in this domain an increasingly pressing need. Yet most public financial resources reduce the task to plain-text SEC 10-K filings paired with a handful of question--answer items. We release Ledger (Long-context Evaluation of Documents for Grounded Extraction and Retrieval), a corpus of 4, 999 digitized corporate annual reports --- full documents with figures, tables, and narrative, not just regulatory filings. Each report is labeled with 31 consolidated financial KPIs to be extracted and linked to the market's reaction at the earnings date. From this data we derive three evaluation benchmarks spanning the difficulty spectrum: a pure page-level KPI retrieval task with TREC-style relevance judgments over 118,048 questions in natural language, a conversational ''needle-in-a-haystack'' single-value lookup, and a full KPI extraction task, both from long, numerically dense reports. We additionally provide human OCR-quality annotations with inter-annotator agreement and the complete extraction, validation, and scoring toolchain. We further demonstrate the dataset's research utility with a case study linking CEO-letter rhetoric to post-publication market impact. An extension to 291 French ESEF filers (1, 153 reports with 24 KPIs) augments the corpus.

candidates.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-based Management of Continuum Resources
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/lilanpei/continuum-intent-compiler.

candidates.title: Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving
candidates.abstract: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.

candidates.title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric structure? We address this question using a cross-persona paradigm across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B-14B, base and instruct). Given responses on one psychological scale from real individuals (N = 272 Taiwanese university students), models predict responses on six other scales. At the behavioral level, larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations; amplification persists after correcting the seven-scale human correlations for measurement attenuation. We then examine whether this structure is reflected internally. Contrastive direction analysis finds geometry aligned with the human matrix in larger instruct variants, but little alignment in base variants under this assay. Across models, geometry strength is associated with behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008; partial r = 0.69 controlling for log size). To relate internal structure to output behavior, a matched activation-probing paradigm shows that probe slopes vary less than behavioral slopes (1.38-1.77 vs 0.52-1.53). A synthetic control shows that ridge probing can inflate these slopes; after subtracting a baseline based on a reliability proxy from another analysis, adjusted slopes remain associated with behavior (r = 0.88). We term the measured probe-behavior gap readout attenuation. These results establish decodability and geometric alignment under the tested assays, without showing that the measured directions mediate the cross-persona answers.

candidates.title: ROSE: Risk-Aware Orthogonal Subspace Navigation for Lifelong Knowledge Editing in Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) require continuous factual updates to stay current, yet lifelong knowledge editing remains a daunting challenge. The primary obstacle is the severe Locality Erosion and Catastrophic Forgetting, where sequential edits inevitably interfere with pre-trained capabilities and prior updates. In this paper, we propose \textbf{ROSE}, a \textbf{R}isk-aware \textbf{O}rthogonal \textbf{S}ubspace navigation framework for lifelong knowledge \textbf{E}diting. ROSE addresses forgetting by aiming to restrict parameter updates to the orthogonal complement of previously edited subspaces. Crucially, it introduces a risk-guided mechanism that utilizes a dynamically computed risk mask to safeguard specific factual parameter subspaces essential for model stability. During inference, ROSE employs a multi-granularity knowledge integration strategy, featuring prototype-anchored semantic gating and perturbation-driven subspace fusion to precisely activate edited knowledge for relevant queries while limiting interference on unrelated inputs. Comprehensive experiments on two prominent multimodal benchmarks show that ROSE is competitive with state-of-the-art approaches across five key metrics, while maintaining outstanding stability over $1,000$ sequential updates. Our code is available at https://github.com/sunlitsong/ROSE.

candidates.title: MADClean: Statistical Profiling and Multi-Agent Large Language Model Reasoning for Automatic Data Cleaning
candidates.abstract: High-quality data is essential for effective decision-making, data analytics, and training machine learning models. Numerous data cleaning tools and systems have been proposed in both academia and industry. Several recent tools utilize Large Language Models (LLMs), but most rely entirely on their unverified reasoning capabilities, struggling to effectively handle dirty datasets with heterogeneous error types. In this demo, we describe MADClean, a tabular data cleaning system that uses statistical profiling and a multi-agent architecture to achieve strong performance in several data cleaning tasks. MADClean uses dedicated LLM agents to recommend cleaning operations, generate executable source code, and iteratively verify and improve its outputs. We show that MADClean reliably handles dirty data across three real-world data cleaning scenarios, and scales to datasets with hundreds of thousands of rows in our evaluation.

candidates.title: Large Language Model as Universal Retriever in Industrial-Scale Recommender System
candidates.abstract: In real-world recommender systems, different retrieval objectives are typically addressed using task-specific datasets with carefully designed model architectures. We demonstrate that Large Language Models (LLMs) can function as universal retrievers, capable of handling multiple objectives within a generative retrieval framework. To address the model expressiveness and inference efficiency issues of generative retrieval, we propose multi-query representation and transferable discriminative mapping layers to model complex user-item relationships, and incorporate probabilistic sampling to reduce computation costs. Finally, our Universal Retrieval Model (URM) can adaptively generate a set from tens of millions of candidates based on an arbitrary given objective while keeping the latency within tens of milliseconds. Applied to industrial-scale data, URM outperforms expert models elaborately designed for different retrieval objectives in offline experiments and achieves a 3.13% revenue increase on our online advertising platform. URM also demonstrates strong performance in impression and GMV for long-tail and cold-start items.

candidates.title: High-fidelity tunnel inspection and defect quantification via enhanced 3D Gaussian splatting and multimodal large language models
candidates.abstract: Timely detection and physically scaled area estimation of tunnel surface defects are essential for structural health monitoring, yet existing automated methods often rely on scenario-specific annotations and show limited generalization in unseen environments. Traditional point clouds also lack photorealistic visual interpretability. To address these limitations, this study proposes a zero-shot tunnel inspection and 3D digitization framework driven by multi-sensor data fusion. Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) and panoramic images are first acquired to provide metric geometry and photometric information. A two-stage method coupling a multimodal large language model (MLLM) with the segment anything model (SAM) then performs zero-shot pixel-level defect segmentation, while an enhanced 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) algorithm uses LiDAR points as strict geometric priors for photorealistic reconstruction. Finally, defect areas are estimated in 3D space using local scale factors. The framework was evaluated on public datasets and a 333 m pedestrian tunnel in Wuhan. The segmentation method achieved mAP@0.50:0.95 scores of 0.5202 and 0.8956 on public leakage and spalling datasets, and achieved an mAP@0.50:0.95 of 0.4246 on held-out real-world tunnel images. The reconstruction method achieved a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 23.4825, a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.8102, and a learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) of 0.4322, outperforming the original 3DGS baseline values of 19.7724, 0.7832, and 0.5616. For regular mural reference targets, the method yielded an average relative error of 2.71% and an average absolute error of 0.165 m 2 . These results support the feasibility of the proposed framework for tunnel defect inspection, with demonstrated cross-scene transferability of the enhanced 3DGS component and physically scaled defect-area estimation under the evaluated conditions.

candidates.title: Filter-then-match: Holistic Schema Matching via Small Language Model Filtering and Large Language Model Reasoning
candidates.abstract: Schema matching (SM) is a critical step in data integration pipelines and serves as a foundation for tasks such as Table Search and Entity Matching. However, applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to SM is prohibitively expensive due to the task's inherent quadratic complexity, which hinders scalable and cost-efficient deployment. In this paper, we investigate two SM scenarios: the most common instance-based scenario where headers and their values are available, and the metadata-based scenario where only metadata is provided (e.g., due to privacy constraints). We propose Fermat, a unified framework designed to address both scenarios effectively. Fermat incorporates a Small Language Model (SLM)-based filtering strategy that significantly reduce the computational overhead of applying LLMs to SM. We also introduce a column synthesis workflow that enables a fully unsupervised solution, effectively mitigating the scarcity of ground-truth data. Additionally, we implement a specialized loss function with hard column mining to counteract the biases of the filter model on imbalanced data, ensuring improved recall of positive candidates. Finally, we conduct comprehensive reproduction and evaluation of recent schema matching methods on both metadata-based and instance-based datasets, providing insights into their generalizability across diverse scenarios.

candidates.title: Disrupting convergence in large language model generation
candidates.abstract: Efforts to reduce homogenization in large language model (LLM) outputs increasingly use prompting interventions, but these interventions often change both the information supplied to models and the instructions governing its use. We experimentally separate this behavioral guidance from a second potential source of variation: the information available during generation. Across 16,200 generations spanning three preregistered studies and two cross-model robustness replications, supplying heterogeneous external cues substantially increased semantic diversity and generally did so more reliably than explicit instructions to produce different responses. Crucially, this effect did not increase monotonically with stronger instructions to use the information. Merely presenting varied cues produced substantial diversification, whereas instructing models to disregard the same information largely eliminated the effect. When cue identities and cue-use instructions were held constant, differentiation instructions increased collective diversity relative to the other experimental conditions and increased departure from models’ default response spaces, whereas convergence instructions reduced such departure. These findings distinguish two sources of variation often conflated in prompt design: informational inputs can supply variation, while accompanying instructions can suppress their influence or further shape the resulting response distribution. Preserving diversity may therefore require designing information environments, not simply better prompts.

candidates.title: Detecting Human-Scale Built Environment Changes With Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Problem, research strategy, and findings Detecting built environment change at the human scale can help planners monitor neighborhood dynamics, target interventions, and provide evidence to support the evaluation of policies and design programs. The growing availability of time-series street-view imagery has made such change detection increasingly feasible. However, existing methods often provide only coarse indications of change rather than precise identification of what has changed and might lack the flexibility to capture diverse forms of built environment transformation, limiting their applicability in planning research and practice. In this study we addressed these limitations by examining the use of ChatGPT to detect fine-grained built environment changes in Guangzhou (China), evaluating its performance, and demonstrating its applications in planning contexts. The results show that ChatGPT identifies a broader range of changes than trained human coders, achieving higher recall (0.813–0.862) but lower precision (0.622–0.792), while demonstrating broadly comparable overall performance. We further applied the approach to identify crosswalk improvements, pedestrian facility enhancements, tree canopy expansion, and building façade renewal, with ChatGPT demonstrating relatively high performance across these applications (F1 scores: 0.810–0.851).Takeaway for practice This study shows how multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can support planning practice by leveraging time-series street-view imagery to detect fine-grained changes in the built environment. By developing and evaluating a prompt-chaining framework, this study has clarified the capabilities and limitations of MLLMs for planning applications. Importantly, planners should treat MLLM outputs as supporting evidence rather than ground truth. Category-guided open-ended prompts can reveal changes beyond predefined event classes, and prompt chaining can decompose complex tasks into transparent and adjustable steps. When applied carefully, MLLMs enable planners to identify and analyze built environment changes at a level of detail that was previously difficult to achieve at scale.

candidates.title: Cite Unseen: Measuring Citation-Channel Vulnerabilities in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Citation-grounded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems expose source URLs alongside answers, extending user trust to cited links. Prior corpus-poisoning research primarily targets answer corruption, overlooking cases where answers remain largely unchanged while citations route users to unsafe destinations. We identify this citation-channel vulnerability and introduce Citation-stage Attack Success Rate (C-ASR) to separate citation manipulation from answer degradation. Across four BEIR corpora, three retrievers, and four generators, changing only the source URL of a single injected document reaches 71% C-ASR on the most vulnerable generator at well under 1% corpus pollution. The attack persists with paraphrased or answer-derived content, while citation behavior differs sharply across generators under our fixed pipeline. These results expose a model-dependent safety surface missed by answer-centric RAG evaluation.

candidates.title: Tasks over Application Manuals: Revealing Gaps in Long-Horizon Procedural Reasoning for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on a wide range of natural language tasks, and recent benchmarks suggest that they are increasingly adept at multi-hop reasoning. However, these benchmarks are typically short-horizon, requiring only a small number of retrieval or inference steps, and provide limited evidence of reliability on real-world tasks that involve following manuals spanning hundreds of pages with complex, interdependent guidelines. In this paper, we introduce Tasks over Application Manuals (TAM), a benchmark for evaluating long-horizon procedural reasoning. We construct TAM by curating real-world tasks from two domains—ICD-10-CM clinical coding (mapping medical conditions to diagnostic codes) and U.S. federal sentencing (computing crime sentencing guideline outcomes, specifically offense levels)—with human-validated labels. Each task requires following an authoritative manual with tens of thousands of rules and executing a sequence of interdependent steps across different sections to produce an exact answer. We evaluate general-purpose prompting approaches, including retrieval-augmented generation, ReAct-style prompting, and an agent-harness baseline on GPT-5, and find that the best exact-match performance remains extremely low: 1% on ICD-10-CM coding and 15.5% on sentencing tasks. These results show that current benchmarks may overestimate LLM reasoning ability and miss a key challenge: reliably following long, rule-based procedures.

candidates.title: ADAPTIVE SPARSE ATTENTION NETWORKS FOR MILLION-TOKEN CONTEXT MODELING
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across diverse natural language pro¬cessing tasks; however, their computational and memory requirements increase quadratically with input sequence length, making million-token context modeling computationally prohibitive. This paper presents an Adaptive Sparse Attention Network (ASAN), a novel hierarchical sparse attention framework designed to efficiently pro¬cess contexts containing up to one million tokens while preserving long-range semantic dependencies. The pro¬posed architecture integrates three complementary components: (i) an adaptive token importance estimator that dynamically identifies informative tokens, (ii) a hierarchical block-sparse attention mechanism for scalable global-local interaction, and (iii) a memory-guided retrieval module that selectively recalls historical contextual represen¬tations during inference. Unlike conventional sparse attention methods employing fixed attention patterns, ASAN dynamically adjusts sparsity according to contextual relevance, thereby reducing redundant computations with¬out sacrificing contextual understanding. Experiments were conducted on long-context language understanding benchmarks including LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, InfiniteBench, and BookSum using contexts ranging from 32K to 1M tokens. The proposed framework achieves a LongBench average accuracy of 91.8%, outper¬forming Longformer (84.7%), BigBird (86.2%), and Mamba-2 (89.4%). On the Needle-in-a-Haystack benchmark, ASAN attains a retrieval accuracy of 98.6% for one-million-token sequences while maintaining only a 7.9% memory overhead compared with standard sparse transformers. Furthermore, the proposed method reduces at¬tention computation by 71.3%, decreases GPU memory consumption by 63.5%, and achieves a 2.9 inference speedup over dense attention transformers. Extensive ablation studies demonstrate that adaptive sparsity con¬tributes a 4.5% improvement in contextual reasoning accuracy, while hierarchical memory retrieval enhances long-document comprehension by 6.1%. These results indicate that ASAN provides an efficient, scalable, and robust solution for next-generation million-token language modeling, enabling practical deployment of founda¬tion models for document intelligence, legal analytics, scientific literature mining, and large-scale conversational AI.

candidates.title: SAVER: Selective and Adaptive Multi-View Routing for Visual Emotion Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Emotions elicited by visual content are formed through the interaction of multiple visual cues rather than a single visual element, and their importance varies depending on the context. This characteristic makes visual emotion analysis not merely a classification problem but a reasoning task that requires the selective integration of diverse visual cues. Existing approaches tend to represent images using a unified feature representation and fail to explicitly model the contributions of different visual cues. To capture the multifaceted nature of emotional cues, we propose SAVER, a framework for query-conditioned visual emotion reasoning. SAVER decomposes visual information into multiple view-specific representations corresponding to distinct aspects, such as facial expressions, scenes, objects, and colorfulness, enabling the explicit modeling of each cue. A semantic-aware routing mechanism dynamically selects and integrates the most relevant views by jointly considering the visual context and query semantics. This selective integration is combined with learnable soft prompts to enable structured emotion reasoning within a vision-language model. Extensive experiments on diverse emotion datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms both vision-based and VLM-based approaches. Qualitative analysis provides interpretable insights into how different visual cues contribute to emotion prediction, highlighting the effectiveness of SAVER in improving both its performance and interpretability. The code is available at https://github.com/leeyubin10/SAVER.git.

candidates.title: RAH: Recursive Agent Harnesses for Long-Context Reasoning through Delegation-as-Code
candidates.abstract: When an agent recurses over a long-context task, should the recursive unit be a bare model call or a full harness with filesystem tools, code execution, and planning? We study this question on long-context aggregation, tasks where a single instance may contain thousands of key--value pairs each requiring individual model reasoning. Coding agents reduce per-entry reasoning to regex heuristics. Recursive language models (RLMs) invoke LLMs recursively but lack tool access. We introduce the Recursive Agent Harness (RAH), in which a parent agent generates and runs an executable script that programmatically spawns full subagent harnesses in parallel for fine-grained workloads and uses structured function calls for subtasks of 1-5 entries. We call this harness recursion and study it against model recursion, recursion over bare model calls as in RLMs, on long-context aggregation. With the backbone held fixed at GPT-5 to match the published Codex and RLM baselines, RAH improves the Codex coding-agent baseline from 71.75% to 81.36% on Oolong-Synthetic (199 samples, 13 context-length buckets up to 4M tokens), a gain attributable to the harness rather than the model. With a stronger backbone, Claude Sonnet 4.5, the same design reaches 89.77%.

candidates.title: Query-Guided RoPE Modulation for Lost-in-the-Middle Mitigation in Long-Context LLMs
candidates.abstract: Long-context language models often neglect information in the middle of the input, a phenomenon known as "lost-in-the-middle". Part of this gap may stem from the long-range decay of rotary position embedding (RoPE), which weakens the positional signal between distant tokens. Existing input compression deletes low-importance tokens, and attention reweighting acts only after RoPE has weakened this signal. RoPE-level methods modify positions directly but apply the same remapping to every query. To address these limitations, we propose QGPM (Query-Guided Positional Modulation), a training-free method that reshapes RoPE positions using query relevance from the model's own attention heads. QGPM builds a broad relevance map for lower layers and a sharp one for upper layers. Low-relevance tokens advance by less than one position on fast-rotating planes, pulling relevant evidence toward the query. Slow-rotating planes keep the original layout, with every token in place. Experiments on NoLiMa and RULER with multiple context lengths show that QGPM improves over base models and strong baselines, with the largest gains on retrieval tasks, and generalizes across multiple backbones. Our code is available at https://github.com/iZHpy/QGPM.

candidates.title: Language-Model Agents Running Verified Subsurface Multiphysics Simulations: Traced Numbers and the Modeling Choices That Still Need Checks
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents can now set up and run numerical simulations from a sentence, but a reported number can be wrong in two ways: the simulator never produced it, or it came from a model that was set up badly. We built GeoAI-THM Studio, an agent harness for OpenGeoSys 6.5.8 in which the language model edits only a typed model tree through 21 tools, a configuration is computed only after its verification cases pass (27 cases; 21 within 1 % of their exact solutions, official benchmarks or consistency checks, all within 2.5 %), and an output guardrail rejects answers whose checked numbers cannot be traced to the run, the model inputs or the request. In 16 runs with gpt-6-luna and gpt-6.1-terra on eight requests in heat, groundwater flow, deformation and solute transport, every number the guardrail checks in every answer was traced in this way, and Claude Haiku 5.5, standing in for a small model during development, passed 20 of 21 test scenarios, from which the eight requests were drawn. Yet both OpenAI models answered how much a 300 W point heat source raises pore pressure wrongly, −0.507 and 0.635 MPa against 0.967 MPa from the exact solution, because both had coarsened the mesh at the source, and gpt-6-luna also around it. gpt-6.1-terra had itself found that halving the elements changed its value by 0.257 MPa and called the result mesh-sensitive, but still reported it, and the scoring script, which checks procedure and provenance, passed both answers. Recomputing every answer on the mesh of its starting example exposed the errors. A sweep of the element size at the source showed the pressure within 3 % of the exact value only when the elements there are no larger than one eighth of the distance heat has spread by the first output, and the released harness refuses coarser meshes. We propose, as a hypothesis for further tests, that each modeling choice left to the language model needs a physics-based check of this kind.

candidates.title: Reconstructing LLM Lineage Trees via Fine-Tuning Path Inference
candidates.abstract: Fine-tuned (FT) derivatives of large language models (LLMs) are now released in large numbers, yet their provenance relies on self-reports and cannot be verified. Misattributed lineage leaves a verifier unable to audit outsourced fine-tuning, confirm license compliance of derived models, or trace vulnerabilities that a parent passes to its children. All three require the direction of derivation, not merely its presence. Existing output-only methods are limited to pairwise derivation tests or undirected lineage estimation, while recovering a directed tree requires white-box access to model weights. We formalize the problem of reconstructing a directed model tree, including internal nodes, under gray-box access, where only teacher-forced log-likelihoods are observed and weights are never inspected. Fine-tuning raises the log-likelihood of the training data, and a child inherits this increase from its parent. Building on this property, we define an asymmetric per-task log-likelihood deviation between any two models as a trace of fine-tuning history, and derive from it an edge weight for each ordered pair of models. We propose TRACE-Edge, which exactly solves for the maximum spanning directed tree under these edge weights, with neither hyperparameters nor tree-structure constraints. We evaluate it on five configurations totaling 25 model trees built from three base models and seven tasks. TRACE-Edge achieves a parent-match accuracy of 0.74 when probed with the fine-tuning examples, and on average outperforms an output-similarity baseline even with held-out probes drawn from the same distribution as the training data.

candidates.title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

candidates.title: Agentic Small Language Models for Closed-Loop Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection
candidates.abstract: With the adoption of the Internet of Things (IoT) in critical infrastructures, investigating security incidents across connected devices has become challenging. Graph-based intrusion detection approaches show promising detection performance. However, an anomaly alert does not explain how the surrounding activity developed, and manually following this evidence is difficult in large provenance graphs that contain many benign events and highly connected entities. Threat hunting is a proactive methodology that searches for hidden or undetected threats and reconstructs the activity surrounding an alert. Existing language-model-based approaches mainly rely on computationally expensive Large Language Models (LLMs) and model-generated graph queries, while directly presenting a complete provenance graph exceeds the reasoning and context capacity of Small Language Models (SLMs). In this paper, we propose ProvNav-SLM, an agentic threat-hunting framework that combines a Graph Neural Network (GNN) with an SLM for provenance investigation. The framework operates through three systematic phases: Detect, where the GNN identifies anomalous entities; Investigate, where an SLM agent repeatedly selects among recorded graph-navigation actions; and Verify, where a rule-based executor retrieves the selected relationships and preserves their links to the collected logs. To support SLM reasoning, the framework transforms large graph neighborhoods into small action groups organized by direction, relation, and entity type. The main novelty of ProvNav-SLM is its ability to perform closed-loop provenance threat hunting with a local SLM while separating graph-wide anomaly detection, semantic action selection, and evidence verification across dedicated components. In an exploratory evaluation on four ProvICS campaigns, the local SLM recovered more target processes on average than the evaluated graph-based rules.

candidates.title: SKIM: Pruning Large Language Model Agents via Selective Knowledge Informed Masking
candidates.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed under structured generation, where grammar constraints enforce output format at inference time. Whereas existing compression methods target unconstrained generation, we first identify a fundamental mismatch: under structured generation, grammar constraints reduce the model's output distribution to valid tokens, and the logits matter most at the small set of positions that decide the agent's action. Motivated by this finding, we propose SKIM (Selective Knowledge-Informed Masking), the first pruning and distillation framework for LLM agents under structured generation, with both stages guided by token role. SKIM partitions token positions into context, decision, and format categories, and this partition drives two complementary axes: (1) category-aware pruning saliency scores that preserve parameters most relevant for decision positions; and (2) an on-policy distillation objective that aligns student and teacher on valid tokens, paired with category-aware feature matching. We evaluate SKIM on tool-calling benchmarks and within multi-step agent loops, across multiple model scales and sparsity levels. SKIM consistently improves accuracy over baselines, with its superiority becoming most striking in high-sparsity regimes where conventional methods struggle, demonstrating the potential of category-aware compression for deployment-time grammar-constrained agents.

candidates.title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
candidates.abstract: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. Specifically, we cast DictLLM as a four-step post-training optimization. First, we obtain shared dictionaries via singular value decomposition (SVD) of input-scaled weight matrices, amortizing rank across grouped layers; second, we sparsify the layer-specific coefficients to the target compression ratio using a dictionary-aware Hessian; and third, we refine the dictionaries given the resulting sparse coefficients. Finally, we aggressively quantize both components using factor-specific Hessian information: input covariance for the dictionaries and the dictionary-aware Hessian for the coefficients. The resulting representation reduces memory footprint by storing a single shared dictionary per layer group, along with sparse layer-specific coefficients. On language modeling and zero-shot reasoning benchmarks, DictLLM consistently outperforms existing post-training low-rank compression methods and pushes the Pareto frontier between model size and performance. DictLLM compresses the original LLaMA-7B model by 5.1x with only a 2.9-point increase in WikiText-2 perplexity, achieving a 3.6x higher compression ratio than the state-of-the-art low-rank method.

candidates.title: AMS-RAG: An Adaptive Multi-Stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework for Intelligent Product Recommendation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) strengthens Large Language Models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge during response generation. However, conventional RAG systems primarily rely on single-stage semantic retrieval, often overlooking structured user constraints such as brand, category, price, and rating preferences. This paper presents AMS-RAG (Adaptive Multi-Stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a unified framework for intelligent product recommendation. The proposed framework integrates Adaptive Query Understanding (AQU), Adaptive Metadata Filtering (AMF), Semantic Retrieval, Adaptive Diversity Re-ranking (ADR), and Adaptive Confidence Scoring (ACS) to progressively refine candidate selection before response generation. The framework was implemented using Sentence-BERT for semantic embedding, ChromaDB for vector retrieval, and FLAN-T5 for response generation. Experiments conducted on an Amazon product dataset containing 1,465 products demonstrate that AMS-RAG achieves approximately 98% search space reduction while maintaining high recommendation quality, with an average Precision and Hit Rate of 0.90. The results demonstrate that adaptive multi-stage retrieval provides an efficient and reliable approach for intelligent product recommendation.
