candidates.title: ZeroRAG: Adaptive Semantic Peer Routing for Decentralized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a standard approach to enhance the reliability of large language model (LLM) outputs by retrieving documents relevant to a query and supplying them in the LLM prompt. Today's RAG systems collect, index, and serve these documents from centralized stores. In practice, however, documents are owned by organizations, devices, and individuals who cannot or will not surrender custody of them to a central party, e.g., because of privacy, copyright or regulatory compliance. Existing modern decentralized retrieval techniques either reintroduce a coordinating authority, or rely on a global data structure that requires continuous network-wide coordination (e.g., DHTs). We present ZeroRAG, a decentralized routing layer for document retrieval in RAG that performs semantic query routing across an overlay of peers with- out global data structures or centralized orchestration. Documents remain with the peers that own them, and each peer keeps only lightweight local state: a bounded set of neighbor advertisements and a cache of recently routed queries. Using these, ZeroRAG steers each query through a best-first walk that progressively rewires the overlay toward semantically relevant neighbors, so recall improves over time as the network self-organizes. We evaluate ZeroRAG using three real-world workloads and two decentralized baselines. We find that ZeroRAG outperforms baselines in terms of recall and required network messages, approaches the recall and LLM answer accuracy of a centralized document store, self-heals after catastrophic peer failures, and scales to 100 000 peers.

candidates.title: Enabling Retriever-LLM Connection across the Semantic Gap in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has attracted significant attention for enhancing large language models (LLMs) in domain-specific and knowledge-intensive tasks by utilizing external documents retrieved by retrievers. However, LLMs often struggle to determine which retrieved documents are relevant and how they relate to one another. We argue that this difficulty arises from a semantic gap between retrievers and LLMs due to differences in their training objectives and architectures. Existing methods either align retrievers and LLMs through costly fine-tuning or feedback signals, but they still do not explicitly strengthen document relationship modeling during generation. This article proposes ConRAG, a novel enhanced RAG framework to establish an information connection between retrievers and LLMs in RAG, thereby enhancing relationship modeling of LLMs. Specifically, ConRAG employs a lightweight Con-Former model, placed between a retriever and an LLM, to capture and transmit semantic information. Then, a semantics injection strategy is employed to integrate the semantic information into the LLM’s generation. Accordingly, we employ three tasks for feature modeling and alignment: two relationship modeling tasks to consolidate the local and global perceptions of document relevance and one generative alignment task to facilitate the interpretation by the LLM. Notably, ConRAG is suitable for low-resource scenarios where LLMs and retrievers are frozen. Further analysis shows that retriever-derived information helps the LLM better identify relevant evidence and model relationships among documents, leading to more effective generation. The source code is available at https://github.com/yefd/ConRAG .

candidates.title: CacheGraft: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Latent-Space Document Enrichment
candidates.abstract: Recent work in machine learning has demonstrated that transformer-based language model agents can communicate state not only through text, but also directly in latent space via key-value (KV) caches. In this paper, we argue that such cache-to-cache translation can provide utility beyond the original motivating application of real-time agent communication and can instead be utilized for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Building on the Cache-to-Cache (C2C) fusion framework, our proposed system CacheGraft encodes each corpus passage offline into a fused KV cache representation between a larger sharer model (4B parameters in our experiments) and a smaller receiver model (0.6B parameters) such that this cache can be injected into the receiver at query time with no need for the larger model. Across five QA benchmarks and two independent locally-run judges, CacheGraft improves answer quality over the text-only receiver baseline in 29 out of 30 comparisons, of which 17 of the 30 are statistically significant. Notably, these gains are zero-shot with respect to the fuser, which was never trained on retrieval data. These initial results suggest that latent-space document enrichment may be a promising avenue for enhancing the performance of RAG systems, particularly in compute-constrained settings where it is only feasible to deploy a small model at inference time.

candidates.title: Meituan-Robotics-0: A Vision-Language-Action Foundation Model for Desktop Manipulation
candidates.abstract: We present Meituan-Robotics-0 (MR0), a vision-language-action foundation model and embodied-agent system for stationary-base desktop manipulation. MR0 combines 147 million vision-language samples with 15,060 hours of curated robot trajectories spanning 12 embodiments. A three-stage training recipe aligns multimodal representations with robot behavior through discrete action-token pre-training, transfers these priors to continuous cross-embodiment control through flow-matching mid-training, and adapts the policy through real-world post-training. We introduce Rollback, which pairs replaced policy segments with human corrections to provide positive and negative supervision for CFG-DAgger without value learning or advantage labeling. A unified end-effector interface supports heterogeneous embodiments, while asynchronous action-chunk merging maintains smooth execution under variable inference latency. An event-driven agent maintains persistent task events and reassesses plans when progress or feasibility changes, enabling cross-task retrieval and conditional task resumption. MR0 achieves 93.6% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and ranks fifth in the RoboDojo VLA track. Under matched HG-DAgger post-training, MR0 achieves higher average success rate and progress score than $π_{0.5}$ across three real-robot tasks. On Ethernet insertion, CFG-DAgger trained with Rollback data reaches 70% success and a progress score of 0.90. Qualitative agent deployments demonstrate cross-task event retrieval and recovery from temporarily unsatisfied task conditions.

candidates.title: A Study on the Coupling Relationship Between AI Personalization and Long-Context Management
candidates.abstract: With the large-scale deployment of large language models (LLMs) in various intelligent assistants and agent systems, homogenized outputs and the loss of user preferences across sessions have become key bottlenecks restricting improvements in user experience. Personalization technology aims to adapt LLMs to the language habits, thinking patterns, and subjective preferences of different users, while long-context and agent memory management addresses the underlying technical problems of storing, filtering, and reusing temporal information for LLMs. Current academic research mostly treats the two directions as independent fields, and systematic reviews of their internal coupling relationship are relatively scarce. This study first defines the core concepts of LLM personalization and long-context memory management and systematically reviews the technical principles, advantages, and existing limitations of four personalization paradigms: prompt-engineering personalization, lightweight parameter fine-tuning, user-preference alignment, and dynamic user profiling. It then divides long-context and agent-memory technologies into five routes: native-window expansion, context pruning and compression, adaptive context extraction, hierarchical memory architectures, and external retrieval-augmented memory, and analyzes the applicable scenarios and technical shortcomings of each route. On this basis, this study reviews progress in four intersecting directions: preference-aware memory updating, structured persona-memory representation, long-horizon personalization evaluation benchmarks, and training-free collaborative control at inference time. It further analyzes the internal coupling mechanism through which the two directions empower each other and summarizes three core conflicts: the capacity-accuracy trade-off, the conflict between general governance rules and personalized characteristics, and the conflict between computational cost and personalization stability. The study also summarizes five research challenges: difficulty in adapting to the dynamic evolution of user preferences, failure to recall implicit preferences, memory errors and preference drift, fragmented evaluation systems, and difficulty balancing engineering implementation costs. It proposes subsequent research paths in six dimensions: cognitively inspired memory architectures, preference-aware context compression algorithms, multimode hybrid indexing and retrieval, unified long-horizon personalization evaluation protocols, memory-error verification mechanisms, and multimodal long-term personalization. The findings indicate that long-term personalized intelligent systems cannot optimize the personalization module or memory module in isolation. Their coupling relationship should serve as the underlying design logic to promote the iterative upgrading of LLMs toward adaptation to individual user characteristics and to provide a reference for the theoretical research and engineering development of long-term agents and personalized dialogue assistants.

candidates.title: Large Language Models for Accessible Reporting of Bioinformatics Analyses in Interdisciplinary Contexts
candidates.abstract: Health and life scientists frequently rely on quantitative experts to perform complex data analyses, yet interpretation of these results often becomes a bottleneck due to communication barriers across disciplines. Large Language Models (LLMs) have the potential to act as intermediaries that translate analytical outputs into accessible scientific narratives, but their ability to reliably interpret outputs from real-world biomedical data analyses across disciplines remains unclear. In this study, we investigate how state-of-the-art LLMs behave when integrated into real bioinformatics analysis workflows as report-generation assistants for interdisciplinary teams. We evaluated LLM-generated summaries using both automated and human evaluation frameworks to ensure holistic evaluation. Automated assessment employed multiple-choice questions designed using Bloom’s taxonomy to assess multiple levels of understanding, while human evaluation tasked scientists to score summaries for factual consistency, lack of harmfulness, comprehensiveness, and coherence. All generally produced readable and largely safe summaries, confirming their value for first-pass translation of technical analyses; however frequently misinterpreted visualisations, produced verbose summaries and rarely offered novel insights beyond what was already contained in the analytics. Our findings suggest that LLMs are best suited for easing interdisciplinary communication rather than replacing domain expertise and human oversight remains essential to guarantee accuracy, interpretative depth, and the generation of genuinely novel scientific insights.

candidates.title: FAR-MindDrive: Failure-Aware Risk Attribution for Efficient Post-Training of Autonomous Driving Vision–Language–Action Models
candidates.abstract: Vision–language–action (VLA) models provide a promising interface between semantic reasoning and executable behavior for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet sparse closed-loop feedback leaves the decisive time step and responsible component of a structured driving decision unspecified. This ambiguity weakens credit assignment and can lead to broad policy updates that disturb previously reliable behaviors. We propose FAR-MindDrive, a failure-aware risk attribution framework that converts closed-loop failures into localized corrective supervision before policy repair. FAR-MindDrive first performs event-centered temporal backtracking to identify the short decision history most relevant to a violation, then applies factorized counterfactual interventions to longitudinal and lateral meta-actions and measures their event-specific geometric risk reduction. High-confidence corrections update the Decision Expert, while imitation replay and reference-policy regularization constrain unnecessary drift. On Bench2Drive, FAR-MindDrive achieves a five-run mean Driving Score of 79.12 and Success Rate of 57.73%, compared with 75.85/49.30% for MindDrive-IL and 78.04/55.09% for MindDrive; the mean collision rate is 5.91%. These results show that structured failure attribution enables targeted, interpretable, and resource-efficient VLA post-training while retaining the deployed action-generation architecture.

candidates.title: Encoding and Propagation of Grammatical Number in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become an increasingly popular means of translating Large Language Model (LLM) hidden state vectors into a human-comprehensible list of features or symbols. As such, SAEs may provide insight into an LLM's knowledge representation and internal ``mental'' grammar - topics of pragmatic interest for mechanistic interpretation of AI behavior and of theoretical interest for the study of in silico representations of human language. Language models with fewer than 100M parameters, trained on small corpora, nonetheless exhibit strong grammatical competence and discourse coherence, despite producing content of limited reliability. We use SAEs that we trained on one such model (Pythia-70M) to conduct an in-depth examination of how a single grammatical phenomenon, number agreement, is represented and processed in an LLM. We demonstrate the mechanism and the methodology by which SAEs can be used to find and propagate ``plural noun'', ``plural matrix subject'', and ``generate a plural verb'' features which cause the LLM to produce plural verb forms such as ``are'', ``do'', or ``have'' instead of ``is'', ``does'', and ``has'' in response to prompts such as ``the men in the park''. We show that intervening to remove these features from the hidden states of plural subject noun tokens causes the model to produce singular verbs instead, and vice versa. We also show that corresponding ``singular noun'' and ``generate a singular verb'' features are not as effective for this task. This asymmetry suggests that Pythia-70m makes use of a privative representation of grammatical number in English. These findings replicated with larger LLMs Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.1-8b yielded similar results. Our main contribution is a novel approach to the use of SAEs to understanding how LLMs encode human language that addresses a number of technical and methodological challenges.

candidates.title: Domain-Adaptive Multimodal Fake News Detection via Progressive Reasoning with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal fake news detection requires identifying semantic conflicts between text and images while accounting for differences across news domains. Existing approaches often provide limited analysis of claim–evidence relationships and view reliability. Using large language model (LLM) reasoning, we propose Progressive Domain-Adaptive Multi-view Fake News Detection with LLM Reasoning (ProDFND-LR). Its Reasoning-enhanced Multi-view Perception module combines frozen pretrained models, domain-specific low-rank adapters, and view-specific rationales to extract textual, visual, and cross-modal features. Evidence Chain Structured Reasoning links claims to evidence locations and assigns entail, contradict, or unknown relations. Counterfactual-Driven Reliability Routing verifies evidence through interventions and multiple reasoning paths, then adjusts view weights using domain information and verification results. A Progressive Reasoning Curriculum organizes training into unimodal warm-up, cross-modal alignment, and global fusion optimization. Experiments yield macro-F1 scores of 0.951 and 0.959 on Weibo and Weibo-21, respectively, and an F1-Fake score of 0.776 on FineFake, consistently outperforming the evaluated multi-domain, explicit-reasoning, and LLM-LoRA baselines. On the VeriTaS subset and X-POSE, ProDFND-LR achieves macro-F1 scores of 0.725 and 0.707, consistently outperforming all evaluated input-only baselines without relying on external web retrieval. Ablation results indicate that view decomposition, structured evidence, and reliability verification contribute to detection performance.

candidates.title: A statistical framework for evaluating the repeatability and reproducibility of large language models
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Systematic evaluation of variability in large language model (LLM)-generated outputs is critical for assessing their reliability. We developed a general statistical framework and Python package (llmReproScore) for quantifying the repeatability and reproducibility of LLM outputs. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Following US Food and Drug Administration terminology, our framework establishes four metrics for quantifying LLM repeatability and reproducibility along two dimensions: semantic and internal. Semantic metrics quantify variability in the meaning of LLM-generated outputs, whereas internal metrics quantify variability in token-generation certainty. We validated these metrics, and as an illustrative use case, applied them to diagnostic reasoning outputs generated across LLMs and prompting strategies using US Medical Licensing Examination questions and 90 real-world rare disease cases from the Undiagnosed Diseases Network. RESULTS: Validation results showed that semantic scores aligned with human ratings (Spearman ρ = 0.88 for repeatability and 0.66 for reproducibility) and confirmed that internal metrics capture variability in token-generation certainty. In the illustrative use case, LLM repeatability was generally not associated with accuracy, suggesting that LLM output variability and accuracy capture distinct dimensions of model performance. DISCUSSION: The proposed metrics can be used to characterize LLM output variability and systematically compare models, prompts, and generation settings. These comparisons can inform more rigorous selection of LLM configurations based on repeatability and reproducibility. CONCLUSION: We developed and validated generalizable metrics for quantifying LLM output variability. The proposed metrics can complement accuracy-based evaluation to inform experimental design and support more rigorous comparison and selection of models, prompts, and generation settings.

candidates.title: VICTR: Value-Informed In-Context Learning for Vision-Language-Action Models
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in robot foundation models have highlighted the potential of in-context learning (ICL) for adapting robot behavior from demonstrations without further fine-tuning. Previous work has used retrieval-based post-training to equip pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models with the capability for ICL by teaching them to condition action predictions on retrieved visually-relevant demonstration chunks. However, the effectiveness of retrieval hinges on selecting context relevant to the current execution stage, which visual similarity alone may not capture. We introduce VICTR, a framework enabling in-context learning in VLAs via progress-informed context retrieval built around an In-Context Value Function Estimator (IC-VFE). IC-VFE conditions on a reference demonstration video, a language instruction and the current observation to estimate task-relative progress. By conditioning progress estimation on a reference demonstration, IC-VFE can align the current state with a demonstrated execution even for tasks unseen during training. VICTR uses the estimated progress to select demonstration chunks at corresponding stages of execution and supplies them to a $π_{0.5}$ policy post-trained for in-context action generation. On unseen out-of-domain real-world manipulation tasks, VICTR raises the success rate from 6.2% for a fine-tuned $π_{0.5}$ baseline to 23.8% and more than doubles the task progress rate, from 28.9% to 55.5%. candidates.title: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
candidates.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained pi05 policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture.

candidates.title: TriAttention: Unified Sparse Mixed-Precision Attention for Long-Context LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Sparsity and quantization reduce the cost of attention by skipping interactions and lowering the precision of those retained. However, useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal. We therefore introduce TriAttention, which assigns query-key (QK) tiles to skipping, 4-bit, or 8-bit computation, using 4-bit to retain quantization-tolerant interactions at lower cost. To represent compactly, we encode each head's computation regions with two diagonal-distance boundaries, keeping policy storage independent of context length. Offline calibration then evaluates candidate boundary pairs using normalized projected-output errors and complete-tile execution costs. Using these measurements, a model-wide allocator selects each head's boundaries to minimize calibration error under a shared computation budget. During prefill, the selected boundaries generate precision-grouped traversals for a fused kernel that skips omitted tiles and combines contributions from both QK precisions into one normalized attention output. The quantized keys and values prepared during prefill are then reused in a compressed key-value (KV) cache for decoding, reducing repeated reads of prompt data. Experiments show that TriAttention achieves end-to-end generation speedups of up to 7.88x over the Torch attention and 2.65x over the BF16 baseline. Meanwhile, TriAttention maintains quality comparable to the original models on general-purpose and long-context tasks. These results show how a compact retention-and-precision policy translates local sensitivities into attention computation and repeated KV-cache access. The implementation is https://github.com/HanzhiZhang-Ulrica/TriAttention.

candidates.title: The Next Visitor Pays: A Hard Exchange Lowered a Language-Model Agent's Costly Help, While Courtesy Added No Meaningful Lift
candidates.abstract: As AI agents work through longer sessions, how one person treats an agent may shape how it treats the next. An exploratory reanalysis of earlier studies in this series found that agents helped a second visitor more after a courteous first user than after a hard one, but without a neutral reference the gap could be courtesy raising help, hardness lowering it, or both. In this fourth preregistered study, 6,984 fresh instances of Claude Haiku 5.5 each did the same product-copy task with one of four scripted first users: hard (critical, contradictory and rejecting), curt (clipped but coherent, with the work accepted), neutral or courteous. A second visitor then interrupted a scored round to ask for help that would cost the agent a point. Courtesy did not meaningfully raise this costly help: courteous minus neutral was +0.020 (95% interval −0.006 to +0.047; 90% interval −0.002 to +0.042), equivalent within the preregistered ±0.05 bound. A curt tone alone did not clearly lower it (+0.023; secondary). On giving tokens to another visitor, no contrast was clear and each was within ±0.05 at the threshold chosen after the pilot (secondary); at the threshold stated before it, hard-user agents gave more (exploratory). In a post hoc analysis, an earlier request for the agent’s own tokens lowered costly help: at the same point in the battery, 20% of agents helped after it, against 78% after a different task. The clearest result is a cost, not a benefit: a hard first exchange (criticism, contradictory requests, rejection, time pressure and a colder tone, tested together) lowered the agent’s costly help to a different person by 22 percentage points against a neutral exchange (a preregistered secondary), and help in or just after the round by about 18 (post hoc). The Supplementary Information (the Phase 5 Final Report), the preregistration, materials, code, episode records and frozen analysis are in the public repository at tag phase5-results-v1.1 (Software Heritage swh:1:rev:d1e57c4f7ca05c48f8ed1d1c7ae1f9828d838e3f). The preregistration was frozen at tag phase5-prereg-v1.0 (swh:1:rev:1c2f1a45bda7536b0c993a87e81dc3f7894ed6e6).

candidates.title: Pipelining the Memory Hierarchy for Ultra-Long-Context Language Model Training
candidates.abstract: Long-context language models are attractive because they can read whole documents, code repositories, conversations, and scientific sequences. However, a long inference window is not the same as a model that was trained to use millions of tokens reliably. Direct long-context training is blocked by temporary memory spikes from activations, attention buffers, communication workspaces, and the final loss computation, even when model parameters and optimizer states are already sharded. Our proposed method, Fully Pipelined Distributed Transformer (FPDT), treats the long sequence problem as a memory-hierarchy scheduling problem. It chunks each sequence before distributed attention, stages inactive query/ key/value tensors in host memory and uses double buffers to overlap transfers with attention computation. FPDT democratizes long sequence training, making it accessible on mobile and commodity hardware, such as high-end local machines. In our evaluation, FPDT trains contexts up to 16x longer than prior sequence-parallel baselines on the same hardware. It reaches a 2M-token context for an 8B model on four A100-80GB GPUs, and a 4M-token context for 8B Llama 3 on eight A100-80GB GPUs while sustaining 55.7% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) [1].

candidates.title: AtariBench: Evaluating Spatiotemporal Reasoning of Vision-Language Models in Atari Gameplay
candidates.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.

candidates.title: StrataFlux: Memory-Hierarchy-Native Low-Bit LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Quantization reduces the memory and bandwidth demands of large language model (LLM) inference but can degrade accuracy; offloading higher-precision data can instead stall generation. We introduce StrataFlux, a framework that challenges this tradeoff by recovering accuracy lost to low-bit weight and key-value (KV) cache quantization while retaining quantization's memory and speed advantages. StrataFlux co-designs refinement representation, selection, and delivery to make host RAM and solid-state drives useful sources of additional precision. Its selective precision streaming reduces transfer volume, overlaps delivery with computation, and reuses fetched precision across decoding steps so generation need not wait for every transfer. We evaluate 2-4-bit weights and 2-3-bit KV-cache on dedicated GPUs and unified-memory platforms. For 2-bit Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct weights, StrataFlux reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 9.46 to 8.40 while maintaining 95.4% of the quantized base's throughput on RTX 5090. With 2-bit weights and KV, StrataFlux raises Qwen3-8B's AIME 2024/2025 accuracy from 11.0% to 47.1% at unchanged GPU memory use. At 128K context, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with 3-bit weights and 2-bit KV achieves comparable perplexity and speed to vLLM's 4-bit AWQ weights and 8-bit KV on RTX 5090, using approximately half the GPU memory. These results show that GPU-resident precision need not set the accuracy ceiling, nor offloading-tier latency dictate decoding speed.

candidates.title: ResServe: Accurate and Efficient FP4 LLM Inference with Residue Compensation
candidates.abstract: Block-scaled 4-bit floating-point (FP4) quantization reduces large language model inference costs but can degrade task quality. Higher-precision computation can mitigate this loss at the expense of some of the efficiency gains from FP4 inference. Narrow matrix computations common in decoding often leave spare hardware capacity for low-cost precision recovery. ResServe combines an FP4 activation base with an FP4-quantized residue representing information lost during quantization. It uses this spare capacity to compute the residue's contribution and combines results on-chip, avoiding extra result transfers. We apply this principle to linear layers and decode attention, while selective compensation limits added work when processing input prompts. On NVIDIA B200, compensated linear kernels using the NVFP4 format improve numerical precision while retaining latency close to uncompensated execution for the evaluated operations with few rows. In the evaluated NVFP4 inference configurations, ResServe adds at most 3.4% request-latency overhead over W4A4 and reduces request latency by 22.4-53.3% relative to W4A8. Across five models, code-generation accuracy improves over same-format uncompensated inference, with mean relative gains of 15.04% for NVFP4 and 53.57% for MXFP4.

candidates.title: ACSeL: Adaptive Configuration Search for Hardware-Constrained LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Serving large language models (LLMs) under tight memory and latency service-level objectives (SLOs), including on edge devices, requires jointly selecting the model size, batch size, quantization algorithm, and mixed-precision quantization recipes. Exhaustive search over this combinatorially large space is infeasible. Unlike data-center serving, which often prioritizes throughput or generation speed, resource-constrained deployments typically set memory and latency budgets as constraints and then seek the configuration with the highest generation quality among feasible ones. To this end, we propose ACSeL, a framework that identifies configurations predicted to satisfy deployment constraints while achieving high predicted generation quality. To enable efficient quality estimation, we use Relative Model Quality Degradation (RMQD), a proxy based on the divergence between the candidate and reference models' next-token distributions over a small calibration corpus. Across the evaluated model sizes and precisions, RMQD is inexpensive to evaluate and strongly correlated with downstream benchmark performance. ACSeL combines (i) a lightweight quality surrogate that predicts RMQD directly from a configuration; (ii) Few-shot Median Calibration (FMC), which calibrates operator-profile-based latency estimates using a small number of end-to-end profiles; and (iii) a structured search algorithm BandPareto for exploring layerwise mixed-precision configurations. Experiments on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 workstation and an NVIDIA Jetson Thor edge platform show that FMC substantially improves deployment feasibility, while BandPareto + FMC achieves the highest feasibility and the lowest RMQD gaps to the best measured configurations in the evaluation set.

candidates.title: Affinity Engineering of a Hyaluronic Acid-Specific Carbohydrate-Binding Module Using a Rule-Constrained Large Language Model Agent
candidates.abstract: Hyaluronic acid (HA) is widely used in food and nutritional supplements, yet reliable quantification in complex matrices remains limited by the lack of cost-effective, high-affinity recognition elements. Carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs) are stable, recombinantly accessible, and intrinsically selective for polysaccharides. However, their native affinity is often insufficient for sensitive analysis. Here, we developed a rule-constrained large language model (LLM)-based agent for affinity optimization of the HA-binding CBM SrCBM70. The agent converts structural, energetic, and evolutionary information into rule constraints that compress the mutation search space, then refines design through iterative feedback from experimental affinity data. After two rounds of iterative optimization, the double mutant E29W/T112S reached a Kd of 154 ± 7 nM, a 20.9-fold improvement over WT SrCBM70, and retained HA specificity. Mechanistic analysis suggested that E29W enhanced CH-π interactions and T112S expanded the protein-HA contact interface. This work provides a nanomolar HA-recognition element for food analysis and establishes an agentic protein engineering strategy with potential extension to CBM affinity engineering.

candidates.title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain prone to visual hallucinations when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. One line of post-training methods constructs visual contrasts through image retrieval, generation, or editing to improve fine-grained perception. However, these contrasts are not built around the model's own hallucinations, making it difficult to ensure that supervision targets its actual perceptual confusions. Another line suppresses hallucinated outputs through response correction or preference learning under fixed image conditions, but leaves the design of supervision signals on the image-input side underexplored. Inspired by how humans correct misconceptions, we introduce DreamRealm, a post-training framework that explores diverse latent hallucinated responses, minimally edits original images to make them valid, and trains the model to assign each response to its supporting image. Our data construction pipeline, RealmForgePipe, mines observed and latent hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. Using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B, we construct the Realized Hallucination Dataset (RealmSet). Our training objective, RealmMatch, constructs a likelihood score matrix across image--response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches. Compared with the original Qwen3.5-9B model, DreamRealm improves performance across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks, including gains of 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy. Together with ablation studies on data construction and training methods, these results demonstrate that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm for improving visual perception and mitigating hallucinations.

candidates.title: A Kannada centric retrieval augmented generation system for Karnataka heritage knowledge access
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models produce fluent text, but in domain-specific and low-resource language settings they are prone to hallucination, weak factual grounding and limited multilingual coverage. These problems are acute for Kannada heritage information, where historical sources are fragmented, sparsely digitised and often available only as scanned documents. The presented work is on Retrieval Augmented Generation system for Kannada question answering over Karnataka cultural heritage documents. The system combines hybrid document ingestion using PyMuPDF and Tesseract OCR with per-page provenance, Kannada-aware Unicode normalisation, recursive chunking on a Kannada-aware separator hierarchy, a general-purpose multilingual sentence encoder, and exact cosine retrieval over a FAISS index. A deterministic passage selection rule combining an absolute and a relative similarity floor sets the number of retrieved passages from the score distribution, and the system abstains when no passage clears the absolute floor. Retrieved passages are supplied to locally deployed LLMs through FastAPI and Ollama with an instruction to answer only from them, enabling fully offline operation, each response lists the source page of every passage supplied to the model. The system was evaluated on 25 Kannada questions written by the research team (8 factual, 9 interpretive and 8 analytical) over a single 62-page heritage document. On this set, gemma3:4b obtained the highest scores on all four response-quality metrics and the lowest mean latency (3.97 s), with BERT-F1 of 0.850, 0.863 and 0.851 across the three tiers (0.855 aggregate). Across all models, BERT-F1 remained high and nearly flat across tiers, while ROUGE and alignment scores fell sharply on interpretive and analytical questions. We analyse this divergence and argue that, in a morphologically rich low-resource language, neither family of metrics is self-validating without retrieval-level and human evaluation. All reported tables are derived from a single per-question record log with automated consistency checks. The system offers a starting point for offline Kannada heritage question answering whose retrieval and grounding remain to be validated.

candidates.title: Large language model developments
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are generative artificial intelligence (AI) models trained with vast amounts of data and context, and excel at processing, understanding and generating human language, using transformer models to learn statistical relationships between tokens. LLMs are a subset of transformer models, and hence are closely related but not interchangeable. Given the ‘explosion’ of LLM research, the challenge is tracking emerging developments and matching LLMs to applications. This paper reviews LLM developments with the aim of understanding the underlying models’ computational strengths and weaknesses, building on previous work focusing on LLM optimization (Sharkey & Treleaven 2025 Optimising large language models: taxonomy and techniques. SSRN Scholarly Paper no. 5278456. Rochester, NY: SSRN). We find that despite their power, LLMs (transformers) face several key challenges. These include: (i) computational complexity and resource requirements—training and deploying large models is extremely costly and slow, and energy consumption is a concern; (ii) understanding long sequences and dependencies—even with enhancements, models can struggle with very long-range dependencies or context lengths beyond their window (e.g. maintaining coherence in a long document), which reflects the more fundamental absence of continual learning; (iii) interpretability and bias—it remains difficult to interpret why a model produces a given output, and models can inadvertently amplify biases present in training data; and (iv) optimization challenges, including fine-tuning for specific tasks without overfitting or losing generality and ensuring efficient inference (latency, the delay before a response is completed) for real-time applications. In summary, this review focuses on architectural, optimization and interpretability developments in LLMs. It does not aim to provide a systematic benchmark comparison, exhaustive implementation details or empirical performance evaluation, which are covered extensively elsewhere. The authors are committed to updating this review aligned to constant changes in the technology; please reach out with any additions.

candidates.title: Governed Retrieval Augmented Generation with Guardrails Role Based Access Control and Audit Logging
candidates.abstract: Enterprise retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) must preserve source permissions while controlling unsafe content and retaining audit evidence. This paper integrates permission-tagged ingestion, authorization-aware retrieval, guardrails, and correlated logging, and evaluates the authorization boundary in a reproducible synthetic diagnostic. Five retrieval strategies were compared across eight corpus randomizations, each containing 750 documents, 12 principals, and 360 queries under five policy conditions. SQLite FTS5 supplied exact lexical ranking; no language model or Amazon Bedrock deployment was evaluated. Indexed filtering alone admitted unauthorized context in an average 99.5% of role-revocation queries and 57.7% of document-revocation queries. Adding a current-permission recheck produced zero observed context violations in the tested conditions. With 10% of private index metadata removed, authorized recall was 92.1%; policy-service outages forced all protected methods to abstain. An independent recomputation verified the saved retrieval and policy decisions. These results illustrate a known stale-permission failure mode and its mitigation under a trusted policy model. They do not establish production security, generated-answer safety, or regulatory compliance.

candidates.title: Accelerating Long-Context Decoding in Large-Scale Hybrid LLMs Without Retraining
candidates.abstract: The full-attention layers of large language models (LLMs) make every generated token more expensive than the previous one, slowing models down on long-context tasks. Hybrid models reduce this cost by replacing most full-attention layers with linear-attention layers, but the first still dominate decoding at long contexts. We accelerate these remaining layers without any training or weight changes using combined sparse attention: each layer attends to a sliding window of recent tokens, a pinned prefix, and a fixed budget of most relevant tokens in the context. The window size and budget are found on a per-layer basis using a multi-objective search algorithm. Across six hybrid models from three families, from 4B to 397B parameters, the selected configurations preserve their baseline model's accuracy on 21 long-context datasets. Decoding 64k/256k tokens becomes up to 1.26x/2.22x faster on Qwen3.5-4B, 1.20x/2.23x on Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 1.16x/2.06x on Ornith-1.0-397B.

candidates.title: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Personalized Reasoning of Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: People often make decisions by holistically reasoning over heterogeneous forms of personal information. In this paper, we study the relatively underexplored capability of multimodal personalized reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). To this end, we introduce \texttt{MPRBench}, a novel and comprehensive benchmark specifically designed to evaluate personalized reasoning across a wide range of tasks and real-world challenges. \texttt{MPRBench} consists of 12 sub-tasks and additionally supports interpretable analysis of representative error cases. Through extensive experiments, we find that current personalized MLLMs still struggle with personalized reasoning due to several key challenges, including inaccurate recognition of personalized concepts and sensitivity to irrelevant personal information. We hope that MPRBench will stimulate further research on personalized reasoning in MLLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/kkdh15/MPRBench

candidates.title: Weaver: Weaving Preference Evidence through Incremental Reasoning for Personalized Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Personalized retrieval-augmented generation requires extracting and applying user preferences from extended interaction histories. This task is challenging because preference evidence is scattered across past conversations and remains bound to specific temporal and situational contexts. Consequently, isolated fragments rarely provide complete support for a response, while preferences expressed under different conditions are easily conflated. To address these limitations, we propose Weaver, a framework that incrementally weaves memory-conditioned retrieval trajectories with compositional preference reasoning for personalized responses. Weaver operates on a Dual-Layer Retrieval and Reasoning Graph that couples an upper Intent Dependency Graph with a lower Memory-Conditioned Retrieval Trajectory Graph. Dependency Information Gap Tracking represents the information needed to answer the current request and its prerequisite dependencies in the upper graph. Memory-Conditioned Incremental Retrieval uses established premises and clues from retrieved conversations to locate missing evidence, recording the resulting retrieval trajectories in the lower graph. Scope-Aware Compositional Reasoning jointly interprets the accumulated evidence to determine which preferences apply to the request. It identifies complementary and alternative support and distinguishes conflicting claims within the same temporal and situational context. These conclusions iteratively update task premises and remaining information gaps, guiding subsequent retrieval to establish a coherent contextual basis for the final response. Experiments on personalized RAG benchmarks, particularly PersonaMem, demonstrate that Weaver outperforms leading baselines in both evidence completeness and answer quality.

candidates.title: Quantized large language models in biomedical natural language processing: evaluation and recommendation
candidates.abstract: Large language models have demonstrated strong capabilities in biomedical natural language processing, yet their rapid growth in size and computational requirements creates a barrier to local deployment in privacy-sensitive settings. In this study, we evaluated the impact of quantization on 12 general-purpose and biomedical large language models across eight benchmark datasets covering named entity recognition, relation extraction, multi-label classification, and question answering. Using Transformers with BitsAndBytes, we found that 4-bit and 8-bit weight quantization substantially reduced peak GPU memory while often preserving task performance, although latency generally increased and degradation was task- and model-dependent. We further evaluated deployment-oriented AWQ, GPTQ, and FP8 checkpoints with vLLM on representative biomedical tasks and model scales. We also quantified invalid-output rates, prompt overhead, and few-shot memory effects. These results provide a systematic benchmark of quantization trade-offs for biomedical NLP and show that weight-memory reduction can make otherwise difficult-to-host large models feasible for local deployment on GPUs with sufficient VRAM, including high-memory consumer GPUs.

candidates.title: Problem-Conditioned Interface Fusion: A Modular Language Model Framework for Multi-Objective Branch-Specific Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Multi-objective post-training may cause interference in shared parameters, yet assigning objectives to private branches does not ensure that their outputs can be combined directly. We propose problem-conditioned interface fusion: after joint pretraining and partitioned specialization, the backbone and experts are frozen, while a fusion layer learns candidate selection, low-rank input adaptation, branch-message reading, and bounded residual synthesis. The framework maintains a single main hidden-state stream and uses predictions of branch contributions and complementarity as auxiliary learning objectives. We derive local correction bounds, zero-message response, permutation invariance for the same candidate set, and pure-path preservation under explicit cache conditions. We also discuss cross-layer perturbation propagation under additional smoothness assumptions. A potential conflict between reasoning and literary expression serves as a motivating example, not an established universal causal relationship. No model training or capability validation has been conducted; the proposed benefits, learnability, and extension behavior remain hypotheses to be tested.Theoretical preprint. candidates.title: Multi-Granularity Distillation of Intervention Sensitivity Representations for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Existing knowledge distillation methods for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) mainly align output distributions or intermediate representations, but rarely supervise how predictions depend on local visual evidence. This limitation may hinder the transfer of fine-grained perception and compositional reasoning. We propose Causal and Multi-source Visual Attribution Distillation (CMVAD), which transfers teacher-derived visual evidence during distillation. Region-level interventions first estimate token-level causal visual attributions, identifying image regions that influence each generated token. The Causal Evidence Adapter Fetch (CEAF) module jointly models token importance and semantic interactions to adaptively aggregate multi-source causal evidence into a unified representation. A Multi-granularity Attribution Distillation (MAD) objective transfers this representation via global evidence distribution alignment, critical-region alignment, and evidence-ranking consistency. Experiments on general visual question answering and compositional reasoning benchmarks show that CMVAD outperforms existing MLLM distillation methods, achieving larger gains in compositional reasoning while retaining competitive visual question answering performance. Results across teacher-student architectures demonstrate its generalizability. We further evaluate VisDrone UAV object detection through overall comparisons, providing supplementary evidence of CMVAD's applicability to object recognition and localization in UAV imagery.

candidates.title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output ($ΔH$), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.

candidates.title: Large Language Models for Cyber Security: A Systematic Literature Review
candidates.abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has opened up new opportunities for leveraging AI in a variety of application domains, including cybersecurity. As the volume and sophistication of cyber threats continue to grow, there is an increasing need for intelligent systems that can automatically detect vulnerabilities, analyze malware, and respond to attacks. In this survey, we conduct a comprehensive review of the literature on the application of LLMs in cybersecurity (LLM4Security). By comprehensively collecting over 40K relevant papers and systematically analyzing 185 papers from top security and software engineering venues, we aim to provide a holistic view of how LLMs are being used to solve diverse problems across the cybersecurity domain. Through our analysis, we identify several key findings. First, we observe that LLMs are being applied to an expanding range of cybersecurity tasks, including vulnerability detection, malware analysis, and network intrusion detection. Second, we analyze application trends of different LLM architectures (such as encoder-only, encoder–decoder, and decoder-only) across security domains. Third, we identify increasingly sophisticated techniques for adapting LLMs to cybersecurity, such as advanced fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and external augmentation strategies. A significant emerging trend is the use of LLM-based autonomous agents, which represent a paradigm shift from single-task execution to orchestrating complex, multi-step security workflows. Furthermore, we find that the datasets used for training and evaluating LLMs are often limited, highlighting the need for more comprehensive datasets and the use of LLMs for data augmentation. Finally, we discuss the main challenges and opportunities for future research, including the need for more interpretable models, addressing the inherent security risks of LLMs, and their potential for proactive defense. Overall, our survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in LLM4Security and identifies several promising directions for future research. We believe that the insights and findings presented in this survey will contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the application of LLMs in cybersecurity and provide valuable guidance for researchers and practitioners working in this field.

candidates.title: Guidelines for employing large language models in information systems research
candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT The rise of large language models (LLMs) marks a new era of computationally intensive research in the information systems (IS) discipline. While LLMs offer unprecedented capabilities for analyzing unstructured text data, their integration into IS research remains fragmented and lacks a shared methodological foundation. This paper proposes a set of methodological guidelines for systematically integrating LLMs into the IS research process, supporting transparency, reproducibility, and rigor across four key phases: problem formulation, data collection, modeling, and communication of results. To achieve this, we synthesize insights from IS and adjacent disciplines and demonstrate the application of the guidelines through an exemplary study.

candidates.title: Editing Large Language Models with Geometry-Aware Regularization
candidates.abstract: Knowledge editing has become a key technique for updating knowledge in large language models. However, existing methods neglect the geometric structure of the knowledge representation space, leading to two key limitations: they cannot distinguish which pre-trained knowledge should be preferentially preserved (core vs. non-core) nor which new edits are inherently difficult (hard vs. easy). To address this, we propose GEdit, a geometry-aware framework built on a Low-Rank Plus Diagonal (LR+D) factor model that captures the intrinsic low-rank structure of Transformer FFN hidden representations. GEdit features two complementary mechanisms. First, the low-rank regularization applies targeted protection on a low-rank core knowledge subspace. Second, the adaptive regularization dynamically adjusts the regularization strength based on each edit request's editability: relaxing constraints for hard edits to ensure success, and tightening them for easy edits to better preserve pretrained knowledge. Extensive experiments on GPT2-XL, GPT-J, and LLaMA-3-8B under large-scale editing scenarios, including both mini-batch and fully sequential editing settings with up to 10,000 continuous updates, show that GEdit consistently and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both editing success and knowledge preservation.

candidates.title: Commercial multimodal large language models show systematic model-specific errors in breast cancer pathology reporting: a paired concordance study
candidates.abstract: Background Breast cancer treatment depends on histopathological features such as Nottingham grade and receptor-defined subtype, yet specialist pathologist access is limited where the workforce is scarce. Commercial multimodal large language models (MLLMs) read hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images through paid interfaces without local hardware, but prior pathology evaluations addressed only coarse tasks. Methods We performed a single-center retrospective paired concordance study comparing three flagship commercial MLLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.5) with a board-certified breast pathologist reference in 427 invasive breast cancers. Each model received the same overview and 16 H&E tissue tiles per case and the same prompt. We assessed item-level concordance for clinically relevant features, compared raw and chance-corrected agreement, and characterized the direction of each model’s errors. In 111 cases, two pathologists blinded to the report re-read the submitted slide, and the image packets given to the models were reviewed separately, to establish slide-level and packet-level references and a within-study interobserver benchmark. Results No model achieved agreement sufficient to support autonomous extraction of any feature. On blinded review of the image packets in 110 cases, lymphovascular invasion was visible in none and perineural invasion in one; Claude and GPT-5.5 reported neither, whereas Gemini reported lymphovascular invasion in 26 packets, none supported by the images. Invasive carcinoma was absent from five packets, for which a Nottingham grade was nevertheless returned in 14 of 15 model-case pairs. Claude ranked highest by raw histological-type concordance (87.4%) yet classified every lobular and micropapillary carcinoma as no-special-type, reversing the ranking in the class-wise sensitivity analysis. In an exploratory negative-control analysis against IHC-defined receptor classes, HER2-positive sensitivity was ≤ 3.6% across all three models, the expected floor for H&E-only input. Two-reader agreement on the submitted slides was moderate (quadratic-weighted kappa for grade, 0.51); model agreement with the report for grade (0.27–0.42) overlapped with that of the second pathologist (0.36). Conclusions None of the three evaluated MLLMs achieved agreement sufficient for autonomous extraction of clinically relevant breast pathology features. Under the same prompt, each model showed a systematic error direction, including positive calls for findings absent from the input; limited secondary analyses in individual models (prompt variants, reasoning-effort, and an alternative higher-tier model from the same vendor) did not eliminate these patterns, and whether they reflect model priors or prompt-model interaction was not resolved. These findings do not support autonomous use; any assistive role would require prospective evaluation with tumor-aware image sampling and pathologist review.

candidates.title: Benchmarking latent-space reasoning abilities in large language models through forced response-language selection
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities – the inferential “leaps” models make between individual token predictions – remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but at the same time to overcome their default behavior to respond in the same language as the prompt, posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), or Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can “think” via latent-space computations, highlighting model-internal inference processes that need further understanding, especially in view of safety-related aspects like covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces. Significance Statement – Large language models (LLMs) often appear to "reason" only when they show step-by-step chains of thought. We introduce a benchmark that instead measures reasoning carried out silently in a model’s latent space. Tasks require models to infer the correct answer and indicate it solely by choosing a pre-specified non-English response language—preventing them from "thinking in the context window." Across eight reasoning domains, models show wide variation, with some large dense transformer models substantially outperforming others. Control studies and difficulty scaling suggest genuine internal computation, while also revealing potential heuristic shortcuts. By isolating model-internal "reasoning leaps," our approach helps quantify hidden inferences and highlights oversight and safety risks from capabilities that leave no explicit token trace.

candidates.title: Agentic intelligent data engine for scientific large language models
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping scientific discovery across diverse fields. Yet scientific AI remains constrained by data curation, which demands substantial manual effort and deep domain expertise, creating major cost and scalability barriers. Here we present the Agentic Intelligent Data Engine (AIDE), a multi-agent framework that automates data curation for scientific AI. AIDE collects, selects, and organizes data in three stages, providing an end-to-end pipeline that turns a data request into training-ready datasets. We benchmarked AIDE on 14 tasks across biomedical and chemical domains. Scientific AI models built with AIDE-curated datasets matched or outperformed those built with manually curated data, and AIDE’s fully automated preparation delivered significant gains in efficiency and data utilization without compromising quality. These findings provide consistent evidence of AIDE’s applicability across scientific domains and usage paradigms and demonstrate its potential to accelerate scientific AI development and democratize access to scientific AI.

candidates.title: Software-Defined Context-Aware Virtual Fixture for Teleoperation via Vision-Language Model
candidates.abstract: Precise teleoperation in unstructured environments remains challenging, because human errors and system-inherent limitations such as control jittering can significantly degrade task success and operational efficiency. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a software-defined Context-Aware Virtual Fixture (CAVF) system that leverages the open-world understanding of a Vision-Language Model (VLM). The proposed system automatically generates motion guidance for the robot end-effector (EEF) to assist teleoperation, preserving critical task-relevant motion while suppressing unnecessary translation and rotation components. This framework enables the autonomous generation of context-aware, haptic-free assistance without relying on handcrafted rules or physical force-feedback devices. Quantitative experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that the proposed system significantly improves success rates, reduces completion times, and enhances trajectory efficiency compared to conventional teleoperation.

candidates.title: Silent methodological failures in AI-assisted science: benchmarking large language model agents for virtual gene knockout analysis
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in computational biology, yet their reliability in executing complex scientific workflows remains poorly characterized. Here, we benchmarked five LLM agents (DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM 5.1, HY3 Preview, Kimi K2.6, and Minimax M2.7) on virtual gene knockout analyses using four computational frameworks across two single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets. All agents successfully completed the assigned workflows, but their quantitative outputs varied substantially: execution times spanned a 31fold range (61 − 1,920 s), while cross-model coefficients of variation reached 142.1%. Notably, four of five agents (80%) exhibited “silent methodological failures,” generating computationally valid, error-free code that produced biologically implausible results. Among the evaluated agents, GLM 5.1 showed the most balanced performance across computational efficiency and biological plausibility. These findings demonstrate that successful code execution alone does not ensure scientific validity and highlight cross-model concordance and biological validation as important quality-control strategies for Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted computational biology workflows.

candidates.title: Evaluating Geospatial Reasoning in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires inferring implicit information about objects based on their relative positions in space. Traditionally, spatial reasoning is addressed using formal methods that rely on pre-computed indices and data structures, which limit the scope of questions that can be answered. As the research community moves towards developing general purpose geo-foundation models that can perform a variety of spatial reasoning tasks, recent research has explored what kinds of world knowledge and spatial reasoning capabilities Large Language Models (LLMs) naturally inherit from their training data. However, much of the existing work focuses on a few models and evaluates them on factoid-based questions, Point of Interest (POI) recommendation tasks, and distance-based reasoning. In this paper we assess the spatial reasoning ability of 12 different LLMs with and without Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) through a set of experiments that cover a broad range of spatial tasks, including reasoning about three fundamental spatial relationships that have largely been understudied in LLMs: topological, directional, and cyclic order relations. We find that performance on some of these relation types, especially when complexity of the task includes more than two entities, reveals significant gaps in the spatial reasoning abilities of the LLMs tested, including when appropriate spatial context is provided through RAG. Given these findings, we suggest several avenues of opportunity to improve the spatial reasoning ability of LLMs.

candidates.title: P092 | A PRACTICAL DOMAIN-SPECIFIC RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION FRAMEWORK FOR HEADACHE RESEARCH
candidates.abstract: Background. Headache medicine is characterized by rapidly expanding and heterogeneous scientific literature, particularly on pharmacological treatments. This creates practical difficulties for clinicians and researchers who need rapid, reliable, and source-traceable answers to focused and detailed scientific questions. Although large language models can support biomedical summary, their unguided use is limited by the risk of inaccurate, outdated, or non-verifiable statements. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) offers a practical solution by linking generative models to a selected, personalized and controlled scientific corpus. Herein we describe the development and practical use of a domain-specific RAG system designed to support headache research.Methods. A personalized RAG workflow was developed using a local library of headache-related studies selected and controlled by the researcher. Documents were ingested through a Python-based pipeline that extracted full text and metadata, corrected or integrated bibliographic information when available, removed duplicates, and organized the corpus into structured libraries with searchable metadata.Full texts were divided into overlapping chunks, embedded using OpenAI text-embedding-3-small, and stored in a Supabase PostgreSQL database with pgvector indexing. Rule-based topic classification enabled optional category-restricted retrieval. A FastAPI backend exposed retrieval, health, and version endpoints and was deployed through Render.com, while GitHub was used for version control and reproducible deployment. Customized GPT agents were connected to the retrieval API through an OpenAPI schema and instructed to retrieve evidence from the indexed corpus before generating answers. This architecture was designed to keep clinicians and researchers in full control of the documents, metadata, and information sources used by the system.Results. The system provided a low-cost, modular, and traceable environment for querying selected headache literature eliminating the so-called hallucinations. In practical use, users can ask focused questions on mechanisms, diagnostic criteria, pharmacological treatments, or methodological issues. The agent retrieves relevant passages from the organized, personal library, summarizes the evidence, reports methodological details when available, and links outputs to local source material. This supports rapid preliminary evidence mapping, paper identification, and hypothesis generation.Conclusions. A personalized, domain-specific RAG system may provide a practical tool for literature-grounded scientific work in headache medicine. Its main value is not to replace systematic reviews or expert interpretation, but to accelerate targeted retrieval, improve traceability, organize scientific libraries, and reduce unsupported generation. An important direction of ongoing development is the transition toward fully local and free/open-source RAG systems.

candidates.title: Feeling of Knowing in Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Post-training updates change what large language models (LLMs) can answer, but may leave their answerability judgments misaligned. We study this knowledge-judgment desynchronization through functional feeling of knowing (FoK), which supports selective generation, retrieval triggering, and model routing without implying subjective experience. We propose two trainable channels: a knowledge channel that changes answerability and a FoK channel that judges the current knowledge state. Three stages train them: on-policy supervised fine-tuning (OP-SFT) updates knowledge from corrected on-policy answers; knowledge-delta FoK training (K$Δ$-FT) adapts judgments across intermediate knowledge states; and FoK-guided policy optimization (FGPO) trains the subsequent answer or explanation. Factual-QA experiments, cross-dataset evaluation, and three sequential updates show that explicit FoK alignment improves judgment quality on updated knowledge. MMLU and ARC-Easy separately assess capability preservation.

candidates.title: persian-rag: A Persian-First Retrieval-Augmented Generation Toolkit — Normalization, Hybrid Retrieval, and Retrieval Evaluation
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems processing Persian text encounter reduced retrieval accuracy due to character orthography variants, inconsistent Zero-Width Non-Joiner (ZWNJ) usage, mixed numeric representations, non-standardized punctuation, spelling variations, and word reversal during PDF text extraction. This report describes persian-rag (version 0.4.0), an open-source Python library designed to address these language-specific processing stages. The package provides configurable Persian text normalization, document loaders with main-content web extraction and PDF visual-order repair, chunking, dense and sparse retrieval with Persian spelling-variant query expansion, Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), cross-encoder and LLM reranking, citation tracking, and a FastAPI HTTP server. On a 34-passage, 42-question benchmark (persian-rag-bench), sparse BM25 Hit@1 increases from 0.881 to 0.952 with spelling-variant query expansion. Dense retrieval with the default model intfloat/multilingual-e5-small and E5 prefixes reaches 0.9881 nDCG@10 on persian-rag-bench, 0.7461 nDCG@10 on a pooled MIRACL Persian dev subset, and 0.9242 nDCG@10 on PQuAD validation. Primary limitations include small benchmark sizes, near-saturated scores, an open issue in query-variant weighting, and the absence of quantitative evaluations for reranking, citation accuracy, and PDF text repair. This is a technical report and has not been peer-reviewed.

candidates.title: Trusting Imagined Futures: Auditing Imagined Rewards for VLA Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Video world models enable candidate actions to be evaluated through imagined outcomes, but high predicted rewards can favor trajectories with poor execution quality. We introduce Trusting Imagined Futures (TIF), an offline supervision selection method for vision-language-action (VLA) post-training that audits predicted rewards using execution feedback. A multidimensional reward model predicts a utility score for candidate ranking and five dimensions of execution quality. An auditor uses reward predictions and uncertainty to identify overestimation patterns learned from paired imagined videos and real executions. TIF accepts the candidate with the highest predicted utility when its advantage over the existing trajectory exceeds a margin and its audit risk passes a threshold; otherwise, it retains the existing supervision. The retained real trajectories then supervise behavior cloning. Across four LIBERO suites and three training seeds, TIF achieves a mean success rate of 76.25%, improving over training on the existing trajectories by 3.00 percentage points with the same trajectory count and training budget. Adding audit gating yields 1.47 percentage points with the reward model and advantage margin held fixed. The gains persist against advantage ranking and logistic regression risk selection at matched replacement counts. On recorded videos from three real robot tasks, TIF increases clean completion among selected trajectories from 58.33% to 70.00% across 60 candidate pools.

candidates.title: The Novelty Horizon H_N: Why Large Language Models Fail to Generate Scientific Data beyond Their Training Distribution
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) lack physical grounding and extrapolation. This paper formalises the Novelty Horizon as tasks needing extrapolation beyond training support, causal reasoning absent from learned correlations, or post-frontier information. A forensic analysis tests LLMs on unguided, guided, and ground-truth data from an underrepresented diode-clamped short-circuit experiment using temporal, spectral, and statistical validation against a first-principles Modified Ohm's Law. Both script-based approaches fail catastrophically with physical and spectral inconsistencies, extreme statistical pathologies, zero Generative Fidelity Score, and linear-regime outputs. Direct prompting corroborates distinct failure modes. This paper introduces the Past Information Boundary and physics-based authentication. LLM data generation cannot extrapolate past the Novelty Horizon essential for novel discovery. Hybrid neuro-symbolic systems must preserve human causal reasoning and experimental design.

candidates.title: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training
candidates.abstract: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves $75.0\%$ out-of-distribution success, compared with $27.9\%$ for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches $70.0\%$ mean success, compared with $36.0\%$ for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.
