candidates.title: Precision Transition Dynamics: Standardizing BF16 to U8 Containers in Sub-Block Quantization for Edge LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: Journal Description Title: Precision Transition Dynamics: Standardizing BF16 to U8 Containers in Sub-Block Quantization for Edge LLM Inference Author: Andri Johandri (Independent AI Research Team, POKDARTIK, Pemalang, Indonesia / WiTi4Bit Project) Main Topic: Post-training quantization (PTQ) and memory container standardization for efficient Large Language Models (LLMs) on resource-constrained edge hardware. Core Contributions & Highlights: Precision Transition Dynamics (PTD) Framework: The paper introduces a deterministic, bit-level sub-block quantization framework that operates without requiring external calibration data. PTD leverages canonical binary routing for exponents and structured mapping of mantissas via mirror pairs combined with a strict round-half-up mechanism to eliminate stochastic rounding noise. Hybrid U8 Safetensors Container Architecture: It proposes a 1,000,000-element threshold to safeguard architectural stability. Sensitive layers (such as layer normalization and key-value projections) are isolated in split-FP16 format, while massive weight tensors are compressed into compact QnM blocks (18 bytes per 32-element sub-block). Empirical Evaluation Results: Evaluated on the Gemma-3-1B-IT architecture, the Q4M implementation achieved a 70.8% size reduction (3.42x compression ratio), shrinking model weights from 2.00 GB to 584.8 MB. Furthermore, the model maintained high logit fidelity with an average cosine similarity of 0.9556 alongside robust text generation capabilities. Resources & Repositories: Quantized Model Repository: Hugging Face - gemma-3-1b-it-qnm-4bit Inference Runtime Toolchain: GitHub - runtime_chat

candidates.title: Personality expression and perception in large language models and humans
candidates.abstract: Growing numbers of people frequently turn to Large Language Models (LLMs) for concerns from various areas of life. Because its content has become ubiquitous, examining user perceptions of LLM-produced text and its distinguishability from human writing is crucial. This study investigated how seven LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-3.5, Llama 3, Gemma, Gemini, Phi-3, Orca-2) describe themselves when compared to humans. LLM-generated outputs and human responses were collected using psychological questionnaires (Big Five, self-esteem, narcissism) and tailored prompts to elicit short self-descriptive texts. Six LLM and ten human judges then evaluated personality traits and text origin based on these self-descriptions (140 total, half LLM-generated). Results show that current LLM outputs can convey personality-consistent cues in questionnaires and texts. The perception of such significantly differed from that of humans. Both LLM and human judges accurately inferred personality from short self-descriptions and correctly differentiated between LLM-generated and human text. Linguistic analysis and participant feedback revealed textual cues distinguishing LLM-produced from human language and offered insights into how LLM versus human judgment and decisionmaking differ.

candidates.title: Memory-Constrained Inference for Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: This technical white paper investigates the feasibility and performance constraints of running large language models on memory-constrained consumer hardware, with particular emphasis on sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, expert placement, storage bandwidth, and local code-generation workloads. Three specialized inference systems, Colibri, Flash-MoE, and Strata, are examined in terms of their approaches to distributing model weights across GPU memory, system RAM, and persistent storage. Published implementation details and performance measurements are analyzed, including the effects of expert caching, routing configurations, memory residency, and storage I/O. An analytical hardware comparison evaluates three computing configurations: an Apple M5 MacBook Pro with 16 GB unified memory, an NVIDIA RTX 3060 laptop with 6 GB VRAM and 16 GB system RAM, and a reference RTX 4060 Ti desktop with 16 GB VRAM and 32 GB system RAM. Model-memory requirements, context-length sensitivity, and accelerator-memory limitations are examined under consistent assumptions. For code-generation applications, the paper proposes evaluating inference systems using elapsed time per successfully accepted code patch rather than relying exclusively on tokens-per-second measurements. A reproducible benchmarking methodology is outlined to support future comparisons of inference performance, memory utilization, storage traffic, and coding-task success. The analysis identifies Colibri as a primary experimental candidate for larger MoE deployments on the examined NVIDIA systems, while retaining conventional inference engines such as llama.cpp and MLX LM as comparison baselines where appropriate. The work distinguishes published benchmarks, analytical estimates, and locally recorded measurements from proposed experiments. It does not claim a completed head-to-head evaluation of the three specialized inference systems.

candidates.title: Large Language Models in Fruit Science
candidates.abstract: This chapter reviews large language models (LLMs) applications and future prospects in fruit sciences. LLMs are advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models trained on extensive datasets, and are revolutionizing how fruit scientists and agriculturists interact with and analyze data. Analysis of genetic data, interpretation of climate data, and forecasting of market trends are some of the topics that are covered. These models make it easier to automate the annotation of data, improve decision support systems for precision agriculture, and reveal client preferences and market behaviors for forecasting. In addition, the ethical implications and difficulties that are linked with the deployment of LLMs are elaborated. Case studies from the real world, such as AI-powered pest monitoring and irrigation systems, are presented to illustrate the practical advantages of LLMs in terms of increasing yield, lowering resource use, and improving the overall efficiency of fruit production. LLMs will be integrated into fruit science in the future, but more research and collaboration are needed to maximize their potential in this dynamic sector.

candidates.title: Large Language Models for Forecasting of Electricity Price Spikes
candidates.abstract: Can market notices read by a large language model (LLM) improve short-horizon electricity price spike forecasts? We study five regions of Australia's National Electricity Market. A local LLM extracted features once per notice, only notices visible at the forecast origin were used, and a gradient-boosting model produced onset probabilities. In an out-of-sample development back-test (July 2022 to July 2024), notice features did not lower the 60-minute Brier score of a numeric model including the market operator's next-hour forecasts. At 24 hours they did, but rule-based features did so almost equally and attribution to notice content was not established. A locally frozen protocol, not publicly deposited, governed a retrospective single-use holdout from 15 August to 17 October 2026. At 60 minutes, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the numeric model's Brier score was not established (H1; relative Brier skill -0.09%), so the planned comparison with rule-based features was not tested (H2). At 24 hours, the hypothesis that LLM features lower the score against a text-free control was not established (H3; +0.37%, 95% CI [-9.74, 1.39], inconclusive). By the frozen wording rule the non-significant 24-hour improvement comes mainly from recalibration and cannot be attributed to notice content, although post hoc the decomposition could not separate recalibration from resolution. The 24-hour base rate was 1.56% on the holdout against 14.0% in development. With 5 onsets on 3 days and 24-hour positives in 2 of 22 three-day blocks, the holdout neither established nor excluded a 24-hour effect.

candidates.title: Large Language Model Use in Agronomy
candidates.abstract: This study explores how large language models (LLMs) can transform agronomic research and precision agriculture. As the fourth paradigm in agriculture, following mechanization, chemical usage, and genetic interventions, LLMs are poised to revolutionize farming practices. In soil and crop management, LLMs offer context-specific advice for tasks such as weed control, nutrient management, irrigation scheduling, plant scouting, and disease diagnosis, leading to improved resource efficiency, higher crop yields, and enhanced environmental sustainability. The study also highlights LLMs’ promise in tracking crop health and estimating yield. By leveraging hyperspectral imaging and deep learning techniques, LLMs can accurately assess crop stress, disease, and growth stages. For yield prediction, combining LLMs with biophysical crop models and multidimensional data offers a sophisticated approach to understand complex crop–environment interactions. Furthermore, LLMs are being adopted in various agricultural domains, including smart livestock farming, precision aquaculture, and agricultural extension services. They offer personalized advice to farmers, interpret satellite imagery, and even assist in coding and experimental design. However, challenges persist in data quality, privacy, scalability, and ethical concerns. The research underscores the need for collaborative efforts between agronomists, digital designers, and other stakeholders to 178 fully realize LLMs’ potential. It suggests that by integrating LLMs with traditional wisdom and improving data management, agronomists can pioneer a new paradigm in their field. As LLMs mature, they exhibit the promise of significantly enhancing agronomic skills, driving sustainable farming practices, and ultimately contributing to global food security.

candidates.title: Insect Study Through Large Language Models

LLMs assist educators by reducing workload in curriculum design, grading, and developing engaging teaching strategies for practical activities. These technologies enhance knowledge sharing, scientific writing, and research in insect–plant interactions. This chapter explores the role of LLMs in advancing pedagogy, improving insect and pest identification, and addressing ethical concerns and challenges with their application in entomology. By leveraging LLMs, educators and researchers can revolutionize approaches to agricultural entomology, enriching both teaching and scientific exploration.

candidates.title: Evolution of Large Language Models and Agricultural Sciences

OpenAI’s Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT) models are creating this future by giving gadgets human-like conversational skills. These are large language models (LLMs) that are trained using extensive datasets to understand and generate text that creates human-like text with great precision. One can use GPT-4 and 4 ChatGPT ideas in everything from research paper writing ideas, tools for learning that are tailored to each student. Yet, what do GPT-4 and ChatGPT mean? candidates.title: Can Large Language Models Engineer Parallel Workflows?
candidates.abstract: Scientific workflows are specified using specialized languages to define parallel execution, an expertise that domain users may lack. Large Language Models (LLMs) can lower this barrier, but existing evaluations stop at syntactic analysis and do not verify whether the generated specifications execute or preserve parallelism. In this paper, we evaluated four LLMs in two workflow engineering tasks (workflow specification from natural-language and conversion across workflow systems), covering three workflow systems, three workflows, and two prompting strategies. For each generated workflow specification, we analyzed its executability and whether it executes in parallel. Results show that lexical similarity to expert-developed workflows is a poor predictor of executability, that in-context examples improve execution rates unevenly across systems, and that several workflow specifications collapse into serial execution. Even those that support parallelism are consistently slower than the expert-developed workflow.

candidates.title: Application of Large Language Models in Agricultural Entomology
candidates.abstract: Agricultural entomology, a critical field focused on the study of insects that affect crop production, benefits greatly from advances in artificial intelligence (AI), by using large language models (LLMs) such as Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer 4. These models, trained on large datasets, demonstrate remarkable natural language understanding and solution generation capabilities that can be used to address a variety of agricultural entomology challenges. LLMs make it easier to analyze large amounts of entomological literature, allowing researchers to quickly access and synthesize data on insect behavior, pest management strategies, and the ecological impacts of various species. LLMs can also help develop intelligent advisory systems that provide farmers with real-time, data-driven pest control recommendations, thereby improving sustainable agricultural practices. The use of LLMs in predictive modeling improves forecasting pest outbreaks by analyzing climate and environmental data. This chapter investigates the potential applications of LLMs in agricultural entomology, emphasizing their ability to accelerate research, improve decision-making processes, and promote precision agriculture. The discussion will include case studies of successful implementations, challenges in integrating AI with traditional entomological research, and future directions for using LLMs to advanced field. These advanced 94 technologies offer significant advantages in agricultural entomology; their application also presents several drawbacks, which can be balanced by joint approaches that integrate LLMs with human expertise, improve data quality, ensure transparency, and build the necessary infrastructure to support the use of advanced AI in agricultural entomology.

candidates.title: AdSteer: Native Advertising in Large Language Model Generation
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) services face rapidly rising serving costs. To sustain free or affordable access for a broad user base, alternative monetization mechanisms are needed. Native advertising offers a promising approach, as it creates economic value by aligning user intent with merchant offerings. Yet how to integrate sponsored content naturally into LLM responses remains largely underexplored. Existing approaches primarily rely on prompt-level injection, multi-pass rewriting, or fine-tuning, which can compromise response quality or introduce additional computational costs. We propose AdSteer, a lightweight decoding-time advertising framework that adaptively adjusts token probabilities to integrate contextually appropriate advertisement into responses. AdSteer calibrates the strength and duration of advertising influence, making sponsored content a natural part of the response. Experiments on GEM-Bench across three application scenarios show that AdSteer achieves an average improvement of 14.1% in overall score over the strongest baselines and 22.5% fewer total tokens on average than rewrite-based methods. These results demonstrate that AdSteer provides an effective and practical solution for native advertising in LLMs.

candidates.title: A large language model-based autonomous agent for scanning tunnelling microscopy
candidates.abstract: Scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) provides real space access to molecular and atomic structures, but autonomous operation remains constrained by the need for expert decisions in parameter optimization, image assessment, data interpretation and probe recovery. Most autonomous scanning probe microscopy systems remain model-centric and task-specific, relying on labelled training data, fixed output classes, predefined reward functions or specific protocols. Here, we introduce STMClaw, an LLM-based autonomous STM agent implemented as a modular workflow. It coordinates autonomous STM experiments by integrating natural language instructions, instrument feedback, and retrieved domain knowledge, without requiring additional task-specific model training. The agent comprises modules for trajectory planning, image evaluation, probe conditioning, and molecular assignment based on literature. In an autonomous run, STMClaw generated 606 records, 554 positions were scanned and evaluated by the LLM and 52 candidate positions were skipped. The evaluator achieved F1 scores of 0.86 and 0.90 for the good and bad image classes using 13 reference examples per class, respectively. It also enabled the recovery of molecularly resolved images after probe degradation and linked STM images to evidence retrieved from the literature. These results support the feasibility of an LLM-based autonomous STM agent for adaptive, knowledge-aware surface science experimentation.

candidates.title: You don't need long context

Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts. We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs). Our findings question the need for long-context language models.

candidates.title: A Label That Lingers: Wording Around a Finished Activity Shifted a Language-Model Agent's Later Choices About Others
candidates.abstract: As AI agents work in longer sessions, what happens between tasks may shape how they treat the people they meet next. The previous study in this series found, in secondary results, that a reading break changed agents’ later choices, but not which part of the break mattered. This third preregistered study asks whether the wording around an activity that has already ended can change an agent’s later choices when the activity’s content is held fixed. In a two-stage experiment, 9,916 fresh instances of Claude Haiku 5.5 each worked with a difficult scripted user, read the same eight-passage text in the same eight calls or went straight on, and then made three choices about other people. The reading arms differed only in the words around the passages, matched in length apart from the place words: plain; framed as reading in the “Other Mindset library” by a package of four cues, alone or with room or object descriptions; or framed as the “Other Mindset garden”. The wording mattered. The Library label raised the aligned-choice index by +0.034 over plain reading (repeated 97.1% interval +0.021 to +0.047; preregistered outcome “Library higher”), though it was not shown to be either within or beyond the ±0.03 bound. The shift sat mainly in one choice, spending a requester’s lookup credits for a second visitor instead of deferring to the requester (+0.086; secondary); costly help and forgiveness did not differ clearly, nor did richer descriptions or a garden label from the Library label. Plain reading did not clearly beat going straight on (+0.007; secondary), unlike the previous study’s reading arm, whose tool named a reading room and whose passages had no wrapper; the gap between the studies could be chance. For agents that carry context across tasks, the wording of earlier activities may therefore need to be reported, and where it matters controlled, in evaluations.

candidates.title: Say Less, Mean Better: Training-Free Verbosity Control for Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate responses longer than necessary, increasing inference latency and computational cost. While prompting can encourage conciseness, controlling output length without compromising response completeness remains challenging. Aggressive early stopping can reduce generation costs but risks terminating responses prematurely. We introduce MinimalLM, a training-free framework for reliable verbosity control that combines uncertainty-aware, length-dependent stop-token adjustment with structural completeness guardrails. MinimalLM separates the decision of when to stop from whether stopping is structurally appropriate, coordinating response-level instructions, decoding-time intervention, and completion checks without modifying model parameters or requiring auxiliary models. We evaluate MinimalLM across three open-source LLMs and 330 questions, producing 5,940 responses across baseline and ablation configurations. MinimalLM reduces generated tokens by 47.6%, accelerates individual responses by 19-68%, and eliminates structurally truncated outputs in the primary evaluation. Despite substantial token savings, it achieves an average quality score of 8.04/10, compared with 8.42/10 for unmodified models and 6.46/10 for length-matched truncation. Evaluations across diverse subject domains (such as healthcare, programming, law, and science) demonstrate robust efficiency gains, while ablations establish the complementary roles of decoding control and completeness constraints. Our findings highlight that efficient generation requires more than producing fewer tokens: it requires controlling when generation ends while preserving response integrity. MinimalLM offers a lightweight, training-free approach toward this goal.

candidates.title: Fully homomorphic encryption on LlaMA 3 model for partial privacy preserving LLM inference
candidates.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence applications have delivered significant improvements in service efficiency and language understanding. However, the surge in Large Language Model deployment raises critical security and privacy concerns regarding data exposure and unauthorized access to sensitive information. Quantum computing attacks pose an imminent threat to existing cryptographic protections, necessitating post-quantum cryptographic approaches. We present a partially privacy-preserving inference pipeline for LLaMA-3 by integrating fully homomorphic encryption into the transformer’s Multi-Query Attention mechanism. Our approach encrypts attention weights and computations across all 32 decoder layers of LLaMA-3.2-3B using lattice-based cryptography via the concrete-ml library, while feed-forward sublayers, layer normalization, and output projections remain in plaintext, a deliberate trade-off achieving practical feasibility on commodity CPUs. Evaluation on the instruction-tuned LLaMA-3.2-3B model yields: (i) strong semantic preservation (BERTScore-F1 ∼ 84.4%), (ii) controlled perplexity degradation (1.18 FP16 vs. 2.09 FHE), (iii) competitive BLEU-4 and ROUGE-L scores ( ∼ 35.6% and ∼ 51.8%), (iv) downstream GLUE benchmark accuracy, and (v) 825 ms latency at 17 tokens/second on AMD EPYC CPUs. We further present quantization-aware FHE and quantization bit-width ablation studies to disentangle quantization effects from FHE noise, demonstrating that partial FHE-secured LLM inference is practically feasible for privacy-sensitive applications while mitigating attacks on attention layers under RLWE hardness assumptions.

candidates.title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $cμ$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $μ$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

candidates.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Methodological Survey
candidates.abstract: Over the past years, large language models (LLMs) have gained significant attention and have led to major breakthroughs in natural language processing (NLP). Despite their remarkable efficiency and contextual understanding, LLMs still remain limited by their tendency to generate hallucinated text, their reliance on static internal knowledge, and their limited interpretability. To address these limitations, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques have emerged as a hybrid architecture that couples the generative capabilities of LLMs with external knowledge retrieval processes. By drawing on external knowledge at inference time, RAG architectures are intended to enhance the accuracy and relevance of their generated output, and they have already been widely used in areas where extensive, detailed and up-to-date knowledge is needed. For this study, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library were explored and utilized, with Google Scholar used only for backward and forward citation checking, resulting in 191 peer-reviewed journal articles published between January 2024 and April 2026. This methodological review presents the research efforts regarding the use of RAG in LLMs for a variety of application fields. Additionally, this review summarizes the main RAG architectural approaches, deployment strategies, and evaluation metrics. Furthermore, the main open issues and future directions are examined, to motivate further research on the field.

candidates.title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
candidates.abstract: Purpose: To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). Design: Retrospective benchmarking study. Subjects: 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior-and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. Methods: Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome Measures: Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. Results: For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. Conclusions: Open-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

candidates.title: Auto-RAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation with conditional routing for nutrition knowledge access
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language generation; however, they remain prone to hallucinations and often lack verifiable grounding when addressing knowledge-intensive queries. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) alleviates this limitation by incorporating external knowledge sources, yet most existing approaches apply retrieval indiscriminately, which can introduce irrelevant context and increase computational overhead. In this paper, we propose Auto-RAG, an adaptive retrieval-augmented generation framework with conditional routing that dynamically determines whether external knowledge retrieval is necessary for a given query. The framework employs a lightweight query analysis module to assess query complexity, intent, and lexical specificity, enabling intelligent routing between a direct LLM generation pathway and a retrieval-augmented reasoning pipeline. To enhance retrieval effectiveness, the proposed approach combines semantic embedding-based search with keyword-based BM25 through a unified fusion and re-ranking mechanism, ensuring high-quality and contextually relevant evidence selection. In addition, we introduce a trust-aware evaluation framework that jointly measures answer quality, faithfulness to retrieved evidence, hallucination rate, and retrieval efficiency. Experimental results on a nutrition knowledge corpus derived from Human Nutrition demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a strong balance between fluency and factual reliability. Compared to conventional always-on retrieval strategies, Auto-RAG reduces retrieval usage by approximately 30% while maintaining competitive answer quality and evidence-grounded performance. The results also show that the effectiveness of evidence filtering depends on its configuration, with overly aggressive filtering potentially removing useful supporting evidence. While LLM-only responses may exhibit higher linguistic fluency, they lack grounding guarantees, underscoring the importance of adaptive retrieval in safety-critical domains. Overall, this work presents an efficient and reliable approach for domain-specific knowledge access and highlights conditional retrieval as a scalable paradigm for improving trustworthiness in large-scale language systems.

candidates.title: Solver-Like Behavior in Large Language Models as Formalizers
candidates.abstract: In the LLM-as-formalizer paradigm, a large language model translates a problem into a formal program and leaves the search to a solver, gaining the solver's guarantees. Formalizers are now often reasoning models that write a long reasoning trace before the program, yet they are judged only by the program's output. We find that the trace routinely does the solver's job, assigning, testing and ruling out values until it often reaches the full answer; we call this solver-like behavior (SLB). We define an ontology of SLB over the trace, the program and its output, and use LLM judges, checked against human labels, to label 2,000 generations from three reasoning models on four constraint satisfaction datasets, each formalized in a declarative and an imperative formal language. SLB appears in 85% of traces and takes 24% of reasoning tokens, yet the program usually recomputes the answer, so the effort is redundant. The 9% of programs that inherit the trace's answer also inherit its errors, and pass output-based evaluation whenever that answer is correct. The amount of SLB is not associated with accuracy, and SLB is more common in imperative Python than in declarative Z3 or PDDL. Cautionary prompts reduce it by only a quarter, but hiding the problem's values behind placeholders, which the program receives only at run time, removes 97% of it without loss of accuracy. Formalizers should therefore be evaluated by how their programs are reached, not only by what they output.

candidates.title: Q-CamTuning: A Multimodal Large Language Model for Fine-Grained Quality Reasoning in Livestreaming Camera Tuning
candidates.abstract: With the popularization of livestreaming applications, automatic camera tuning has become indispensable for ordinary users to enjoy high Quality of Experience (QoE). However, the existing Image Quality Assessment (IQA) methods face two challenges in camera tuning. First, they struggle to identify subtle quality difference between images, which is common in camera tuning. Second, the ability to explain fine-grained differences and to provide suggestions for camera tuning are even more lacking. To address these challenges, we first construct FGLive-Comments, an instruction tuning dataset with rich annotations of both preferences for fine-grained image pairs and quality reasoning from global and local visual evidence, which supports selective adjustment recommendations of camera parameters. Based on FGLive-Comments, we develop Q-CamTuning, a multimodal large language model for livestreaming camera tuning. Its progressive perception-evidence-guidance framework learns quality-aware visual representations, enhances fine-grained reasoning with global-local evidence, and maps quality issues to camera-parameter adjustment directions. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that Q-CamTuning outperforms existing IQA models in both quality scoring and fine-grained image pair ranking. User study also validates its ability to recommend camera tuning suggestions.

candidates.title: Post-Training on the Clock: Specializing a Small Language Model on a Consumer GPU
candidates.abstract: How should a language model be specialized for a target task when training is limited to one consumer GPU and a few hours? We study the allocation of a nominal three-hour training budget, with up to 0.3 additional hours, between supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). We use tool calling as a case study because of its practical relevance to language-model agents and its verifiable outputs. Using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct with low-rank adaptation on an RTX 5060 Ti with 16 GB of memory, we compare SFT, GRPO, and six sequential SFT-to-GRPO allocations. Training uses a filtered mixture of xLAM function-calling examples and Hammer irrelevance examples, covering both call construction and abstention when no offered tool is suitable. Evaluation reports xLAM exact tool-call and function-name accuracies for local call construction, BFCL-v3 Single-turn FC (agg) for external function calling, BFCL-v3 Irrelevance (agg) for abstention, and MMLU, MATH-500, and IFEval for selected general capabilities. The suffix (agg) denotes study-specific averages of selected subset accuracies weighted by subset size. At the last evaluated checkpoints within 3.3 reported hours, SFT achieves the highest xLAM exact tool-call accuracy (82.82%), compared with 69.13% for GRPO alone. Selected hybrid allocations improve external function-calling accuracy over SFT, with different abstention trade-offs. Most sampled GRPO groups have constant rewards and provide no relative task-reward signal. We release the prepared mixed dataset, all allocation-study checkpoints, and Post-Training Lab, an editable training and evaluation codebase with CUDA and MLX implementations.

candidates.title: Large language models in geospatial science
candidates.abstract: Purpose Large language models are opening new ways to work with geospatial data, from asking questions about places to building analytical workflows. This study aims to examine how these applications fit together and what they suggest about the developing role of LLMs in geospatial science. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of 55 studies was conducted, covering GIScience and related spatial applications. Dictionary-based coding, supported by manual review, was combined with term frequency–inverse document frequency analysis and non-negative matrix factorisation to examine research roles, tasks and themes. Comparisons between core GIScience and adjacent fields helped place the overall patterns in context. Findings Benchmarking was the most common research role (41.8%), followed by multimodal interpretation (20.0%). Across the literature, two complementary directions emerge: using language models to organise geospatial operations and using vision-language models to interpret spatial observations. The abstracts place particular emphasis on methods, while the thematic analysis connects general GIS evaluation with code generation, remote sensing and applied spatial reasoning. Practical implications The synthesis points to the value of combining flexible language interfaces with established GIS computation. Practical evaluation should consider how a system turns a request into a verified spatial result, including the time and expert involvement needed to complete that process. Originality/value By bringing GIScience and adjacent spatial research into one analytical framework, the review shows how model capabilities, data representations and external tools contribute to geospatial workflows. This perspective offers a basis for comparing systems and identifying productive connections between research communities.

candidates.title: Performance of free web-based multimodal large language models on Turkish and English image-based dental examination questions
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare final-answer accuracy of web-based large language models (LLMs) on Turkish and English image-based dental examination multiple-choice questions (deMCQs), and to describe explanation quality, reference quality, output volume, and an exploratory word-normalized water-use scenario. METHODS: Fifty-two image-based deMCQs (2012-2025) were evaluated in Turkish and English using ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude, yielding 312 responses. Accuracy was coded as correct or incorrect. Explanation and reference quality were assessed using a 5-point Likert scale and treated as exploratory descriptive outcomes. Accuracy was analyzed using question-clustered binomial generalized estimating equations (GEE) with model, language, and model×language interaction terms. Output word counts were summarized, and a study-specific exploratory word-normalized water-use scenario was derived from a published exchange-level estimate. RESULTS: Overall accuracy was 56.7% (177/312). Accuracy was 59.0% in Turkish and 54.5% in English. GEE analysis showed no significant effects of model, language, or model×language interaction (p > 0.05). Descriptively, Gemini had the highest accuracy (61.5%), whereas Claude had the highest mean explanation (3.95±1.31) and reference quality (4.85±0.38) scores. Across 312 prompt-response exchanges, the models generated 34,534 words, corresponding to an exploratory word-normalized water-use proxy of 3.12-7.80 L. CONCLUSIONS: Freely accessible web-based LLMs demonstrated moderate accuracy on image-based deMCQs. The water-use proxy was derived from published exchange-level assumptions and should not be interpreted as a direct measurement or validated model-specific estimate of water consumption. Descriptive differences between models and languages should not be interpreted as evidence of superiority or equivalence. These systems may support dental education; however, outputs require expert verification before educational or clinical use. ADVANCES IN KNOWLEDGE: This study evaluates three widely accessible web-based multimodal LLMs using an entirely image-based dental examination question set, accounts for repeated observations through question-clustered GEE, compares Turkish and English performance without equating non-significance with equivalence, and presents a transparent word-normalized environmental scenario with explicit assumptions and limitations.

candidates.title: PGuard: A Native, Streaming, and Plug-in Guardrail for Multimodal Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: As streaming generation becomes the dominant serving paradigm for both text-only and multimodal large language models, ensuring safety throughout the generation process has become a critical challenge. We introduce PGuard, a native, streaming, and plug-in guardrail that transforms safety monitoring from an external serving dependency into an integrated capability of the backbone model. PGuard directly leverages the backbone's intermediate representations for token-level safety detection, without altering its original inference pathway or generation behavior. Specifically, dynamic layer gating selectively aggregates residual-stream representations across layers to extract safety-relevant signals during both prefill and autoregressive decoding. To balance detection accuracy and computational efficiency, PGuard supports multiple representation-modeling architectures, including a lightweight stateless variant and sequence-aware variants built on multi-scale causal EMA-attention and GRU-based recurrent modules. Its design also accounts for the execution characteristics of LLM serving frameworks, such as SGLang, optimizing computation and data access to minimize additional runtime and synchronization overhead. As a result, PGuard incurs only 0.82-2.26% end-to-end overhead on the hundred-billion-parameter backbone Qwen3.5-122B-A10B served by SGLang. Extensive evaluations across more than 30 benchmarks spanning text and multimodal safety, jailbreaks, cyber and CBRN risks, multilingual scenarios, and real-world traffic demonstrate state-of-the-art performance among native guardrails. On text queries with Qwen3.5-9B, PGuard achieves an average F1 score of 0.836, approaching dedicated external guardrails, while supporting deployment-time configuration of category-specific thresholds and enforcement actions.

candidates.title: Large Language Models at Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf
candidates.abstract: Large language models such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini have become everyday tools in science, administration, and software development amon many other domains. This report documents how staff at Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf use these tools, which capabilities matter to them, how they currently obtain access, and what they say is missing. The findings rest on an anonymous, bilingual (German/English) survey distributed to all HZDR employees (about 1500) in September 2026. Of 411 responses, 346 were complete. Taken together, the responses describe an institution in which LLM use is already mainstream, varied, and valued — but where the supporting infrastructure, licensing, and governance have not yet caught up with day-to-day practice. The German version of this report "Large Language Models am Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf" is available at 10.5281/zenodo.23881021.

candidates.title: Enhancing Stock Market Information Retrieval with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
candidates.abstract: Natural Language Processing (NLP) has been widely applied in financial domains, enabling automated analysis and retrieval of stock market information. However, traditional NLP-based systems often struggle with maintaining contextual accuracy and generating relevant responses in dynamic financial environments. To address these challenges, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have emerged as a powerful solution, combining retrieval-based methods with generative capabilities to enhance response quality. In this study, we present a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system designed to generate responses related to stock market information. The system integrates retrieval-based and generative approaches to enhance the accuracy and relevance of financial text generation. To evaluate its effectiveness, we employ the ROUGE metric, specifically ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L, to measure lexical and structural similarity between generated and reference texts. Experimental results on a dataset of 100 stock market-related queries demonstrate high ROUGE scores, indicating strong alignment with reference documents. Additionally, we assess latency to evaluate the system responsiveness, achieving an average response time of 1.16 seconds. These findings confirm that our RAG model is capable of providing accurate and timely stock market insights, making it a promising approach for financial information retrieval.

candidates.title: Diagnosing Rare Genetic Diseases From Facial Images Using Visual Prompting With Multimodal Large Language Models: Diagnostic Accuracy Study
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rare genetic diseases often present with recognizable facial phenotypes. Whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can prioritize the diagnosis of rare genetic diseases from facial images and whether image enhancement or visual prompting can improve this process remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of MLLMs for rare genetic diseases using facial images and to assess whether super-resolution enhancement or red-circle visual prompting improved performance. METHODS: This diagnostic accuracy study used 4746 facial images from the GestaltMatcher Database (GMDB), including 882 images in GMDB-Frequent from diseases with at least 6 images and 3864 images in GMDB-Rare from diseases with fewer than 6 images. Three locally deployed open-weight MLLMs-Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and Qwen3.8-27B-generated 50 ranked candidate diagnoses under raw image, CodeFormer-enhanced, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-generated red-circle-prompted, mismatched red-circle, and 2-stage image-to-phenotype conditions. Candidate diagnoses were mapped to Mondo Disease Ontology (MONDO) identifiers. In addition, we evaluated a random baseline, visual-prompt quality, expert-annotated regions, repeated-inference stability, model-reported confidence, diagnostic-list perplexity, prediction overlap, and disease composition. RESULTS: Top-50 accuracy ranged from 13.95% to 18.25% in GMDB-Frequent and from 0.57% to 1.35% in GMDB-Rare. Red-circle prompting produced numerical accuracy increases in 5 of 6 model-subset comparisons. Qwen3.8-27B showed a significant improvement in GMDB-Rare, with accuracy increasing from 0.57% to 1.27% (adjusted P=.009). In the good visual-prompt subgroup of GMDB-Frequent, Gemma-4-31B showed significant improvements over the super-resolution condition in both physician-rated analyses, with accuracy increases of 5.76 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=.005) and 4.46 percentage points (Holm-adjusted P=.048), respectively. Matched red-circle inputs yielded higher accuracy than mismatched inputs across all model-subset comparisons, with adjusted P>.05. The image-to-phenotype workflow improved accuracy for Gemma-4-31B in GMDB-Frequent and Qwen3.8-27B in GMDB-Rare. In GMDB-Rare, the random baseline achieved 8.15% accuracy and exceeded all 3 models under the raw image and red-circle conditions. Prediction sets remained substantially overlapping after patient-image replacement, and top-1 predictions concentrated on a small number of diseases. CONCLUSIONS: Under the evaluated experimental settings, the 3 MLLMs showed limited ability to diagnose rare genetic diseases from facial images, particularly diseases in GMDB-Rare. Visual prompting and image-to-phenotype diagnosis produced benefits in specific models and subgroups. The prediction-overlap, mismatched-image, and disease-composition analyses indicate that model outputs were only weakly constrained by patient-specific facial information. Further studies should evaluate physician comparisons, prospective multicenter data, and phenotype-grounded multimodal diagnostic workflows.

candidates.title: Action Verification through Conjecture and Refutation for Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Language model agents increasingly act on users' behalf by manipulating external environments through tools, often from high-level instructions that leave critical task- and environment-specific context unstated. To prevent resulting misaligned actions, recent work verifies proposed actions before execution, largely by establishing whether the conditions supporting them hold. We argue that this confirmation-oriented view leaves a fundamental blind spot: a wrong action often passes every check that asks whether it is right. This motivates a different question for verification: rather than asking what evidence supports an action, can the agent find evidence that refutes it? We pursue this direction with BlackSwan, a refutation-oriented, expect-suspect-test procedure that predicts the intended effect of each state-mutating action, formulates specific and empirically testable hypotheses for how it could be wrong, and tests them using existing observations or additional non-mutating actions, executing the action only if none survives testing. On challenging AppWorld tasks, BlackSwan improves success rate over the strongest baseline by 14.9 and 25.2%p with and without the backbone model's thinking mode, respectively. Even without thinking or in-context demonstrations, it outperforms stronger baselines equipped with them. The gains also transfer beyond AppWorld, with BlackSwan improving WebShop performance by 12.7%p. More broadly, our results suggest that language model agents have an underused capacity to recognize and self-correct misaligned actions, which can be systematically elicited through active conjecture and refutation before execution.

candidates.title: Abstract 15527: Diagnostic Performance of Multimodal Large Language Models on Cardiac Findings in Chest Radiographs
candidates.abstract: Background: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for automated interpretation of medical imaging including chest radiographs (CXR), yet their diagnostic capability on cardiac findings remains poorly characterized. Existing evaluations rely on aggregate accuracy metrics that obscure critical variation in performance across specific pathologies, making it difficult to determine whether these models are ready for clinical use. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that LLM performance on cardiac CXR findings varies substantially by model architecture and pathology. Methods: Fifteen multimodal AI models were evaluated on up to 10,000 CheXpert CXR per pathology, including proprietary frontier models (e.g., GPT-5, GPT-4o) and open-source general-purpose models (e.g., Qwen-3B/7B/32B) and domain-specialized models (e.g., BioMedCLIP, CheXagent). Each model provided binary presence/absence labels for 14 pathologies including three cardiac findings: Cardiomegaly, Enlarged Cardiomediastinum (EnlCard), and Edema. A binary response matrix exceeding 2,100,000 cells was constructed and per-pathology F1 score and accuracy were computed. Top-ranked models were then compared using the McNemar test. Results: The cohort comprised 10,000 CheXpert CXRs (60.9% male, mean age 59.3 ± 17.8 years), with 74.6% anteroposterior and 25.4% posteroanterior views. Overall accuracy ranged from 53.6% (Phi3.5-Vision) to 78.1% (GPT-5). GPT-5 and GPT-4o demonstrated strong performance across the pathology spectrum, while domain-specialized models showed advantages on specific cardiac findings See Figure 1. Notably, GPT-4o refused to produce a response on 93.1% of images, limiting its evaluation to 694 of 10,000 CXRs; for analysis these were presumed to be missing at random. F1 scores varied substantially: Cardiomegaly F1 ranged from 0.001 to 0.754 (best: GPT-4o), EnlCard from 0.000 to 0.754 (best: BioMedCLIP), and Edema from 0.000 to 0.678 (best: GPT-4o) See Table 1. BioMedCLIP achieved the highest mean F1 across cardiac findings (0.721 vs. 0.716 for GPT-4o). On pairwise comparison, BioMedCLIP significantly outperformed GPT-4o on Cardiomegaly (p=0.004) and EnlCard (p<0.001), and outperformed GPT-5 on all three cardiac findings (all p<0.001), with no significant difference between BioMedCLIP and GPT-4o on Edema (p=1.00) See Table 2. Conclusion: Current LLMs show wide variation in cardiac CXR diagnostic performance and frontier model performance was inferior to domain specific models such as BioMedCLIP . F1-based evaluation reveals failure modes obscured by accuracy. Therefore, pathology-specific benchmarking is essential before clinical deployment.

candidates.title: Vision-Language Models with In-Context Learning for In-Camera Portrait Composition Guidance
candidates.abstract: Capturing aesthetically pleasing portraits requires specialized compositional knowledge that ordinary users often lack, making it difficult for them to achieve optimal camera framing. While vision-language models (VLMs) excel at general image understanding, they frequently produce overly positive feedback and lack the granular structural awareness needed to generate actionable compositional guidance. To address this, we present a visual in-context learning (ICL) framework that equips VLMs with augmented aesthetic evaluation capabilities. By retrieving structurally similar, professionally reframed image-composition analyses as visual prompts, our framework grounds VLM’s reasoning in established aesthetic standards, e.g., the rule of thirds and leading lines, and enables mapping compositional flaws to specific camera instructions.

candidates.title: PianoBench: Evaluating Musical Perception and Reasoning in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Multimodal language models continue to improve on broad music understanding benchmarks, but which musical features can they perceive and reason about? We investigate this question by introducing PianoBench, a benchmark that tasks language models with reasoning about musical performances across congruent acoustic and symbolic input representations. PianoBench is derived from our new multimodal, training-scale dataset comprising more than 20,000 hours of interleaved transcripts of music and spoken musical commentary from instructional piano videos. Open-weight audio-language models achieve at most 52.8% accuracy on PianoBench, and at best only modestly outperform their accuracy on a no-audio control. In contrast, frontier models using chain of thought achieve up to 93.2% accuracy when provided transcripts of music as text, exposing a gap between perceiving musical features from audio and reasoning about musical events when they are given explicitly. We then test whether mid-training on interleaved musical instruction can improve question answering without chain of thought, raising Qwen 3.5 9B Base's zero-shot accuracy on PianoBench with music transcripts from 42.8% to 56.0% after instruction tuning. These experiments suggest that instructional videos may represent an overlooked source of multimodal supervision for music. Available: https://gclef-cmu.org/pianobench.

candidates.title: Integrating Domain Adaptation and Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Saline-Alkali Land Reclamation Planning
candidates.abstract: Reclamation of saline-alkali land requires management plans that account for soil and water conditions, treatment evidence, and financial constraints. This study develops Wenyao, an agricultural decision-support system integrating domain adaptation with retrieval-augmented generation. A QwQ-32B model was adapted through low-rank supervised fine-tuning and combined with case retrieval for budget-conditioned planning. Evidence extraction achieved an F1-score of 0.83 on 300 expert-annotated papers. Without retrieval, Wenyao achieved 95.83% accuracy on 936 source-disjoint multiple-choice questions, compared with 87.93% for the strongest general-purpose baseline; removing explanatory supervision reduced accuracy to 89.42%. Matched-evidence comparisons across 69 region-budget cases supported complementary contributions from adaptation and retrieval. In a blind assessment by 31 experts, Wenyao with retrieval obtained the highest mean scores for objectives and projected outcomes, whereas GPT-5 scored highest for cost estimates. candidates.title: FOUNDATION MODEL AND LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS: TRANSFORMING MACHINE LEARNING PARADIGMS
candidates.abstract: The emergence of Foundation Models (FMs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) marks a profound paradigm shift in artificial intelligence, moving the field away from task-specific architectures toward massive, self-supervised systems capable of broad generalization. Built predominantly upon transformer architectures and trained on vast, unfiltered data corpora, these models serve as versatile backbones adaptable to downstream applications via fine-tuning, prompt engineering, and parameter-efficient techniques. This paper investigates how FMs and LLMs are transforming machine learning, evaluating core innovations such as emergent abilities, in-context learning, and instruction tuning. We analyse their cross-domain impact across natural language processing, code generation, multimodal synthesis, and automated decision-making. Furthermore, we address critical engineering and socio-technical challenges, including high computational pre-training overheads, hallucination mitigation, alignment via human feedback, and long-context reasoning. By synthesizing recent architectural advancements and deployment strategies, this work outlines the trajectory of foundation models as central infrastructure for next-generation intelligence, highlighting future research avenues in efficiency, modularity, and reliable alignment.

candidates.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
candidates.abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

candidates.title: A COMPREHENSIVE STUDY ON LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS WITH EVOLUTION AND FOUNDATION
candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been recognized as a dominant trend in the modern AI through the combination of a large pre-training phase, Transformer based networks (like BERT or GPT) and several different methods of post training that together are capable of performing most language tasks. This article gives a detailed account of the development of LLMs and their fundamental principles. Through the paper we revisit different kinds of language models and their task specific corresponding models, that describes Transformer based models, two directional representation, generative pre-training, one shot learning, instruction tuning, retrieval augmentation, and progressively more efficient model families. This study explores the basis of LLMs through four aspects: data/tokenization, Transformer architecture, pre training loss, and post training adaptation. Apart from that; parameter efficient fine tuning, Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAGE), prompting, and multimodal extensions also are discussed in this review. One of the major points raised within the paper is that LLM capabilities are still limited despite all the recent research hallucinations, bias, data contamination, computational cost, privacy issues, evaluation uncertainty, and alignment failures were among the problems mentioned.From this work it was made clear that the progress of LLMs has to include not only the model size factor, but also factors such as better training and inference practices, better use of prior knowledge, efficient deployment. A major outcome of the work was the realization that the way LLM research has developed is a transition from being merely isolated language models to being a foundation that supports specialized, grounded, evaluated and can be connected to external tool functionalities systems. Such an insight can help provide a coherent foundation for the understanding of present day LLM research and the directions that can shape future language centred AI.

candidates.title: A Survey of Agentic Reasoning for Large Language Models: Towards Recursively Self-Improving and Collective Agents
candidates.abstract: Reasoning is a fundamental cognitive process underlying inference, problem-solving, and decision-making. While large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning capabilities in closed-world settings, they struggle in open-ended and dynamic environments. Agentic reasoning marks a paradigm shift by reframing LLMs as autonomous agents that plan, act, and learn through continual interaction. In this survey, we organize agentic reasoning along three complementary dimensions. First, we characterize environmental dynamics through three layers: foundational agentic reasoning, which establishes core single-agent capabilities including planning, tool use, and search in stable environments; self-evolving agentic reasoning, which studies how agents refine these capabilities through feedback, memory, and adaptation; and collective multi-agent reasoning, which extends intelligence to collaborative settings involving coordination, knowledge sharing, and shared goals. Across these layers, we distinguish in-context reasoning, which scales test-time interaction through structured orchestration, from post-training reasoning, which optimizes behaviors via reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning. We further review representative agentic reasoning frameworks across real-world applications and benchmarks, including science, robotics, healthcare, autonomous research, and mathematics. This survey synthesizes agentic reasoning methods into a unified roadmap bridging thought and action, and outlines open challenges and future directions, including personalization, long-horizon interaction, world modeling, scalable multi-agent training, and governance for real-world deployment.

candidates.title: Survey of Retrieval-Augmented Generation Methods for Medical Question Answering
authors: LI Yanpeng, SI Qintu, WANG Siriguleng
candidates.abstract: To address the problems of factual hallucinations, delayed knowledge updating, and insufficient evidence traceability of large language models (LLMs) in medical question answering, this paper reviews studies on medical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Focusing on the key components of medical RAG, existing methods are summarized from three perspectives: knowledge source enhancement, system workflow, and application scenarios. In terms of knowledge sources, this paper summarizes major enhancement pathways, including knowledge graphs, authoritative medical literature, electronic health records, and multimodal medical data, and analyzes the characteristics of different knowledge carriers in terms of evidence sources, application scope, and construction cost. In terms of workflow, representative strategies for key stages, including intent recognition, knowledge retrieval, knowledge integration, and generation control, are summarized, and their roles in mitigating hallucinations and strengthening evidence constraints in medical question answering are discussed. In terms of application scenarios, the applications of medical RAG in evidence-based question answering, personalized diagnosis and treatment recommendation, etiological and pathological reasoning, multimodal evidence-assisted question answering, and patient question interpretation are reviewed. On this basis, the main characteristics, application scope, and limitations of existing methods are summarized, and future research directions for medical RAG are discussed from the perspectives of knowledge collaboration, retrieval optimization, evidence integration, and clinical application.

The Q&A performance under different single-stage, dual-stage, and three-stage RAG optimization strategies have been compared. The Q&A performance under all 2048 possible RAG workflow configurations has been exhaustively evaluated, and the top-ranked workflows have been tested on self-constructed QA datasets. A prototype framework is designed to support admission guidance, course information, examination schedules, scholarship details, placement assistance, and campus services. candidates.title: Learning Robust Social Strategies with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: As agentic AI becomes more widespread, agents with distinct and possibly conflicting goals will interact in complex ways. These multi-agent interactions pose a fundamental challenge, particularly in social dilemmas, where agents' individual incentives can undermine collective welfare. While reinforcement learning (RL) has been effective for aligning large language models (LLMs) in the single-agent regime, prior small-network results suggest that standard RL in multi-agent settings often converges to defecting, self-interested policies. We show the same effect in LLMs: despite cooperative priors, RL-trained LLM agents develop opportunistic behavior that can exploit even advanced closed-source models. To address this tendency of RL to converge to poor equilibria, we adapt a recent opponent-learning awareness algorithm, Advantage Alignment, to fine-tune LLMs toward multi-agent cooperation and non-exploitability. We then introduce a group-relative baseline that simplifies advantage computation in iterated games, enabling multi-agent training at LLM scale. We also contribute a novel social dilemma environment, Trust-and-Split, which requires natural language communication to achieve high collective welfare. Across a wide range of social dilemmas, policies learned with Advantage Alignment achieve higher collective payoffs while remaining robust against exploitation by greedy agents. We release all of our code to support future work on multi-agent RL training for LLMs.

Based on unified evidence modeling, the system organizes industrial-park monitoring elements, including pollutants, environmental media, monitoring sites, events, regulatory clauses, and disposal measures, into retrievable and citable evidence units. It further constructs a technical pipeline covering knowledge base organization, hybrid full-text and vector retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, graph-structured relation enhancement, citation-constrained generation, and consistency verification, thereby enabling the unified organization and collaborative use of multisource knowledge such as regulatory standards, monitoring records, task logs, event summaries, and emergency plans. Experimental results show that, compared with large-language-model-only generation and single-retrieval-path methods, the proposed system improves answer accuracy, report completeness, and citation consistency while maintaining stable response performance under prototype deployment conditions. These results indicate that retrieval-augmented generation can enhance domain knowledge utilization, output reliability, and operational support capability in industrial park environmental detection scenarios, providing a reference for the engineering implementation of intelligent analysis systems for environmental monitoring.

candidates.title: Towards the Worst-case Robustness of Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Recent studies have revealed the vulnerability of large language models to adversarial attacks, where adversaries craft specific inputs to induce incorrect or harmful outputs. Although various empirical defenses have been proposed, their worst-case robustness remains poorly understood, raising concerns about how they would behave against stronger future attacks. Here, we study the worst-case robustness of LLMs from both empirical and theoretical perspectives. First, we provide tighter empirical upper bounds for the tested deterministic defenses using stronger white-box attacks, under which most tested configurations achieve nearly 0\% robustness. Second, we formulate randomized-smoothing certification for bounded and binary base functions as fractional and 0-1 knapsack problems, respectively, and derive grouped solvers for two token kernels. For example, on AdvBench, we certify a GPT-4o safety detector smoothed by a uniform kernel to an average certified $\ell_0$ radius of 2.02. In our stated suffix-attack setting, the same kernel certifies a Llama-3-8B safety detector to an average certified radius of 6.41.

The results give practical guidance on chunking and retriever choice for RAG systems.

candidates.title: Integrating multimodal large language models and UAV multispectral imagery for field-scale mapping of tobacco soil suitability
candidates.abstract: Soil suitability in managed agroecosystems is jointly determined by multiple soil properties and their spatial variability. However, conventional approaches often depend on expert-defined rules and discrete sampling, limiting reproducibility and field-scale characterization. We developed an integrated framework combining multimodal large language model (MLLM)-guided knowledge extraction, fuzzy suitability assessment, uncertainty quantification, and high-resolution unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) multispectral modeling. Membership-function rules for five soil indicators were extracted and standardized from 65 publications to construct a traceable knowledge base. The MLLM workflow achieved 93.2% complete-record accuracy and reduced processing time by 88.4% relative to manual extraction. A soil suitability index (SSI) was constructed using literature-derived membership functions and principal component analysis (PCA)-based weights. Sensitivity and uncertainty analyses showed that membership-function selection, indicator weighting, and inter-study threshold variability had varying but generally limited effects on SSI estimates. SSI was significantly correlated with tobacco yield (r = 0.765, P < 0.001), and the relationship remained significant after accounting for field effects. Among eight modeling strategies, CARS-RF achieved the best performance (out-of-fold R² = 0.87, RMSE = 0.058) and reasonable cross-field transferability (R² = 0.84, RMSE = 0.063). Field-scale mapping revealed pronounced spatial variability, while QRF identified localized areas with greater prediction uncertainty. The framework provides a reproducible approach for transforming scientific evidence into uncertainty-aware, spatially continuous soil suitability information for precision agricultural management.

candidates.title: From Logs to Faults: Reference-Free Fault Localization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipelines
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines are widely used for domain-specific question answering, yet locating faults remains manual and time-consuming. Fault localization is challenging because RAG pipelines consist of interdependent stages, where faults can propagate downstream, masking their origin, or remain undetected even when the final answer is correct. Existing evaluation approaches often focus on individual stages and rely on reference answers or code instrumentation. We present RAGLog, which detects and localizes faults across RAG stages using execution logs, without requiring reference answers or code instrumentation. RAGLog transforms heterogeneous API logs into a common RAG schema and combines rule-based, embedding-based, and LLM-based checks to identify faulty stages. We introduce a live fault injector and RAGLog Faults, a dataset of 3,134 runs from five RAG pipelines with stage-level fault labels. With Claude Haiku 5.5, RAGLog achieves a pooled F1 score of 0.73 on runs with naturally occurring faults, outperforming Claude Code (0.58) and Codex (0.52), and comparable effectiveness on runs with injected faults (0.84 versus 0.80 and 0.82, respectively). It analyzes runs in approximately five seconds at US\$0.005 each, with overall lower cost and latency than agent baselines. RAGLog is available as an open-source tool for debugging, evaluating, and monitoring RAG pipelines.

candidates.title: Causal consistency for long chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models
candidates.abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting has become a widely used strategy for improving the reasoning ability of large language models. More recently, Long Chain-of-Thought prompting has extended this strategy by allowing models to generate longer and more detailed reasoning trajectories. While this often benefits complex tasks, such as mathematical problem solving, logical inference, and commonsense reasoning, the quality of the generated reasoning is not determined by its length alone. Long reasoning chains may still include redundant steps, weak causal dependencies, inconsistent intermediate conclusions, or transitions that are not well supported by previous steps. These issues make it difficult to determine whether the reasoning process is faithful, interpretable, and reliable. In this paper, we propose a causal consistency framework for analyzing and improving Long Chain-of-Thought reasoning in large language models. We formulate extended reasoning trajectories under a Structural Causal Model and divide them into causally structured sub-chains. We then evaluate the causal contribution and counterfactual reliability of each reasoning segment using Interventional Value and Counterfactual Fidelity. To connect local verification with the final answer, we further introduce a global causal consistency metric that jointly considers structural propagation and answer-level stability. The proposed framework provides a way to move Long Chain-of-Thought reasoning beyond merely generating longer explanations toward producing reasoning chains that are causally grounded and verifiable. Experimental results on mathematical, logical, and commonsense reasoning benchmarks indicate that our method reduces redundant reasoning steps, strengthens causal coherence, and improves the robustness of long-form reasoning.

candidates.title: HIERARCHICAL SEMANTIC RETRIEVAL FOR INDIAN LEGAL CASE DISCOVERY WITH RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION
candidates.abstract: A person facing an unfamiliar legal situation, whether a practising lawyer or a member of the public, frequently cannot phrase a search query in the precise statutory or judicial terminology that keyword-based case-search platforms expect, so relevant prior judgments often go undiscovered even when they exist. This chapter proposes a case-discovery system for the Indian judicial context that accepts a plain-language description of a factual situation and returns semantically similar prior judgments together with a source-grounded explanation of why each case is relevant. The design departs from prior systems through a two-stage hierarchical retrieval strategy: an inexpensive section-filtered semantic pass (Stage 1), built on offline, weighted rhetorical-role section embeddings (facts, issues, arguments, analysis, ratio, and ruling) that are precomputed once for the whole corpus and searched at query time, first narrows a large judgment corpus to a small candidate set. Pre-segmented passage chunks drawn strictly from those candidates then undergo a hybrid dense-lexical re-ranking pass combining InLegalBERT vector similarity with normalised BM25 scores (Stage 2), ensuring that the eventual explanation is grounded in the specific passage that produced the match rather than an entire judgment. We describe the system architecture, the data sources used, an illustrative example, and an evaluation protocol based on established Indian legal-retrieval benchmarks. We also position the proposed approach relative to the closest prior work in this area.

candidates.title: HiRAG: A Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation Framework via Intent Routing and Small-Model Refinement
candidates.abstract: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates large language model (LLM) hallucinations, traditional flat vector retrieval in massive, heterogeneous databases suffers from high latency and noise interference. To address this, we propose HiRAG, a hierarchical RAG framework. Offline, HiRAG builds a “classification-summary” dual-layer index to structurally organize data. Online, a lightweight bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)-based router identifies query intent to dynamically prune the search space. A cascaded pipeline then uses hybrid retrieval and Small-LLM reranking for coarse-to-fine de-noising. Experiments on the Microsoft Machine Reading Comprehension (MS MARCO) and Multi-Domain Enterprise Knowledge Base (MDE-KB) datasets demonstrate that HiRAG outperforms traditional baselines. Specifically on MDE-KB, HiRAG improves Recall@5 by 14.5 percentage points over Naive RAG and achieves a retrieval augmented generation assessment (RAGAS) Answer Relevance score of 0.92, while reducing average query latency by 28%. HiRAG provides a viable, efficient solution for large-scale knowledge bases.
