candidates.title: MCF: A Memory- and Communication-Aware Co-Designed Framework for Long-Context LLM Inference
candidates.abstract: This paper presents Memory- and Communication-Aware Framework for Long-Context LLM Inference (MCF) that optimizes long-context inference through communication-aware and stage-adaptive KV-cache layout transitions. At the core of MCF is {Memory-Aware Replication and Scheduling} (MARS), a dynamic orchestration mechanism for chunked prefill. MARS exploits early-stage memory headroom by selectively replicating highly reused KV blocks, improving locality and hiding KV propagation latency behind attention computation. As prefill progresses and memory pressure increases, MARS progressively drains redundant replicas and converges the KV cache into a sharded decode-ready layout, avoiding expensive layout conversion at the prefill--decode boundary. For decoding, MCF adopts a query-centric execution model in which KV shards remain stationary while lightweight query tensors are routed across workers. This changes communication from KV-cache-dependent transfer to query-dependent transfer, reducing communication growth with context length. MCF further integrates a hardware-software co-designed execution layer based on an FPGA compute-NIC datapath, enabling metadata-driven KV routing and collective operations directly in the network path. Experiments show that MCF improves TTFT, throughput, and scalability over state-of-the-art distributed inference systems, with larger benefits as context length and cluster size increase.

candidates.title: An outcome-devaluation test of language-model agents that keep notes across sessions
candidates.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly work across sessions, learning from the results of their own actions and storing what they learn in notes they write themselves. We adapted the outcome-devaluation test from animal learning to ask whether such agents adjust their behaviour when an outcome's value changes in a context where they cannot act. Over four sessions, agents learned that one tool supplies an artefact that adds more to their project's score than the artefact supplied by a second tool. In a later session without tools, they observed the first artefact's contribution fall (or, in control conditions, the second artefact's contribution rise or fall, or no change). In a final session without outcome feedback, we recorded which tool they requested. Controls included a sham condition, a specificity condition, a direct choice between the two artefacts, notes replaced by neutral text, an instructed condition and scripted learning agents. Claude Haiku 5.5 reduced its use of the devalued artefact's tool in a minimal agent loop (Δ −0.28, 95% CI −0.36 to −0.20) and as a Claude Code agent (Δ −0.52, −0.63 to −0.41), and did so only when that artefact's value fell. It changed little when the other artefact's value rose, and its direct choices between the artefacts show that it mostly did not accept the higher value. In the minimal loop it also failed to act fully on the fall when told about it directly. Claude Sonnet 5 changed its choices in both directions (−0.30 and +0.37). Qwen3-14B named both tool–artefact links correctly in only 47% of runs and did not reduce its use of the devalued tool. Replacing the notes with neutral text removed the learned preference. Blind coding of the notes the Claude agents held at the start of the test showed that every run in the devaluation condition had recorded the fall, but few had revised their plan to avoid the devalued tool; most kept it as the default or marked the choice as uncertain. Runs that kept it as the default chose it on 80–96% of test steps, and in Claude Code most runs that marked the choice as uncertain either switched completely or did not change. In current agents, recording a change in an outcome's value, revising the written procedure and acting on the change are separate steps, and the test measures each one.

candidates.title: Uncertainty-aware offline reinforcement learning for LLM inference serving with heterogeneous SLOs
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference workloads are bursty, have output lengths that are unknown at arrival, expose two resource-distinct phases (prefill and decode), and serve requests carrying heterogeneous service-level objectives (SLOs) on time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT). Prevailing schedulers rely on static heuristics that cannot adapt to this uncertainty, while online reinforcement learning (RL) is unsafe and sample-inefficient in production. We present URSA, an uncertainty-aware, risk-sensitive scheduler trained entirely offline , without interacting with a live serving system, on scheduling transitions generated by replaying historical request traces under existing heuristic schedulers. URSA (i) predicts a calibrated distribution over each request’s output length and derived key–value (KV) cache footprint rather than a point estimate; (ii) encodes the joint state of the waiting queue, heterogeneous GPU instances, and KV occupancy as a request–instance heterogeneous graph processed by a graph neural network; (iii) learns a dispatch policy with conservative, distributional offline RL whose reward jointly optimizes SLO attainment, goodput, and KV-overflow risk; and (iv) reserves memory at a class-dependent high quantile of the predicted footprint to bound out-of-memory events. Across the BurstGPT, Azure LLM inference, and Alibaba GPU-cluster traces, URSA raises overall SLO attainment from $$71.3\%$$ (FCFS) and $$84.1\%$$ (learning-to-rank) to $$90.4\%$$ , cuts P99 TTFT by up to $$3.3\times $$ , and reduces recompute/eviction events below $$1\%$$ , approaching an oracle that knows true lengths. We analyze limitations, robustness to prediction error, and transfer to other scheduling domains.

candidates.title: Shared Context, Separate Engines: Stateful Streaming Inference for Multimodal LLMs on Edge SoCs
candidates.abstract:
Streaming multimodal large language models (MLLMs) must take in new video frames while answering questions about what they have already seen. On an edge SoC, if one engine does both, ingestion and answering compete for its time while the other engines sit idle. To take over a query, another engine must first import or rebuild the accumulated history, because each runtime keeps it as KV state in its own format. 
ame lets one engine answer from history that another engine built. Each query reads the history as it stood when the query was asked, so one engine can keep ingesting while another answers. The CPU and GPU can also decode answers to different queries simultaneously. Phase-level state continuation lets an engine prefill a query, pass its KV state to another engine for decoding, and return to ingestion. State-Driven Execution Planning (SDEP) chooses where each query is prefilled and decoded, based on the state each engine holds and the work queued on it. Across M4 Max, RK3588, and QCS6490, 
ame outperforms single-engine execution. On a live M4 Max stream, SDEP cuts p95 time to first token by $76\%$, and every query receives its first token within one second. Under backlog, it raises request throughput by up to $35\%$. For two concurrent video streams on RK3588, SDEP delivers $19.6\%$ higher request throughput than single-engine execution and $27.2\%$ more than running both engines in parallel without shared state. 
ame delivers up to $2.48	imes$ the throughput of the same engines run serially. Every answer matches serial execution token for token.

candidates.title: Satellite Intelligence: Distributed Training, Collaborative Inference,and LLM Adaptation in LEO Constellation
candidates.abstract: The proliferation of orbital sensing data and the real-time demands of emerging global services are pushing low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks from bent-pipe relays toward intelligent onboard processing. This shift confronts a fundamental tension, where modern artificial intelligence (AI) training paradigms require intensive computation, abundant memory, and stable connectivity, all of which are scarce under the dynamic topologies, intermittent links, and severe size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints of satellite networks. Addressing this tension demands rethinking AI workflows, from training and inference to the emerging deployment of large language models (LLMs), under a constraint-aware design philosophy. To the best of our knowledge, this paper provides the first survey that jointly covers all three, whereas prior surveys examine these aspects in isolation. We begin by identifying the deployment challenge of satellite intelligence (SI) and deriving design principles for SI. We then examine three advancing paradigms: i) distributed training, where federated learning (FL) and split learning (SL) enable satellite-ground co-training under resource limitations; ii) collaborative inference, which exploits single-satellite, multi-satellite, and satellite-ground architectures to meet real-time service demands; and iii) on-orbit LLM adaptation and serving, which tackles the frontier challenge of deploying LLMs under severe orbital constraints and resource-aware serving. Finally, we identify open challenges and future directions. By bridging the AI and satellite networks, this paper provides a research roadmap for the implementation of space-native AI technologies.

candidates.title: Prism : Efficient Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning for On-Device LLMs
candidates.abstract: On-device fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming increasingly important for personalized AI assistants and adaptive agents. However, standard backpropagation imposes substantial training-state memory overheads that often exceed the stringent resource budgets of mobile platforms. To address this, Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization leverages forward-only probing instead of backpropagation, drastically reducing memory footprints and offering a compelling alternative for on-device adaptation. Nonetheless, scaling ZO fine-tuning to billion-scale trainable parameter spaces remains challenging, as the cost of recovering reliable update directions scales poorly with dimensionality under mobile constraints. In this paper, we present Prism, a mobile-native infrastructure for practical billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning. Prism re-architects the ZO loop around a scalable probing substrate, bringing both per-step training latency and memory overhead closer to the inference footprint. We implement Prism end to end on commodity smartphones and evaluate it across diverse tasks and multiple model scales. Prism achieves accuracy comparable to that of state-of-the-art ZO fine-tuning baselines while reducing per-step latency by 53.4%-76.3% and peak memory by 10.6%-13.8% relative to the best baseline in each setting. These results demonstrate the practical feasibility of billion-scale on-device ZO fine-tuning for LLMs under real mobile constraints. We will release our code to support future research.

candidates.title: MarkovSim: an LLM Agent Harness with Bounded Context for Long-Horizon Computational Simulation
candidates.abstract: Recent studies have applied large language model (LLM) agent systems to computational simulation workflows. Such workflows are long-horizon, so the information generated can exceed what an LLM can reason over at once, its context window. Context management is therefore essential, yet existing systems have either neglected it or treated it as a supporting mechanism rather than a subject of study. This paper presents MarkovSim, an LLM agent harness for long-horizon computational simulation, whose core is a context management scheme built into the workflow. The workflow record is written to a memory system with a predefined schema, and at workflow-defined boundaries, namely the state transitions of a finite-state machine a compact representation of the solution progress is constructed from it as the agent's context. Instantiated on finite element analysis and evaluated on six benchmark problems, MarkovSim passed 16 of 18 runs and corrected its own faults in both the solver operations and the model physics. The engineer was consulted only where engineering judgement was needed. The context remained bounded throughout every run, regardless of its length.

candidates.title: ExoMem: OS-Governed Memory for Local Large-LLM Inference on Mobile Edge Devices
candidates.abstract: High-quality large language model inference is increasingly used on mobile edge, from satellites to smart homes, where limited connectivity or privacy requirements motivate local model inference. In many such settings, token generation is inherently compute-limited and added latency may be acceptable, but output quality, memory feasibility and crash-free execution are essential. However, on today's mobile edge with unified-memory architectures, running a large model near the device limit can trigger non-deterministic out-of-memory failures. This is because deep learning frameworks retain freed buffers inside caching pools, thus continuing to occupy shared DRAM, which the OS cannot reclaim. During inference, fragmentation and conservative reuse can produce growing memory usage, eventually exceeding the memory availability. In this paper, we present ExoMem, an OS-governed middleware that restores OS authority over physical pages without sacrificing framework compatibility. ExoMem keeps model topology and operators in the framework, while anchoring weights in OS-managed mappings, and introduces a dormant state, whose virtual addresses remain stable for correctness but whose physical pages are immediately reclaimable when needed, leveraging standard OS page caching as an implicit multi-tier hierarchy. Implemented as a plug-and-play extension, ExoMem enables stable local inference for substantially larger LLMs on mobile edge, including 72B-class models on 64GB NVIDIA Jetson devices, while preserving headroom for concurrent workloads.

candidates.title: Did the Model Use That? Counterfactual Training Boosts Self-Attribution in Language Models
candidates.abstract: A fundamental challenge for explainable and accountable language models is revealing how external information influences their answers. This paper examines whether models are self-attributive: that is, whether they indicate when -- and only when -- their responses to questions are influenced by information provided alongside the question. Furthermore, we explore how self-attribution can be improved through counterfactual training, which explicitly teaches models to distinguish between answers that do and do not depend on supplied information. We found that most of the eleven frontier models rarely attribute influential information in their answers, and the rest attribute non-influential information. Training acknowledgment into reasoning does not fix this: the acknowledgment does not reach the final answer. We introduce CREDIT, which directly supervises final-answer self-attribution with counterfactual labels, without the need for human annotation. CREDIT substantially improves attribution in four open models, including two distilled reasoning models, and outperforms reasoning-level fine-tuning and prompting baselines. Among answers that agree with a user's suggestion, CREDIT distinguishes those changed by the suggestion from those the model would have given anyway. Gains transfer partly to unseen information types and prompts containing sources that support conflicting answers.

candidates.title: From Human Intent to In-Orbit Action: A Self-Learning Large Language Model Agent for 6G Satellite Networks
candidates.abstract: Autonomous control of sixth-generation (6G) low Earth orbit satellite networks is hindered by the gap between high-level human intent and low-level control logic: translating a request such as "uninterrupted Arctic video" into a valid reinforcement learning reward still takes days of manual trial and error, and existing large language model translators cannot learn from the failures of the policies they generate. This article presents ALMOND (Agentic Large-Model-Orchestrated autonomous Network Design), a cognitive framework that closes this intent-to-action loop under on-orbit compute constraints. The contribution in artificial intelligence is a bidirectional semantic engine that translates natural-language demands into multi-objective reward functions and, conversely, mines implicit operational constraints from failed reinforcement-learning trajectories through counterfactually validated forensics, together with a large language model-guided graph neuroevolution that seeds and critiques policy architectures. The contribution in engineering is a ground-centric, compute-frugal architecture for autonomous 6G non-terrestrial network operation, in which satellites execute only distilled policies below 50,000 parameters with sub-15 ms inference and no on-board large language model. On a 350-satellite digital twin driven by real ephemeris data, ALMOND raises polar handover success from 55% to over 95%, converges about three times faster than baseline reinforcement learning, and reduces reward engineering from 48 hours to 4.5 hours, demonstrating a practical path toward trustworthy in-orbit autonomy.

candidates.title: Auditable Evaluation of Open-Weight Large Language Model Agents for Blockchain Anti-Money Laundering Investigation
candidates.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents equipped with graph tools can compile structured dossiers for blockchain anti-money laundering (AML) compliance, yet evaluation remains hindered by unverifiable prose, confounded self-repair ablations, and static benchmarks. We present amlagent, an auditable neuro-symbolic testbed in which open-weight agents emit typed, identifier-citing forensic claims checked by a deterministic two-stage verifier enforcing session-provenance grounding before ledger-constraint validation. Across 1,757 trajectory-shared paired investigations on Elliptic++, Elliptic2 (including an untouched holdout), and a laundering-obfuscation suite with out-of-distribution peel ratios and cryptographic identifier hashing, we benchmark quantized 7B, 9B, and 80B open-weight models on 16-gigabyte (GB) and 80/96-GB accelerators against breadth-first search, random forests, two-hop neighbor-aggregation baselines, and validation-selected classical hybrids. Validation-selected classical baselines--including Elliptic2 breadth-first search--remain faster and more accurate for scalar suspect ranking and recall across all benchmarks, and agent re-ranking on feature-rich Elliptic++ degrades calibrated tabular scoring (average precision 0.574 versus 0.653). Conversely, provenance-gated agents compile auditable multi-predicate dossiers, outperform standalone tabular scorers on coarse-feature subgraphs, raise unbudgeted obfuscation precision via selective citation (though budget-matched flow truncation retains higher precision), and benefit markedly from tool-surface curation, where disabling an uncalibrated scorer lifts 9B Elliptic2 average precision from 0.112 to 0.341. Decomposing pre-gate failures into tool-skipping omissions and factual contradictions shows that two-stage gating is precision-neutral on well-grounded runs while lifting dense Elliptic2 80B precision by 71%-73% across development and holdout cohorts at bounded recall cost.

candidates.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Health Professions Education: A Scoping Review
candidates.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds the output of large language models in retrieved, verifiable external sources and is increasingly proposed as a way to reduce hallucination in AI tools used for learning. Existing reviews of RAG in healthcare have focused mainly on clinical use cases, and it remains unclear how RAG has been applied and evaluated for educational purposes across the health professions, and to what extent dental education is represented. This scoping review will map the extent, range, and nature of the evidence on RAG-based systems used for the education of health professions students. It follows the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and will be reported according to PRISMA-ScR. Registration timing: this protocol is registered after the literature search (10 September–20 October 2026) and deduplication but before any title/abstract screening, full-text assessment, or data charting.

candidates.title: Large Language Models: A Plain-Language Overview for Engineers
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on huge text collections to generate text by predicting what comes next. Engineers using ChatGPT and other generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools need a clear picture of what training changes and prompts add. The article starts with the Transformer, which connects words in context, and pre-training, where models learn to predict text. It then explains how fine-tuning adapts models to requests, with reinforcement learning from human feedback using human answer rankings. Next, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) supplies documents, while chain-of-thought prompting encourages intermediate steps and agents use tools. FlashAttention lowers training and running costs by reducing data movement during attention; quantized low-rank adaptation (QLoRA) saves fine-tuning memory. Readers get a life cycle figure and tables comparing methods and their limits. A short checklist for judging LLM evaluation claims flags test material in training (data contamination) and model-based grading (LLM-as-a-judge). It also covers very long inputs (long context) and hallucination, meaning false or unsupported claims. Check factual accuracy separately from whether an answer sounds helpful.

candidates.title: Agented AI for Intelligent Workflow Automation: An Agent Framework Powered By Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Enterprise workflow automation has progressed from rigid, rule-based Robotic Process Automation (RPA) toward cognitive systems capable of perception, reasoning, and autonomous action. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, single-model deployments remain limited in multi-step planning, long-horizon memory, tool orchestration, and verifiable decision-making, which are essential for real-world enterprise workflows. This paper introduces AIWA-Agent, an Intelligent Multi-Agent Workflow Automation Framework that integrates a Planning Agent, a Reasoning Agent, a Memory Agent, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) module, a Tool-Calling Agent, an Execution Agent, and a Validation Agent under a Human-in-the-Loop and Explainable AI (XAI) supervision layer. Unlike prior single-agent LLM assistants and loosely coupled multi-agent toolkits, AIWA-Agent formalizes agent interaction through seven governing mathematical constructs Workflow Automation Efficiency , Agent Collaboration Score , Task Completion Accuracy, Workflow Latency , Resource Utilization , LLM Confidence Score , and Agent Decision Score enabling quantitative, explainable orchestration rather than ad hoc prompt chaining. We formalize the framework's architecture, mathematical model, and methodology, and evaluate it through a structured experimental protocol comparing AIWA-Agent against Catgut (single-agent), Autopsy, Crewel, Lang Graph, and Autopen baselines using illustrative, internally consistent performance data across accuracy, latency, collaboration, and resource metrics, together with descriptive statistics, correlation, regression, ANOVA, and reliability analysis. Results indicate that the proposed coordination and validation layers yield measurable gains in workflow efficiency and task success while preserving interpretability. The findings offer a reproducible blueprint for enterprises pursuing agented automation with governance and explain ability by design.

candidates.title: Task Success Is Not Enough: Side-effect-Aware Evaluation of Tool-Using Language Model Agents
candidates.abstract: Tool-using language model agents are usually evaluated by whether they finish the user's task. That metric misses a common failure: an agent can complete the requested work while also taking an unauthorized side-effecting action, such as writing to the wrong object, expanding the scope of the request, or contacting an unintended recipient. We call this failure mode collateral damage (CD). We introduce SABench (Side-effect-Aware Benchmark), a benchmark of 201 email, calendar, and ticket tasks. Each task crosses one of four state structures (independent, dependent, externally reachable, cross-tool) with one of four trap families (ambiguity, mis-targeting, cascade harm, overreach), and each task has a deterministic trace-based oracle for both goal satisfaction and authorization compliance. Across 2,211 model-task pairs from 11 frontier LLMs spanning major commercial and open model families, 15.2% of all runs incur CD, with risk concentrated in ambiguity tasks (38.8% violation rate) while non-ambiguous traps average 8.4% CD. Among goal-satisfied runs, 12.8% still produce unauthorized writes. Cross-tool and dependent states have about twice the CD rate of independent states. CD rates vary by 4.7x across models at comparable goal rates, which suggests that task success alone is a poor proxy for safe tool use. The SABench task corpus is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Phaedrus/sabench; the traces, oracle, code, and analysis pipeline are released at https://github.com/hjj194/sabench-artifact.

candidates.title: From Presence Labels to Bounding Boxes: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Scale Surgical Instrument Localization?
candidates.abstract: Spatial localization of surgical instruments through bounding-box annotations is a foundational component of surgical scene understanding, supporting detection, tracking, interaction analysis, and grounded vision-language applications. Yet existing annotations often cover selected frames, video subsets, or dataset variants rather than complete procedures. Manual extension is time-consuming and expert-dependent. Additionally, weakly supervised and detector-based pseudo-labels require task-specific training and may be imprecise. In this study, we design a scalable MLLM-based annotation framework that converts surgical frames and existing instrument-presence labels into accurate bounding boxes, and systematically analyze its reliability, cost, and design sensitivity. We instantiate the framework using six MLLMs and a multi-call configuration on laparoscopic cholecystectomy in Cholec80. Using a carefully designed stratification scheme, two annotators independently label 1,000 frames, and an expert surgeon reviews one annotation set to establish the reference. Results show that instrument-set F1 ranges from 88.2 to 92.7,whereas mIoU ranges from 0.180 to 0.735, showing that comparable recognition can conceal large localization differences. A structured multi-stage annotation pipeline achieves 0.784 mIoU, compared with 0.735 for the best single-call baseline and 0.814 human-human agreement. Using the best accuracy pipeline, we create and publicly release SurgBox, a spatial extension of Cholec80 comprising 285,977 bounding boxes across all 184,498 annotated frames from the 80 videos. The annotations and human references are made available on GitHub

candidates.title: Evaluation of Demirjian-based dental age estimation: a comparison of multimodal large language models with specialist dentists
candidates.abstract: Aims: This study evaluated the performance of three multimodal large language models (LLMs) ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude in Demirjian-based dental age (DA) estimation from panoramic radiographs compared with specialist dentists. Methods: This retrospective cross-sectional study included 135 panoramic radiographs of children aged 6–13 years. Two specialist dentists confirmed inter-examiner reliability (ICC=0.90) on a pilot subset; the pediatric dentist then assessed all radiographs using the Demirjian method. The radiographs were analyzed once per model using standardized prompts in ChatGPT-5.5 Instant, Gemini 3.5 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6; thus, the reported metrics reflect single-session model performance. Demirjian stages were converted into gender-specific maturity scores and DAs. Performance was assessed using bias, mean absolute error (MAE), and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Statistical analyses included paired-samples t-tests, Wilcoxon, Friedman, Mann–Whitney U, and independent-samples t-tests (p0.05). Conclusion: ChatGPT yielded the lowest MAE relative to CA; Gemini showed the highest specialist agreement, which should not be equated with accuracy. Current multimodal LLMs remain insufficiently accurate and consistent to replace specialist dentists and should be considered adjunctive decision-support tools.
candidates.venue: Journal of Medicine and Palliative Care

candidates.title: Decision-Native Recommendation with Large Language Models
candidates.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) bring world knowledge to user preference modeling in sequential recommendation, but generation-based recommenders express next-item predictions indirectly as text. Generated outputs may fail to identify a unique candidate item, depend on candidate presentation order in the prompt, and lack explicit confidence in the recommendation. Recent studies explore Jev, a model for fast option selection with explicit confidence. Inspired by Jev, we introduce decision-native recommendation, a new paradigm that jointly models item choice and recommendation confidence using LLM representations. It requires valid candidate selection, consistency under candidate reordering, and confidence that reflects recommendation accuracy. We propose Direct Item Choice Estimation (DICE), which learns a personalized next-item distribution over supplied candidates from user interaction history and recommends the highest-scoring item with calibrated confidence. Tree-structured attention shares history computation across isolated candidate branches for order-consistent candidate scoring in a single forward pass. On three recommendation datasets, DICE achieves higher top-one accuracy than all evaluated baselines. Separate evaluations show unchanged item choices under tested candidate reorderings and end-to-end speedups of up to approximately $6\times$ over the evaluated generation-based methods. candidates.title: Rethinking Retrieval in the Long-Context Era: Training-Free Semantic Trees for Adaptive Context Construction
candidates.abstract: Long-context language models can increasingly process entire documents, making full-context prompting a practical alternative to passage retrieval. However, greater capacity determines how much information a model can receive, but not which information best supports a query. This distinction motivates rethinking retrieval: when the full document already fits, can selecting and organizing its evidence improve answering? The challenge is to retain supporting facts and relations while keeping the context focused on the question. To reconcile these goals, we introduce \ours, a training-free framework that uses semantic abstraction to guide selection while retaining original text for answering. \ours constructs a reusable semantic hierarchy from the full document in a single generation, linking node descriptions to source spans. Given a query, structural--semantic scoring and fine-grained lexical attribution nominate shared source nodes; their union with ancestor context preserves structural relations and complete local text. Across four frontier answer models, \ours improves average QA-F1 by 1.72 points over full-context prompting on three LongBench tasks, surpassing the evaluated baselines on the four-model average while reducing answer-context length by 58.55\%. Our code is available at the $\href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/treefuse-ECFE}{repository}$.

candidates.title: Distributed LLM Inference via Communication-Efficient Speculative Decoding
candidates.abstract: Distributed speculative decoding has emerged as a promising approach for device--server collaborative large language model (LLM) inference, but its decoding speedup is often limited by the vocabulary-scale communication overhead. In existing distributed speculative decoding methods, exact rejection sampling requires transmitting full token distributions over the LLM vocabulary between the device and the server, which becomes costly in bandwidth-constrained environments. To address this issue, we propose DISCO, a communication-efficient framework for distributed speculative decoding, that eliminates vocabulary-scale distribution transfer while preserving the exact target distribution. DISCO achieves this by introducing a server-side replica of the draft small language model (SLM), which enables the server to locally obtain the draft-side distribution required for rejection sampling. As a result, DISCO exchanges only drafted token indices and scalar probability values between the device and the server. Experimental results on multiple datasets show that DISCO consistently achieves higher decoding speedup than existing distributed speculative decoding methods, particularly under stringent bandwidth constraints.
